title: Overcrowding concerns arise at Baltimore ICE facility - WBAL-TV
description:
BALTIMORE — Concerns are growing about overcrowding issues at Baltimore's immigration facility as the U.S. Supreme Court allows third-country deportations to resume.
Baltimore ICE facility faces overcrowding allegations despite judge's order Separately, Baltimore's immigration detention facility faces allegations of overcrowding and poor conditions.
U.S. District Judge Julie Rubin has cited Baltimore's ICE facility for failing to comply with her March ruling addressing overcrowding and health concerns.
A WBAL-TV 11 News Investigates review of ICE data collected after the order revealed that the Baltimore facility was overcrowded 60% of the time.
Also in March, Maryland's attorney general filed a federal lawsuit in an effort to obtain records detailing conditions at Baltimore's ICE facility.
text:
BALTIMORE —

Concerns are growing about overcrowding issues at Baltimore's immigration facility as the U.S. Supreme Court allows third-country deportations to resume.

A U.S. Supreme Court order issued Tuesday halts an appeals court ruling and allows the Trump administration to continue third-country deportations, a policy that allows U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to send undocumented migrants to countries to which they have no connection.

Last week, the Trump administration canceled a flight carrying 70 people to three different countries after a federal court ruled migrants should have the opportunity to contest such deportations.

"People who are currently in detention, or maybe aren't even in detention right now, but have been granted withholding of removal or relief under the Convention Against Torture, they are at serious risk of being deported to a country that they have never been to," said Briana Arnold, an immigration partner attorney at Killian Law Group.

Immigration attorney raises risks

Arnold explained that migrants could face significant risks if deported.

"The two main issues are, No. 1, that these detainees are being persecuted or even tortured in these third countries. And, No. 2, a lot of them are being sent to the country that the United States granted them protection from," Arnold told WBAL-TV 11 News Investigates.

She also raised concerns about the lack of due process for migrants.

"They are at serious risk of being deported to a country that they have never been to."

"The United States is really just throwing up their hands and saying, 'Once you are there, you are their responsibility.' And, in many cases, it violates a lot of their rights," Arnold told WBAL-TV 11 News Investigates.

The Supreme Court's order allowing third-country deportations is not final, as the high court is expected to hear arguments on the policy in December to determine its legality.

Baltimore ICE facility faces overcrowding allegations despite judge's order

Separately, Baltimore's immigration detention facility faces allegations of overcrowding and poor conditions. U.S. District Judge Julie Rubin has cited Baltimore's ICE facility for failing to comply with her March ruling addressing overcrowding and health concerns.

"In these tiny cells, they'd pack up to 50 or 60 people where there was no room to even sit, much less lay down — even if people were there for several days,” said Amelia Dagen, senior attorney at the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights.

Rubin's March order required a minimum of 31 square feet of space per person, access to medication and routine medical screenings.

Dagen told WBAL-TV 11 News Investigates that the Baltimore facility was not providing access to medications, showers or toothbrushes, and that cells and bathrooms were not being cleaned.

"We're seeing very many days that were higher ... sometimes over 70 people."

"Pretty quickly after the March order, we started hearing from people who were at the Baltimore holding room that this wasn't happening," Dagen told WBAL-TV 11 News Investigates. "It was inconsistent at best."

A WBAL-TV 11 News Investigates review of ICE data collected after the order revealed that the Baltimore facility was overcrowded 60% of the time.

"The total facility population is 45 people, and, unfortunately, we're seeing very many days that were higher than that, sometimes over 70 people," Dagen told WBAL-TV 11 News Investigates.

Rubin is now requiring the Baltimore ICE field office to file a report every two weeks to ensure compliance with her March order.

Also in March, Maryland's attorney general filed a federal lawsuit in an effort to obtain records detailing conditions at Baltimore's ICE facility. In September, the government denied the allegations of overcrowding.

ICE has not responded to requests from WBAL-TV 11 News Investigates for comment.

text:
PONCE, Puerto Rico —The US Department of Homeland Security inaugurated today a new joint facility during a ribbon-cutting ceremony marking a major investment in CBP and Coast Guard operations and mission readiness in southern Puerto Rico.

The new DHS joint facility, in the Port of Ponce, will house US Coast Guard Resident Inspection Office Ponce and the U.S. Customs and Border Protection Air and Marine Operations Ponce Marine Unit.

These units support CBP and Coast Guard personnel responsible for maritime safety and prevention, border security, inspections and law enforcement operations in the region.

“The Ponce Marine Unit plays a critical role in detecting, interdicting and responding to maritime threats across Puerto Rico’s southern approaches,” said Christopher Hunter, Director of the Caribbean Air and Marine Branch. “This new facility gives our agents the modern operational, maintenance and coordination space they need to work seamlessly with Coast Guard and local partners, strengthen border security, and protect the people and commerce that depend on a secure Caribbean maritime domain.”

The nearly $22 million project included demolition of the former facility, construction of a new two-story, 9,650-square-foot complex with dedicated office, training, operational, security and maintenance spaces. Additionally, the site features a 1,880-square-foot boat maintenance bay, improved pier and boat ramp infrastructure, upgraded utilities, parking, and emergency backup power.

The award, design and construction of this turn-key project was accomplished in partnership with CBP, AMO, USCG, the Coast Guard’s Facilities Design and Construction Center, the CBP Office of Facilities and Asset Management.

"This project is a tangible, long-term investment that reinforces Department of Homeland Security operational readiness and critical infrastructure protection across the Caribbean,” said Capt. Luis J. Rodriguez, Commander of U.S. Coast Guard Sector San Juan. “Our Coast Guard and CBP teams in this new facility can operate, communicate and coordinate faster and more effectively with local law enforcement and port partners strengthening our collective capability to secure waterways, support vital commerce, and safeguard the Caribbean maritime domain."

The DHS joint facility is immediately next to the United States Custom House in Ponce, the oldest existing customhouse in Puerto Rico. Built in 1841, this adobe building of the Spanish era is historically and architecturally significant and is listed on the U.S. National Register of Historic Places.

Expanding this regional maritime footprint, the U.S. Coast Guard assumed control of historic regional lighthouses near Ponce in 1933, including the Cardona Island and Caja de Muertos Lights while the Port of Ponce itself served as a vital logistics hub during World War II.

Today, DHS, CBP, and the Coast Guard work together to secure the nation’s borders, safeguard maritime commerce, and support public safety throughout Puerto Rico and the surrounding region.

text:
Management & Training Corporation, a Utah-based private prison firm, has signed a contract with Immigration and Customs Enforcement to operate a detention facility in Marana, according to a statement from the company on Wednesday afternoon.

The contract was signed on Sept. 29, 2026. MTC said it anticipates the facility will begin operating within two months. The statement described a facility with a 775-bed capacity and a staff of about 338 full-time employees.

In July 2025, MTC purchased the land parcel — a shuttered prison once operated by the same firm — from the Arizona Department of Administration. The purchase, along with murmurs of an imminent detention center, has drawn scrutiny and ire among residents and immigrant rights advocates, who have pointed to concerns over human rights and rising death rates in ICE detention facilities.

In February 2026, the Department of Homeland Security published a performance work statement on a federal database, outlining a potential agreement between ICE and MTC.

But for months, a contract was not signed. As recently as mid-September, AZPM inquired about the contract’s status.

“We don’t have any updates to provide at this time,” a company spokesperson said in a Sept. 17 email.

As the contract appeared dormant in the public eye, members of Pima Resist ICE (PRICE) said they observed regular activity at the site, such as “trucks that work for plumbing companies and just general contractors,” PRICE member Bennett Burke told AZPM.

“We don't have any official notice of anything, but the work is happening,” Burke said earlier this month. “So we know that they're proceeding with getting the facility ready.”

For months, PRICE has pushed back against the planned detention center, often urging the Marana Town Council to take the same stance. The council has repeatedly declined to pass a resolution opposing the facility.

“We aren’t done fighting this thing. Not by a long shot,” said Kristin Downing, another member of PRICE, in a statement Wednesday. “We have been talking with legal experts, doing research, building alliances, and exploring creative ways to make sure this camp never opens. We care too much about our community to just give up.”

The details of the contract remain unclear. The document did not appear in a public database of federal contracts during several searches Wednesday afternoon.

A years-long history in Arizona

Management & Training Corporation, or MTC, has a years-long history in Arizona.

The site of the detention center — an expanse of land near the Marana Regional Airport — was once a private prison operated by MTC through a contract with Arizona’s Department of Corrections.

The minimum security prison held approximately 500 male inmates. At the end of 2023, Gov. Katie Hobbs ended the state’s contract with MTC, citing financial reasons. That decision shuttered the facility.

In its statement announcing the new contract Wednesday, MTC cited its nearly 30-year history in Marana, adding that the company would focus on “operating the facility safely and professionally, meeting and exceeding ICE’s National Detention Standards (NDS), and providing compassionate care to the people entrusted to us.”

The firm, however, has received criticism in past years — including a state-led review under Republican leadership.

In 2015, Republican Gov. Doug Ducey terminated a separate agreement with MTC after riots broke out in a Kingman prison operated by the firm. A state review reported that the prison was understaffed, that inmates held hunger strikes and that employees were “poorly paid,” NPR and KJZZ reported at the time.

A recent investigation from The Intercept and LOOKOUT News reported that when MTC operated the Marana prison in 2022, the company failed to report sexual assault allegations.

Note: This story has been updated to include comments from PRICE. This is a developing story and will be updated as new information becomes available.

text:
President Donald Trump hosted hundreds at the White House on Wednesday for a Hispanic Heritage Month celebration, where he bragged about his record support from Latino voters in the 2024 election and argued that his economic policies are bringing them prosperity and that his immigration policies are protecting their communities.

“Two years ago, we won more votes from the Hispanic Americans than any Republican president in history, and we won more than almost anybody that’s ever run for office,” Trump told the room of Latino supporters inside the East Room.

The president also framed his administration’s economic agenda as restoring opportunity for Hispanic families, saying, “Under the Trump administration, that American dream is back, and it’s bigger and better than ever before.”

But U.S. Rep. Analilia Mejia, the first Afro-Latino to serve in the United States Congress, told theGrio that Trump’s support among Latino voters has waned and that his policies are bringing anything but good to their communities. The freshman congresswoman called the president’s actions “destructive” and slammed his attempts to pit Latino and Black communities against each another.

“It’s interesting to watch him try to pander to a group, but his actions, as always, speak louder than his words,” said Mejia, who has represented New Jersey’s 11th Congressional District since April, filling the vacant seat previously held by now-Governor Mikie Sherrill.

Congresswoman Mejia said Latino communities are “living in fear” amid the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement, which has included mass detentions and deportations—some of which have resulted in deaths and have been found to be unconstitutional by federal courts. Mejia said that fear has been “irrespective of their immigration status.”

Despite the president’s claims during the 2024 campaign that his administration would only target violent criminals, data shows that a majority of those detained by ICE are non-criminals.

“I see it every time I visit Delaney Hall, meeting people who were either following the law, had court dates, have work permits, were captured at work sites or at schools or even hospitals, and what it is creating is a sense of fear within the Latino community and in the broader community,” said Mejia.

During his Hispanic Heritage Month remarks, President Trump often veered away from discussing Hispanic heritage and the contributions of Latinos to American culture, instead highlighting the construction of his $600 million ballroom and other White House renovations. The president told the group of Latinos that they would be “the first people of consequence to ever step on the new ballroom floor.”

Rep. Mejia scoffed at the president’s fixation with construction as millions of Latino communities struggle to afford the country’s rising cost of living and are losing jobs.

“I’m not surprised that he would take the limited opportunities that he grants himself to engage with my community in an authentic way, and instead pivot to his own narcissistic greatest hits,” she told theGrio. “This president has, by throwing these tariffs like they’re Mardi Gras beads, looking for loopholes, despite what our Supreme Court has stated, is driving up the cost of construction, new home construction, and homes overall, impacting a very large Latino workforce.”

Congresswoman Mejia also called out Trump’s efforts to drive a wedge between Latino and Black communities, in which he has repeatedly claimed immigrants were stealing jobs from Black workers.

“We know that the othering, the ostracizing of immigrant communities, and pitting one immigrant community against another [community] is a tactic often utilized to weaken the majority of people who disagree with you,” said Mejia. “So, of course, Donald Trump…hopes that we will fight each other instead of focusing our energies on addressing the fact that he’s creating a healthcare crisis in this country by not only allowing the ACA tax credits to expire but by gutting Medicaid and Medicare.”

The New Jersey lawmaker added, “He’s lowering people’s quality of life and, frankly, life expectancy. It has a disproportionate impact on both Black and Brown communities, and he’d much rather tell us that it’s each other’s fault instead of admitting that it’s his regressive and destructive policies that are causing the most harm.”

text:
Press Releases

Attorney General Tong Opposes Unlawful DHS Rule Fast-Tracking Asylum Seekers into Removal Proceedings Without an Interview

(Hartford, CT) -- Attorney General William Tong, as part of a coalition of 21 attorneys general, submitted a comment letter opposing the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) new rule limiting affirmative asylum applicants’ opportunity to participate in an asylum officer interview and explain why they cannot safely return home. The interim final rule (IFR) permits U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to refer these asylum applications directly to the Executive Office for Immigration Review’s (EOIR), placing applicants in adversarial removal proceedings in immigration court. DHS estimates the rule could result in roughly 130,000 future affirmative asylum applicants being referred without an interview each year and could affect up to 444,000 cases already pending in EOIR’s asylum backlog. The IFR could further strain an already lengthy process for asylum claims, potentially leading to significant delays or case dismissals that would take an additional financial and mental toll on individuals and families navigating the asylum system.

“Willful ignorance is the proposed immigration policy of the federal government. Trump wants to refuse asylum applicants the basic opportunity to tell their story before funneling them into removal proceedings with life and death implications. This is a cruel betrayal of everything this country has stood for since our founding, and I stand with attorneys general across the country in opposition,” said Attorney General Tong.

The IFR pushes asylum applicants directly into an adversarial court proceeding, where an Immigration and Customs Enforcement prosecutor argues against their claim, with the denial rate reaching 94% in June 2026. Further, because immigration judges now frequently deny asylum claims without giving the individual a full merits hearing, many may not even receive a day in court at all. According to the Center for Victims of Torture, 44% of asylum seekers, asylees, and refugees in the U.S. are torture survivors, and the interview portion of the immigration process provides crucial time to explain why an applicant is seeking asylum, particularly for unaccompanied minors and applicants who cannot afford legal representation.

In the comment letter, Attorney General Tong and the coalition argue the IFR violates federal law and is particularly harmful for unaccompanied children, who under the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act are entitled to have their asylum claims heard through USCIS’s non-adversarial adjudicatory process, not EOIR. Attorney General Tong and the coalition further assert that the IFR:

• Ignores the evidentiary importance of a non-adversarial asylum interview and does not justify departing from decades of policy;

• Harms state residents by increasing the risk of detention and removal, disrupting employment authorization, and making legal representation even more difficult to obtain for many asylum applicants;

• Will strain state-funded legal service providers, healthcare clinics, and immigrant integration resources, as well as undermine law enforcement interests;

• Strips unaccompanied children of the non-adversarial asylum process Congress guaranteed them under federal law, forcing kids who often have no attorney to navigate an adversarial system built for adults;

• Increases the psychological distress experienced by asylum seekers and their families, compounding trauma many have already experienced fleeing persecution;

• Undermines tax revenue and business income, given immigrants’ critical role in the workforce and broader economy;

• Abandons compliance with the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) by circumventing notice and comment requirements when the Rule went immediately into effect on July 28, 2026; and

• Fails to consider reasonable alternatives, such as limiting the rule to future applicants, preserving interviews for unaccompanied children, or hiring more qualified asylum officers.

In sending this letter, Attorney General Tong joins the attorneys general of California, Colorado, Delaware, District of Columbia, Hawai‘i, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, and Washington.

text:
Joint letter led by Church World Service and Refugee Council USA warns tens of thousands of refugees are caught in a ‘deadly bureaucratic trap’

WASHINGTON, D.C.—Ahead of Thursday’s deadline for states to end Medicaid eligibility for many refugees in U.S. communities, Church World Service (CWS) and Refugee Council USA issued a joint letter signed by 58 other refugee-serving, religious, veteran, refugee-led, humanitarian and community-based organizations calling for an end to the green card processing freeze and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’ (USCIS) ‘re-vetting’ initiative that targets resettled refugees.

In July 2025, Congress passed legislation, H.R. 1, mandating that refugees and other humanitarian entrants without green cards will be cut off from Medicaid, Medicare and CHIP eligibility. Meanwhile, USCIS has continued its adjudication pause on over 100,000 refugee green card applications, leaving resettled refugees in a deadly bureaucratic trap. The two policies combined will leave many refugees without health coverage, which will have devastating consequences, particularly for those who count on Medicaid for lifesaving care. Though children and pregnant women in some states will continue to be able to access Medicaid through programs like CHIPRA 214, tens of thousands of pending green card applicants will lose their health coverage as soon as tomorrow, Oct. 1.

In tandem with frivolous ‘re-vetting’ of already arrived refugees, the administration is destabilizing decades of precedent and putting new members of our communities in harm’s way.

As the undersigned organizations stated in today’s letter:

This bureaucratic trap has ensnared refugees across the country. If left unaddressed, it is a trap that will have deadly consequences. It is also certain to exact enormous costs on state and local communities already struggling with cost shifts and broad cuts to federal support. These are conditions that must be treated, and local hospitals and health care systems – in addition to food banks, churches and congregations, and local nonprofits – will take on the burden of doing so unless the administration steps in and begins processing refugee green cards again.

The U.S. government promised resettled refugees permanent protection and the opportunity to rebuild their lives in safety. Providing basic support to these refugees in the first years after they arrive is an investment in our economic growth and security. Across administrations, data shows that when properly supported during the resettlement process, refugees and asylees bring massive fiscal benefits.

CWS Chief Strategy Officer, Erol Kekic, called for an immediate end to burdensome and superfluous directives that negatively impact refugees:

Tomorrow, refugees across the country will lose health coverage on which they depend. Many did exactly what the law requires, applying for their green cards months or even years ago. But the Trump administration has halted green card processing for most refugees, leaving them with no clear path to eligibility for life-sustaining benefits. For some, the consequences of being cut off from Medicaid could be deadly.

At the same time, the administration continues to target refugees with an unjust “re-vetting” initiative, subjecting individuals who have already cleared the most rigorous screening in the U.S. immigration system to unnecessary scrutiny and re-traumatization. Church World Service calls on the Trump administration to immediately and fully resume the processing of refugee green card applications and end the re-vetting of refugees.

Executive Director of Refugee Council USA (RCUSA), John Slocum, said:

Stripping refugee arrivals of their eligibility for health care and food assistance was already devastating to vulnerable populations who fled violence and persecution. To compound that harm by pausing or in any way delaying refugees’ green card application processing and adjudications is beyond cruel. At every turn, the Trump administration has destabilized and disrupted the diverse social fabric of our communities. Coupled with the “re-vetting” of resettled refugees—as a pretext to wrongfully attack their refugee status—these policies have real-world, deadly consequences, and our communities both bear witness and the cost.

More than 45 years ago, Congress decided that refugees who qualify shall receive lawful permanent residence. We therefore urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and USCIS to:

Resume full adjudication of refugee I-485 applications immediately and commit publicly to clearing the backlog.

Immediately establish, a dedicated channel through which members of Congress and legal representatives can request expedited adjudication for applicants facing termination of medical coverage.

End the unnecessary re-vetting of refugees who have already cleared the most rigorous screening in the U.S. immigration system.

For more information on the rights of refugees, eligibility for necessary medical care, or to speak with one of our experts, contact media@cwsglobal.org. Visit CWSglobal.org to learn more about the current State of Play,

text:
BUFFALO, N.Y. — The Trump administration is moving to cancel $810 million in federal funding already approved by Congress, setting up a new fight over presidential spending authority and raising questions about the impact on refugee services in New York.

More than $567 million of the proposed cuts are tied to refugee and entrant assistance programs.

The administration sent Congress the rescission request Friday, targeting funding across 11 federal accounts. The White House says its immigration and refugee policies have dramatically reduced the number of people entering the United States and argues the remaining money is excess funding that is no longer needed.

The administration is attempting to cancel the funding through what is known as a “pocket rescission,” in which a president submits a rescission request close enough to the end of the fiscal year that the money could expire before Congress completes its review.

But the Government Accountability Office, Congress’s nonpartisan watchdog, says the administration cannot use the process to force congressionally approved funding to expire.

In a five-page letter sent to congressional leaders, GAO pointed to the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, which governs how a president can seek to withhold or cancel money appropriated by Congress.

GAO said the president may ask Congress to rescind funding but cannot withhold the money through its expiration if Congress has not approved the request.

The White House disputes that interpretation.

Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought criticized GAO’s finding in a post on X, accusing the agency of being partisan. The administration has argued that the Impoundment Control Act does not expressly prohibit pocket rescissions.

The dispute comes as the federal fiscal year ends Tuesday.

Potential impact in New York

New York state data shows 10,654 refugees received services in the state during federal fiscal year 2024. About 97% were served in upstate New York, with Erie County among the five counties serving the largest number of refugees.

Assemblymember Jon Rivera, a Buffalo Democrat, said refugee resettlement has played a role in filling workforce gaps and revitalizing neighborhoods in Western New York.

“A hit to this would kind of devastate certain sectors of the economy,” Rivera said.

Rivera said New York continued supporting refugee resettlement agencies during President Donald Trump’s first term, even as some agencies elsewhere closed amid declines in refugee admissions.

“Places like Buffalo, because New York state had continued to fund their refugee resettlement agencies, they were able to receive more people,” Rivera said.

U.S. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand also criticized the latest rescission request.

“The Trump administration rescinding this congressionally approved funding is completely illegal and wrong,” Gillibrand said in a statement to Spectrum News 1.

Gillibrand said repeated attempts to cancel federal funding are creating uncertainty for service providers in New York.

What happens next

The dispute is part of a larger disagreement between the Trump administration and Congress over presidential authority to withhold money lawmakers have already appropriated.

The administration used a similar maneuver involving billions of dollars in foreign aid last year. That dispute reached the U.S. Supreme Court, which allowed the funding to remain withheld in an emergency order but did not make a final determination on the broader legality of pocket rescissions.

GAO is not a court, meaning its latest finding does not by itself compel the administration to release the funding.

With the fiscal year ending, the immediate question is whether the administration makes the money available, allows it to expire or faces another legal challenge over its attempt to cancel the funds.

title: Washington Employers Must Notify Workers About Federal Immigration Inspections Starting ...
description:
Starting October 1, Washington employers must notify their workers when a federal agency announces plans to inspect employment eligibility paperwork.
It applies to any business that employs one or more workers in Washington, including the state, state agencies, and local governments.
That notice gives the employer three business days to produce its I-9 forms and related records.
It also has space for you to fill in where you will post inspection notices and how you will otherwise communicate them.
Workers, former workers, anyone injured by a violation, and organizations whose members include such people, including unions and advocacy groups, can sue in court.
text:
Starting October 1, Washington employers must notify their workers when a federal agency announces plans to inspect employment eligibility paperwork. They must also follow up with individual notices once the government reports what it has found. The Immigrant Worker Protection Act (IWPA), which was signed by Governor Bob Ferguson earlier this year, gives employers just five business days to act, and also requires every employer to hang a new workplace poster whether or not an inspection ever happens. The Attorney General’s Office just released the poster, model notices, and employer guidance, so the time to act is now. Here’s what the law requires and eight steps to take with October 1 upon us.

Who’s Covered?

The law reaches just about every employer in the state. It applies to any business that employs one or more workers in Washington, including the state, state agencies, and local governments. There is no small-business exemption.

What Triggers the Notice Obligations?

The law focuses on Form I-9 inspections, often called I-9 audits, which usually start when Homeland Security Investigations delivers a Notice of Inspection. That notice gives the employer three business days to produce its I-9 forms and related records.

The Washington law defines “federal agency” broadly, though. It covers any agency that enforces or helps enforce federal civil immigration law or employment eligibility inspections. It expressly includes on-duty officials from the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of Labor, and the Justice Department’s Immigrant and Employee Rights Section.

Obligation 1: Post the New Poster (Starting October 1)

Every employer must display the AG’s poster where workplace notices are customarily posted. The poster explains the law’s notice rights to workers. It also has space for you to fill in where you will post inspection notices and how you will otherwise communicate them. It’s available in English, Spanish, Russian, Vietnamese, Ukrainian, and Chinese (Mandarin) on the AG’s IWPA page.

Obligation 2: Notify Workers Within 5 Business Days of an Inspection Notice

Within five business days of receiving notice of an inspection of I-9 forms and related worker records, you must give written notice to each worker and to the worker’s union, if any. The notice must include:

A copy of the agency’s Notice of Inspection; and

The following information, in English and the state’s five most common non-English languages:

The name of the agency conducting the inspection

The date you received the notice

The types of records sought and any other identified purposes, to the extent you know them

Contact information for an AG-approved statewide immigrant and refugee rights organization

You must deliver this notice in two ways:

Post it where workplace notices are customarily posted, and keep it posted until the inspection is complete; and

Send it directly to workers through your usual method of communication, using at least one of the following: hand delivery, mail with proof of delivery, email with proof of transmission, or text message with proof of transmission. A text can link to a copy of the notice on a web page.

The law lists acceptable forms of proof, including dated electronic transmissions and time-stamped photos of postings, plus other records kept in the ordinary course of business. Proof is rebuttable, so keep good records.

Obligation 3: Notify “Affected workers” Within 5 Business Days of the Results

Within five business days of receiving the results, you must give each “affected worker,” meaning anyone the results identify as possibly lacking work authorization or as having deficient I-9 forms or work authorization documents, and their union:

A copy of the agency’s written results notice

A written explanation of the obligations the results create for you and the worker

A description of the deficiencies that relate to that worker

The deadline for correcting any deficiencies

A mutually agreed date and time for a meeting to correct the deficiencies, or options for dates and times, within the correction period

Notice that the worker has the right to representation at that meeting

The AG also publishes a model “Notice to Affected Employees” in all six languages.

2 Possible Paths for Enforcement

The law provides two possible paths for enforcement:

The Attorney General can investigate on its own or in response to complaints, issue civil investigative demands, and sue. For notice violations, courts must award $500 for each instance in which an employer failed to provide a required notice to a worker. That amount doubles for willful violations. A court may waive or reduce the amount if the violation was inadvertent, caused no actual harm, and was promptly corrected in good faith.

Private lawsuits are also available. Workers, former workers, anyone injured by a violation, and organizations whose members include such people, including unions and advocacy groups, can sue in court. If the court finds a violation, it awards the greater of actual damages or statutory damages of 40 times the state’s hourly minimum wage per plaintiff, per violation. At the 2026 minimum wage of $17.13, that’s $685.20 per plaintiff per violation. Prevailing plaintiffs can also recover attorneys’ fees and costs. Because statutory damages are calculated per worker, a single missed notice at a large worksite can add up fast.

8 Steps to Take

Here are eight steps you should take as the new law takes effect.

1. Hang the poster by October 1. Post it at every location where workers actually report, not just headquarters. Fill in where and how you’ll communicate inspection notices.

2. Build a five-business-day playbook.Decide who receives a Notice of Inspection, who calls counsel, who completes the model notice, and who sends it.

3. Pre-stage the model notices. Download all six language versions of both AG notices so you aren’t hunting for them mid-inspection.

4. Pick your delivery method and test your proof. Confirm that you have current email addresses or mobile numbers for workers, including seasonal, remote, and field staff. Make sure your system generates dated proof of transmission.

5. Identify your union contacts. If any workers are represented, know exactly who receives notices on the union’s behalf, and check your CBAs for shorter deadlines.

6. Plan for the results phase. Know which language you use with each worker and be ready to offer meeting times within the federal correction period.

7. Review your self-audit and reverification practices. Make sure internal audits are consistent, nondiscriminatory, and no broader than federal law requires.

title: Attorney General James Sues Trump Administration to Protect Housing Counseling for New Yorkers
description:
“Housing counselors help New Yorkers buy their first homes, keep the homes they have, and stay on top of rent and other bills,” said Attorney General James.
In announcing the move, the administration attacked housing counseling grantees as “radical groups” and “far-left” organizations, faulting them for positions such as believing that housing is a human right.
In the lawsuit, Attorney General James emphasizes that Congress already rejected the administration's attempt to end this program.
The president's Fiscal Year 2026 budget proposed eliminating housing counseling funding entirely.
Attorney General James argues that HUD's actions violate the Administrative Procedure Act, the federal housing counseling statute, and federal appropriations laws.
text:
NEW YORK – New York Attorney General Letitia James today sued the Trump administration to stop it from cutting off funding that helps New Yorkers buy their first homes, stay in the homes they have, and manage their rent and finances. The lawsuit, filed on the last day of the federal fiscal year, challenges the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development's (HUD) refusal to award approximately $56.1 million that Congress set aside for housing counseling nationwide, part of the president’s so-called “pocket recissions.” That funding is set to expire at midnight tonight, and New York stands to lose more than a million dollars in support for thousands of vulnerable New Yorkers statewide.

“Housing counselors help New Yorkers buy their first homes, keep the homes they have, and stay on top of rent and other bills,” said Attorney General James. “For decades, Congress has awarded funding to support these critical efforts. Now, the Trump administration is cruelly running out the clock so these funds disappear at midnight. I am going to court tonight to make sure New York families can still get the help they need.”

“With housing costs on the rise thanks to the dangerous policies pushed by the Trump administration, canceling this funding threatens to push even more Americans to the brink,” said Governor Kathy Hochul. “Here in New York, we’re not backing down, and with the support of Attorney General James, we’re pushing back on the federal government to restore this funding and deliver for our residents.”

For nearly 60 years, HUD has funded programs that give homeowners, homebuyers, and renters the information they need to succeed in the housing market, including guidance on financial management, financial literacy, and property maintenance. Every year since 2013, the New York State Housing Finance Agency has received up to $1 million in housing counseling funds from HUD. The agency then passes the grant money on to 22 HUD-certified housing counseling organizations statewide, each of which receives between $20,000 and $100,000 per year.

In March 2026, HUD opened applications for this year's funding, set an anticipated award date of August 3, 2026, and said it expected to make about 175 awards nationwide. New York submitted its application on May 22, 2026, and HUD confirmed it was complete, but then went silent. Without explanation, New York never received any of the expected federal housing counselor funding. Some New York counseling organizations have already begun the work these funds were meant to cover.

On September 25, 2026, just five days before the funds were set to expire, President Trump announced a pocket rescission of nearly $1 billion in federal spending, including the housing counselor program. A pocket rescission is a request to Congress to cancel funding, sent so late in the fiscal year that the money lapses before Congress can act. In announcing the move, the administration attacked housing counseling grantees as “radical groups” and “far-left” organizations, faulting them for positions such as believing that housing is a human right. None of these claims have anything to do with the counseling services funded by Congress.

In the lawsuit, Attorney General James emphasizes that Congress already rejected the administration's attempt to end this program. The president's Fiscal Year 2026 budget proposed eliminating housing counseling funding entirely. Congress refused that proposal and fully funded the program in the appropriations law signed on February 3, 2026. In the same law, Congress included a measure expressly barring agencies from eliminating or reducing a program unless Congress enacts the change.

In 2024, this funding helped New York prevent more than 250 evictions and almost 300 foreclosures and helped nearly 300 first-time homebuyers close on their first home. Now, as a result of the president’s pocket rescission, over 7,000 households in New York are at risk of losing access to one-on-one counseling services, and nearly 2,800 households may lose financial assistance to improve their living conditions.

Attorney General James argues that HUD's actions violate the Administrative Procedure Act, the federal housing counseling statute, and federal appropriations laws. Federal law requires the HUD Secretary to make financial assistance available to HUD-approved housing counseling agencies and state housing finance agencies, which the administration is now refusing to do. Attorney General James also argues that HUD acted arbitrarily by basing its decision on the perceived political views of grantees, a factor Congress never authorized, and by ignoring the harm to more than 2,200 housing counseling agencies and 6,700 housing counselors nationwide who rely on this funding.

Attorney General James is asking the court to declare HUD's actions unlawful, block HUD from letting the funds lapse, and preserve the funding past today's deadline so New York can ultimately receive its award.

text:
MINNEAPOLIS (CN) — The Justice Department filed a judicial misconduct complaint Wednesday against nearly all of Minnesota’s federal judges regarding comments they made to The New York Times over the government’s handling of immigration cases.

The complaint follows a Times article published this month titled “Trump’s Minnesota Surge Threatened Democracy, Judge Warns,” which focused primarily on U.S. District Judge Patrick Schiltz’s views on Operation Metro Surge.

Six of the seven members of Minnesota’s federal bench spoke with reporters regarding the immigration crackdown, the Times says in the article.

Schiltz sat with the Times for a rare 90-minute interview, where he reportedly said the Trump administration has a “disregard for court orders” — harkening back to a brief yet heated order the George W. Bush appointee issued in February.

According to the Justice Department, Schiltz also told the Times the administration’s noncompliance clogged the court to a “near standstill” and posed a threat to the rule of law.

“If anything is a ‘grave threat to the rule of law,’ it is judges who repeatedly and brazenly exceed their authority,” the Justice Department says in the complaint.

While Schiltz attributed much of the issue to staffing shortages and “incompetence,” he reportedly warned failing to uphold the legal system risks sliding into “anarchy or… authoritarianism” — a position the Justice Department said is outrageous.

Federal officials also name U.S. District Judge John Tunheim, a Bill Clinton appointee, in the complaint over a statement he made to the Times claiming immigration agents weren’t arresting, in his view, dangerous criminals.

The Justice Department said Schiltz and Tunheim’s comments and conduct are “egregious” — claiming the two judges violated the Code of Judicial Conduct that ethically prohibits judges from making public comments on pending cases or political statements.

“Our complaint alleges that federal judges in Minnesota used their official judicial office to pander to the press about immigration policies,” Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said in a press release. “Judges who covet publicity rather than follow the rule of law by adjudicating cases or controversies undermine the public’s confidence in an impartial jury.”

Officials note even harmless statements to the press can create a perception of bias and indicate a judge may be motivated to decide issues in a way that prompts media attention.

The Justice Department requests that any judges who spoke to the Times about immigration cases recuse themselves from all current and future matters involving Homeland Security, given the concerns about impartiality.

“Public confidence in judicial impartiality cannot survive if judges seek out media attention and pander to the press,” Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. said in the press release. “Regrettably, judges in the District of Minnesota have done just that — by disregarding their ethical duties and launching a partisan press campaign, these judges advance their policy preference, allowing criminal illegal aliens to run free in Minnesota.”

Federal officials note many key immigration cases and criminal prosecutions against “anti-immigration enforcement agitators” are currently active or on appeal to the Eighth Circuit, making the judges’ public comments especially inappropriate.

The feds go even further to turn the blame for a judicial backlog back on the bench, referencing an Eighth Circuit decision that reversed the legal interpretation many Minnesota judges had on detention.

“As a matter of Eighth Circuit precedent, the flood of habeas petitions alleging a statutory violation and the resulting drain on government resources that led to several instances of unintentional noncompliance with court orders was the result of these and other district judges’ own legal errors,” the Justice Department says in the complaint.

The complaint is addressed directly to Chief U.S. Circuit Judge Steven Colloton, a Bush appointee, of the Eighth Circuit, which will handle the review and investigation into the supposed improper conduct of Minnesota judges.

Throughout Operation Metro Surge and in the following months, judges in Minnesota have been flooded with a mass of petitions from those challenging their detentions. Schiltz previously threatened Trump administration officials with contempt over violating court orders in such cases.

“As legal-ethics experts have confirmed, our judges were acting well within the ethical rules that apply to federal judges in speaking to The New York Times,” Rebeccah Parks, a District of Minnesota public information officer, told Courthouse News in a statement Wednesday. “Indeed, in February of this year, the Committee on Codes of Conduct issued an advisory opinion to emphasize that federal judges may ‘speak and write on core judiciary matters such as advocacy for the rule of law and judicial independence.’ Our judges acted within this capacity."

description:

In California, every ICE detainee is held in a private detention facility operated by a private corporation on private property under contract with the federal government.
Earlier this year, detainees at two ICE detention facilities in California, California City and Golden State Annex, held a boycott to protest increasing prices and gross profiteering at commissaries at these facilities.

text:
SACRAMENTO – Today, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed into law Senate Bill 941. Authored by California State Senator Steve Padilla (D-San Diego), the bill would prohibit the excessive markup of products sold at private detention facilities in California.

In California, every ICE detainee is held in a private detention facility operated by a private corporation on private property under contract with the federal government. California is currently home to seven such facilities, including two located within Senator Padilla’s district.

Commissaries at such facilities are often operated by third-party vendors that set prices without meaningful oversight. Reports from oversight and advocacy organizations document excessive pricing and inadequate access to basic necessities in private detention facility commissaries: a bar of Irish Spring soap was marked up by 75%, ramen noodles by 100%, Colgate Baking Soda and Peroxide by 139%, and canned tuna by 300%.

Earlier this year, detainees at two ICE detention facilities in California, California City and Golden State Annex, held a boycott to protest increasing prices and gross profiteering at commissaries at these facilities.

“As Trump’s monstrous deportation policies rip families apart, it is unacceptable California companies hike up the price of basic goods, all to profit off the backs of detainees forced into inhumane conditions,” said Senator Padilla. “SB 941 prioritizes people over profits to ensure this type of corporate greed does not continue in California.”

SB 941 prohibits the sale of commissary items in private detention facilities at prices exceeding a 35 percent markup above vendor cost. This extends California’s existing commissary price protections, established under SB 474 (The BASIC Act), to ICE detention facilities.

SB 941 is sponsored by California Collaborative for Immigrant Justice, the California Department of Justice Office of the Attorney General, and Immigrant Defense Advocates.

“Governor Newsom’s signing of SB 941 is a meaningful victory for people in detention and their families. Detained people themselves helped shine a light on abusive commissary prices through organized boycotts, and today California has responded by putting people before profit,” said Edwin Carmona-Cruz, Executive Director of California Collaborative for Immigrant Justice. “Immigration detention is unjust and exploitative. This law creates an important protection to reduce that exploitation."

“With the signing of SB 941, private vendors will no longer be able to run up massive profits off of the desperation of immigrant detainees,” said Attorney General Bonta. “My office’s review of conditions at immigration detention facilities across California has found repeated failures to provide adequate clothes, food, and hygiene products for detainees. As California confronts the Trump Administration’s inhumane mass detention and deportation campaign, I’m grateful for Senator Padilla’s championship of SB 941 and the Governor’s support of this legislation.”

“SB 941 sends a clear message that California puts people before profits. Families with loved ones in detention should not be forced to pay inflated, predatory prices simply to provide basic necessities and maintain a sense of dignity during an already difficult time,” said Jackie Gonzalez, Co-Executive Director at Immigrant Defense Advocates. “By putting reasonable limits on commissary markups, this bill protects California families from exploitation and ensures that private companies cannot profit unchecked off people’s hardship and separation.”

Senate Bill 941 passed both houses of the Legislature with bipartisan support last month.

text:
The Trump administration used funds from the Department of Homeland Security to air TV ads featuring President Donald Trump in recent days, according to sources familiar with the matter.

Federal budget records indicate the money was moved into a U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) account for "commemorative events" on Sept. 19 and federal contract data shows that a contract of $20 million was awarded the next day to the LMD Agency, a Maryland-based advertising agency for a "National Media Campaign." Days later, the ads began airing.

CBP is the the agency within DHS that is responsible for securing the nation's border and ports of entry. The funds appear to have been drawn from Trump's signature tax and spending bill passed in 2025. The bill provided $6.2 billion for a variety of border security improvements, but also for "commemorating efforts and events related to border security."

LMD Agency did not immediately respond to ABC's request for comment. The Wall Street Journal first reported the source of the federal funds.

DHS has been known to use funds for advertising campaigns, including spending millions of advertisements encouraging people who are in the country illegally to self-deport.

The federal government has spent at least $1.7 million to air three different TV ads featuring Trump in recent days, according to an estimate from AdImpact, which tracks and analyzes political ad spending across TV, digital and connected TV channels.

Critics say the ads could violate federal propaganda law. The White House has defended them as “public service announcements” and drawn comparisons to past examples ofadministrations that created PSA's to highlight new drug coverage under Medicare and signups for the Affordable Care Act exchanges.

DHS directed inquires to the White House. In a statement to ABC News, a White House spokesperson said: "These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad. The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic. We should be proud of our country."

Democrats on the Senate Appropriations Committee responded by sending a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin demanding he answer questions about the breakdown of the funds, whether the ads are expected to continue, and DHS's role in facilitating their airing.

text:
WASHINGTON — The Justice Department filed a complaint Wednesday against federal judges in Minnesota over their remarks to the media about the pressure on their courthouse during the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement surge.

The complaint alleges the seven judges — nominated by Democratic and Republican presidents — violated judicial ethics by speaking to The New York Times about their experience dealing with a flood of cases during last winter’s Operation Metro Surge crackdown that led to thousands of arrests in the Twin Cities.

The complaint escalates the department’s battle with the federal judiciary, which has halted administration priorities, dismissed high-profile prosecutions and accused government lawyers in some cases of failing to comply with court orders.

The department is demanding that the judges recuse themselves from all criminal or civil cases involving the Department of Homeland Security, Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters, because of what he described as “obvious bias they have shown” in their remarks to the newspaper.

“When we have a situation like we have now, where you have a judge, a couple of judges, just not only violating the canons in our view, but also showing bias in what they’re saying, we have no choice but to act to defend not only our prosecutors, but also DHS,” Blanche said.

The judge at the center of the story, Patrick Schiltz, accused the government in January of failing to comply with nearly 100 court orders. He said in a ruling that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, a part of DHS, “is not a law unto itself.”

Schiltz, who was nominated by Republican President George W. Bush and served as a law clerk for Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, told the newspaper that what happened in Minnesota’s federal court last winter “created a grave threat to the rule of law.”

In a statement Wednesday, a spokesperson for the Minnesota court said legal experts have confirmed that the judges were acting “well within the ethical rules that apply to federal judges” in speaking to the newspaper. Schiltz also said in a statement that his comments did not violate any ethical rules.

“Indeed, in February of this year, the Committee on Codes of Conduct issued an advisory opinion to emphasize that federal judges” may speak or write “on core judiciary matters such as advocacy for the rule of law and judicial independence,” Schiltz said in a statement. “That is exactly what I did.”

The complaint was filed with the chief judge of the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which oversees federal judges in Minnesota.

The Republican administration has railed against what it describes as “activist judges” who officials say are intent on thwarting Trump’s agenda. Yet some of the most critical and unfavorable court rulings have come from judges nominated by Trump and other Republican presidents.

title: Man shot by ICE in Austin will stay in custody, but will not return to ICE detention center
description:
Garces Perez had an immediate removal order at the time of the shooting due to him missing a court date.
Bazan said he interviewed Garces Perez and the other ICE officer involved, who is named as D.F.
Lawyers say Garces Perez needs surgery Garces Perez's lawyers have demanded he be provided medical care.
Garces Perez originally had a hearing in San Antonio, where his lawyers were going to argue for his release, but that was canceled.
The shooting of Garces Perez has led to multiple protests in Austin, including one on Sunday at the site of the shooting, which drew over 150 people.
text:
Wilber Garces Perez, who was shot in the back by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent earlier this month, will remain in custody after a federal court hearing in Austin on Wednesday.

He will not return to the ICE detention facility he was initially taken to in South Texas, according to Daniel Woodward, an attorney with the Texas Civil Rights Project. Instead, he will remain in federal court custody.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Texas charged Garces Perez, a citizen of Venezuela, with assaulting, resisting, interfering and impeding a federal officer. He faces up to 20 years in federal prison if convicted.

Prosecutors argued that due to Garces Perez fleeing from authorities, having connections in Venezuela, including his parents and his child, and because he faces time in federal prison, he is a flight risk and danger to the community.

Shane McMahon, the criminal defense attorney for Garces Perez, argued that his client had been trying to go through the process of obtaining legal residency in the United States. Garces Perez had an immediate removal order at the time of the shooting due to him missing a court date. He applied for an appeal, but it was denied.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Dustin M. Howell, who presided over the hearing on Wednesday, agreed that Garces Perez was a flight risk, but disagreed with prosecutors that he was a danger to the community.

The prosecution's argument for Garces Perez being a danger stemmed from him allegedly striking an ICE officer with his vehicle, attempting to hit an officer with his car after a chase and disregarding the safety of the public while he fled from officers.

Unreleased body-cam footage shown in court

Rick Bazan, a Department of Homeland Security special agent, said neither he nor his team interviewed the ICE agent who shot Garces Perez, identified in court documents as L.G., as part of their investigation. Bazan also said he did not ask L.G. if he was hit by the vehicle. A separate DHS unit is investigating the shooting.

Bazan said he interviewed Garces Perez and the other ICE officer involved, who is named as D.F. in the arrest affidavit. He also said he used body camera footage from the ICE officers and footage from local businesses to piece together the sequence of events.

Prosecuting attorneys showed body-camera footage from the incident, which has not been released to the public. The footage showed a car chase with the ICE agents as they pursued Garces Perez.

The officer, D.F., who was wearing a body camera, began calling the Texas Department of Public Safety for backup and lost sight of his partner and Garces Perez about six minutes into the pursuit, the video showed. He then turned off his camera before calling L.G. to find out where he was. Bazan testified that the car chase was partly in residential neighborhoods.

The chase lasted about eight minutes, according to Bazan. During questioning by McMahon, the defense attorney, Bazan said he did not ask D.F. why he turned off his camera.

The ICE agents first found out Garces Perez was in the United States illegally after seeing Garces Perez walk into a restaurant and running his license plate through a database, Bazan said.

The ICE officers then waited for Garces Perez to leave the restaurant and drive off, so that they could conduct a traffic stop and arrest him in a less populated area, according to Bazan.

The video showed both officers approaching Garces Perez’s car during the initial stop, and the ICE agent, L.G., talking to Garces Perez in Spanish, according to the body camera footage presented in the courtroom.

L.G. identified himself as an immigration officer and asked Garces Perez to put the car in park and step out of the car multiple times. Garces Perez said he would move the car and park it. L.G. then replied they would move the car for him, according to the body camera footage. The back and forth continued with both sides repeating themselves.

Garces Perez then rolled up his window and sped away, the video showed. According to court documents, prosecutors accused Garces Perez of hitting an officer on the torso with his side mirror. McMahon, the defense attorney, said it was not clear, in the courtroom video, to what extent the car made contact with the officer.

According to court documents, officer L.G. caught up with Garces Perez and crashed into his car, forcing it to spin out. In an interview with Bazan, officer D.F. relayed that the other officer, L.G., had told him he feared Garces Perez was trying to hit him with his car.

McMahon then showed a social media video of L.G. getting out of his car after the crash, running behind Garces Perez’s car and shooting three times through the rear back window.

Lawyers say Garces Perez needs surgery

Garces Perez's lawyers have demanded he be provided medical care. He has had a bullet lodged in his back since the shooting 10 days ago and appeared in court in a wheelchair. Garces Perez occasionally winced in pain during the court proceedings.

"He is facing permanent immobility and sepsis," said Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, a lawyer working on his immigration case, "and medical professionals are calling for surgery for him. Throughout the hearing today, he was wincing in pain, and it's difficult for us to see our client in such pain."

Garces Perez originally had a hearing in San Antonio, where his lawyers were going to argue for his release, but that was canceled.

The shooting of Garces Perez has led to multiple protests in Austin, including one on Sunday at the site of the shooting, which drew over 150 people.

WASHINGTON (OSV News) — The U.S. Supreme Court temporarily allowed the Trump administration to carry out third-country deportations — removals to a country where a person who had migrated to the United States has no ties — while a challenge to that policy continues.

The high court granted Sept. 29 the Justice Department’s emergency request to put on hold a lower court ruling that the Department of Homeland Security’s policy permitting the removal of migrants to so-called third countries is unlawful, but it also agreed to hear a challenge to the policy in December.

As part of its efforts to enforce hardline immigration policies, the Trump administration has carried out deportations of some immigrants who lack legal authorization to live and work in the U.S., known as “third-country” removals. The people subject to these orders are sent to countries not specifically identified in their removal orders or to countries with which they have no preexisting ties or citizenship.

Thousands sent to countries they have no ties with

The Migration Policy Institute estimated that about 15,000 third-country deportations occurred between Jan. 20, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2025. Some estimates say about 25,000 people have been deported in such arrangements to date.

In one such notable case, the Trump administration sought to deport Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national, to African countries including Uganda and Liberia, after a judge protected him from deportation to his country of origin due to concerns about gang violence against his family.

“The decision by the Supreme Court to allow third country deportations, even temporarily, violates human dignity and places immigrants in danger. It is akin to a U.S. citizen without legal status in England being deported to North Korea,” Kevin Appleby, senior fellow for policy and communications at the Center for Migration Studies of New York and the former director of migration policy for the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, told OSV News.

James Percival, general counsel for the Department of Homeland Security, said in a post on X, “A bad day for criminal illegals and open borders activists alike.”

Percival added, “It’s not too late to get $3,000 and a flight home,” a reference to a policy permitting what the department calls an “exit bonus” for those who voluntarily self-deport.

Appleby said that he hopes the Supreme Court “will rule differently when they hear the merits of the case, but in the interim the lives of thousands of persons will be placed in jeopardy.”

Advocates say third-country policy violates Catholic teaching

Catholic social teaching on immigration balances three interrelated principles: the right of persons to migrate in order to sustain their lives and those of their families, the right of a country to regulate its borders and control immigration, but also a nation’s duty to regulate its borders with justice and mercy.

Dylan Corbett, executive director of the Hope Border Institute, a group that works to apply the perspective of Catholic social teaching in policy and practice to the U.S.-Mexico border region, told OSV News, “Deporting people to countries they’ve never known, where they have no family, no language and no protection, isn’t enforcement. It’s banishment and it’s punitive.”

“As Pope Leo reminds us, human dignity has no passport, and even a temporary green light for this practice puts real lives at risk,” he said.

Christian migrants, particularly Catholics, are the most vulnerable demographic to mass deportation in the U.S., a joint report, “One Part of the Body,” published by evangelical and Catholic groups in 2025, said. According to demographic data as of the end of 2024, the report found that 10 million Christians make up 80%, and Catholics 61%, of those vulnerable to deportation under Trump administration policies implemented in 2025.

title: Trump administration escalates feud with federal judges | CNN Politics
description:
The Justice Department filed a judicial misconduct complaint against nearly all the federal district judges in Minnesota, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced on Wednesday, escalating tensions between the Trump administration and the judicial branch.
While the ethics complaint is pending at the federal appeals court that oversees Minnesota’s federal bench, Blanche is calling on the district court judges to recuse from DHS-related cases.
The Trump administration has tried various tactics to strike back at judges they see as hostile to President Donald Trump’s agenda.
The Committee on Codes of Conduct for the Judicial Conference — a policy-making entity for federal judges that Roberts oversees — ultimately offered more nuanced guidance.
(The administration denied the allegations, and Bove was later confirmed to a position on a federal appeals court based in Philadelphia.)
text:
The Justice Department filed a judicial misconduct complaint against nearly all the federal district judges in Minnesota, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced on Wednesday, escalating tensions between the Trump administration and the judicial branch.

The administration’s demand that the judges be disqualified from immigration-related cases was prompted by a recent New York Times article in which the judges described the Justice Department’s failure to comply with court orders during an immigration-enforcement surge as a grave threat to the rule of law.

In their comments, the judges focused on how DOJ staffing shortages appeared to inhibit the administration in its ability to comply with their orders — similar to comments they have previously made in legal settings. But Blanche on Wednesday said the comments were “overtly political” in violation of judicial rules and that they reflected an “an obvious bias” against the Department of Homeland Security.

While the ethics complaint is pending at the federal appeals court that oversees Minnesota’s federal bench, Blanche is calling on the district court judges to recuse from DHS-related cases.

The demand, however, may not have much impact, as previous efforts and public complaints have gone nowhere — and the bar for disqualification of judges is high.

A spokesperson for Minnesota’s US district court said that the interviews the judges gave were within the bounds of judicial ethics, including guidance issued to judges in February that emphasized their ability to speak and write “on core judiciary matters such as advocacy for the rule of law and judicial independence.”

“Our judges acted within this capacity,” Rebeccah Parks said.

The Trump administration has tried various tactics to strike back at judges they see as hostile to President Donald Trump’s agenda. That has included an unsuccessful DOJ lawsuit — filed against the entire federal bench in Maryland — challenging an order covering that court that limited the ability of the administration to quickly remove migrants who are fighting their deportations.

Top Trump officials have also been willing to use exceptionally sharp language to publicly call out judges by name for rulings they disagree with.

As courts across the country have faced aggressive public pushback from the president and his allies for rulings that blocked Trump policy initiatives, judges have sounded alarms about how the heated rhetoric has raised the specter of threats and intimidation.

“These judges talked to the media, or at least to the New York Times, about cases, some of which are ongoing, in a matter that the department views as a clear violation of their ethical duties,” Blanche said.

Rules for judges for speaking to the press

The latest Justice Department campaign against Minnesota’s federal court taps into a debate in the legal world over whether it’s appropriate for judges to criticize the administration’s actions in commentary outside the confines of a legal proceeding.

The extraordinary legal disputes that arose from unprecedented actions taken by Trump and his deputies at the beginning of his second term led to notable examples of judges speaking out — both in on-the-record contexts, and in anonymous interviews with press outlets — about their concerns of an assault on democratic norms. Their comments at times took aim not just at the Trump administration, but also at the Supreme Court for how it has frequently reversed lower court rulings against the administration with little explanation why.

Sen. Chuck Grassley of Iowa and Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, the Republican chairs of the Senate and House Judiciary Committees, called on Chief Judge John Roberts to put a kibosh on judges talking to the press — particularly when done in an anonymous fashion — in a letter last November highlighting the criticism against the Supreme Court.

The Committee on Codes of Conduct for the Judicial Conference — a policy-making entity for federal judges that Roberts oversees — ultimately offered more nuanced guidance.

An ethics advisory issued for judges in February said there was room in “some circumstances” for them to offer “measured defense of judicial colleagues from illegitimate forms of criticism and attacks that risk undermining judicial independence or the rule of law.”

The advisory said that violence, intimidation, disinformation and threats to defy court orders were all examples of “illegitimate” activity judges could speak out about. But it also instructed judges to consider the “tone, context, and form” of what they’re saying — including in situations where a judge is speaking anonymously to the press.

The handful of judges quoted in the New York Times report were speaking on the record, not anonymously, though the report said the outlet spoke to seven judges in total. One of them, an appointee of Trump’s during his first term, seemed to refer to the recent ethics guidance.

“We are allowed to speak out about judicial independence,” Judge Nancy E. Brasel told the New York Times. “And so we should, in order to keep it.”

Blanche on Wednesday, however, argued that the comments were political in nature and that they touched on cases that were still pending, in violation of judicial rules. The Justice Department’s complaint targeted the six active judges who participated in the story — a seventh active judge on the court did not talk to the Times.

Gabe Roth, executive director for the judicial ethics organization Fix the Court, noted that Blanche has departed from DOJ norms by attending partisan rallies while leading the department.

(Blanche, when asked Wednesday about his attendance at political events, insisted that he did not violate DOJ policies.)

“If DOJ doesn’t want judges to speak to the New York Times about the agency’s aberrant practices in federal court, it should spend more time fixing those practices and less time filing frivolous misconduct complaints,” Roth said.

DC judges weigh ‘grim’ DOJ claim that courts can’t probe its defiance of their orders

Separately this week, a powerful appeals court in DC was weighing judges’ powers to address government defiance of their orders in court.

The DOJ has asked the DC US Circuit Court of Appeals to shut down the effort by Judge Jeb Boasberg to obtain information from the administration about its decision to move forward with removals of certain Venezuelan migrants to an El Salvadoran prison in March 2025, after the judge issued an order seeking to halt the deportations.

How the appeals court resolves the DOJ’s appeal could shape what other judges can do when they believe that the government is willfully not following their orders.

At a hearing in the appeal Tuesday, Circuit Judge Nina Pillard said hat the administration’s arguments would seem to put the federal courts at the “mercy of the executive” branch.

“If the executive branch can determine, ‘We do not want to be stopped by a court. If we are, we will ignore it and do our best to, you know, keep our noses clean,’” Pillard said, laying out her “grim” interpretation of the Trump administration’s stance in the case. “’But if the court thinks there’s a problem, we in the end will be in charge of whether that problem is tracked down.”

The administration claims it did not violate Boasberg’s orders, which it argues were unclear. The Justice Department says that any efforts by him to further investigate the matter would be an unconstitutional usurpation of the executive branch’s prosecutorial powers.

In a back and forth with ACLU attorney Lee Gelernt, who was defending Boasberg’s handling the case, Circuit Judge Greg Katsas, a Trump appointee, acknowledged what had been unsaid, but obvious: If Boasberg was allowed to make a final referral for a criminal contempt prosecution, it is assumed that the Trump Justice Department would not act on it.

He and two other DC circuit judges, all Trump appointees, have already agreed in earlier stages of the appeal with the administration’s stance. However, the full circuit court, which leans left, is now considering the dispute. Several Democratic appointees on the court expressed their concerns Tuesday with administration’s approach.

Two judges referenced comments allegedly made by Emil Bove, a former Trump personal attorney who was then the No. 3 official at the Justice Department. Bove was accused by a whistleblower of telling other administration officials as they plotted the deportations that DOJ might need to tell courts “f**k you” if they sought to halt the removals.

(The administration denied the allegations, and Bove was later confirmed to a position on a federal appeals court based in Philadelphia.)

Separation of powers “runs two ways,” said DC Circuit Judge Patricia Millett at the Tuesday hearing. “It’s not a one-way street in favor of the executive branch.”

This story has been updated with additional information.
