text:
Human rights advocates asked a United Nations panel to intervene Wednesday to help end a new U.S. government practice of withholding from families and lawyers the whereabouts of thousands of detainees facing deportation.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement removed the names of detainees with final removal orders from its Online Detainee Locator System on Sept. 15 in an apparent effort to speed up their deportations. The change, which ICE did not announce and has not explained, applies to more than 16,000 of the nearly 69,000 detainees who are in ICE custody.

The move has interfered with detainees' ability to challenge looming deportations by impeding access to their lawyers while devastating families who lost track of their loved ones, immigration lawyers say.

A coalition of more than 30 groups who advocate for noncitizens in the U.S. petitioned the U.N.'s Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances to declare the policy a violation of international law and to push for its end.

“A system with no transparency is a system with no accountability, and that should terrify all of us,” said Sarah Decker, an attorney at the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, one of the petition's signatories. “Disappearing people into a network of remote detention sites, hiding their whereabouts, and cutting off their access to outside help is the definition of an enforced disappearance."

Separately, on Wednesday, more than 45 House Democrats led by Reps. Luz Rivas and Veronica Escobar urged ICE to restore the names to the locator, calling the practice of concealing them “contrary to foundational principles of the American legal system.”

ICE's parent agency denied Wednesday that its practices amount to disappearing people, saying all detainees “have opportunities to communicate with their family members and lawyers.”

“The appropriate process due to an illegal alien with final deportation orders is removal, plain and simple,” the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement. “That said, DHS has a stringent law enforcement assessment in place that abides by due process under the U.S. Constitution.”

Detainees can typically call relatives if they have money in their commissary accounts, while calls to their legal representatives are supposed to be free.

Approximately 1.4 million people living in the U.S. are subject to final orders of removal. That typically means an immigration judge has ruled they should be deported and the decision has been upheld on appeal or not appealed. They still have several legal options to challenge their detention and deportation. Federal judges have ruled thousands of times that detainees should be released or granted bond hearings.

The petition to the U.N. said the policy has already “obstructed legal counsel from accessing their clients in detention, preventing interventions to seek immigration relief, challenge unconstitutional detention, and block unlawful deportations.”

It cited examples of several detainees, including a mother and 7-year-old daughter who were challenging their detention at a Texas facility but lost access to their lawyers as they faced deportation to Venezuela. Only after a judge ordered ICE to disclose their whereabouts did the agency do so, about 18 hours later, and release them from custody, the petition said.

One man reported intense stress and that the “darkest thoughts imaginable went through" his mind after the whereabouts of his elderly disabled mother were abruptly removed from the system, according to the petition.

The petition said ICE's online locator, launched in 2010, has become “an even more crucial tool” as President Donald Trump's administration has carried out a sweeping campaign to arrest and deport people who are in the country illegally. It noted that the U.N. working group had lobbied for the locator’s creation and its 2024 expansion to include people detained by the Border Patrol.

The petition asked the U.N. group to urge ICE to publicly list all detainees’ locations within an hour of their arrest and give detainees’ lawyers 24 hours’ notice before a transfer. The U.N. group, which was formed in 1980, helps families locate loved ones who have reportedly been subjected to enforced disappearance by government agents. It has five members and is currently chaired by Grazyna Baranowska of Poland.

text:
A Michigan nurse has been charged with a federal misdemeanor after authorities alleged she helped an injured immigration detainee leave a hospital while he was in federal custody, according to court filings.

Chloe Renae Freeman, 33, of Whitmore Lake, was charged with instigating or assisting the escape of a person under arrest, according to a criminal complaint filed August 28 in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan. The charge carries a maximum penalty of one year in prison and a fine.

Freeman was working as a registered nurse at Trinity Health Ann Arbor Hospital when the alleged escape occurred on May 28, according to an affidavit filed with the complaint.

Read More on News

The allegations are contained in an affidavit from FBI Special Agent Michael Wagner submitted to establish probable cause. Freeman has not been convicted of the charge, and the complaint represents the government's account of events.

Attorney Matthew G. Borgula told Newsweek that Freeman, who has pleaded not guilty to the charges, will not be making any public comment at this time.

“The individual referenced is no longer employed by Trinity Health Ann Arbor. Because this is an active legal matter, we are unable to comment on the specific allegations or ongoing court proceedings,” Trinity Health Ann Arbor told Newsweek.

Newsweek has contacted the Department of Homeland Security, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection, for comment.

President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign has expanded immigration enforcement across the country, prompting protests, legal challenges and opposition from immigrant-rights groups. Federal authorities have also accused U.S. citizens and protesters of interfering with immigration enforcement operations, while federal immigration agencies have faced allegations of due process violations, excessive use of force and racial profiling.

U.S. Border Patrol agents conducted a targeted immigration enforcement operation in Ann Arbor the night of May 28 involving a man identified in court records only by the initials OBP, according to the affidavit.

Federal authorities described the man as a native and citizen of Mexico who had previously been removed from the United States in December 2022 and had not received permission to reapply for admission.

Agents approached the man at about 9 p.m. near Washtenaw Avenue and Pittsfield Boulevard, according to the affidavit. Authorities allege he ran from the agents, tripped over a curb and struck his face on the pavement.

After taking him into custody, agents observed bleeding from his head and provided first aid for cuts on the bridge of his nose and a small contusion on his forehead, the filing said. Emergency medical personnel were called and determined that he required further evaluation.

He was subsequently taken to Trinity Health Ann Arbor Hospital while remaining in Border Patrol custody, according to the affidavit. The government described his detention as an administrative immigration arrest rather than a criminal arrest.

At the hospital, medical staff ordered a CT scan. A CT technologist told investigators that after the scan, two nurses, including Freeman, arrived and directed the technologist to keep the patient in the CT room rather than return him to his hospital room, according to the affidavit.

The government alleges Freeman later returned and retrieved him.

Hospital badge records showed Freeman used her badge to enter the CT room at approximately 11:31 p.m., said the affidavit. Security footage cited by investigators allegedly showed the detainee leaving through the hospital's ambulance bay doors about a minute later.

Authorities said they had been unable to locate him as of the filing of the complaint.

During a June 18 interview with hospital investigators, Freeman admitted allowing the man to leave, the FBI affidavit alleges.

According to the government's account of the interview, Freeman said she knew the patient was in immigration custody but did not believe he remained in custody at that moment because immigration agents were not physically present with him in the CT room.

Freeman allegedly told investigators that she removed the man's IV and escorted him through the ambulance bay doors. The affidavit alleges she also said she disagreed with ICE separating people from their families and knew she "was going to set him free."

"Freeman told the interviewers that she did not agree with ICE separating people from their families and that she knew she 'was going to set him free,'" Wagner wrote in the affidavit.

She also acknowledged that the man's injuries could have been life-threatening, according to the affidavit.

Prosecutors allege Freeman took the man out of the hospital before his medical care had been completed and before he had been properly discharged.

Freeman made her initial appearance before U.S. Magistrate Judge David R. Grand on September 29 and was released on a $10,000 unsecured bond, court records show. A preliminary examination is scheduled for October 20.

The Trump administration has expanded the role of federal law-enforcement agencies in its immigration crackdown, with ICE working alongside Border Patrol, the FBI, the Drug Enforcement Administration, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, and the U.S. Marshals Service on immigration-enforcement operations.

The administration has also changed where immigration authorities may conduct enforcement. On January 20, 2025, then-Acting Homeland Security Secretary Benjamine Huffman rescinded a Biden administration policy that had restricted ICE and Customs and Border Protection enforcement actions in or near so-called protected areas, including hospitals, schools and places of worship. The replacement directive eliminated categorical restrictions and instructed officers to use discretion and "common sense" when deciding whether to conduct enforcement actions in such locations.

text:
PARIS (CN) — On Wednesday, the Paris Criminal Court found 13 men guilty of charges including involuntary homicide for their role in the tragic sinking of an inflatable dinghy that left 31 people dead in 2021.

Just before delivering the verdict, the presiding judge — the court asked journalists not to publish her name — said investigations and debates shed light on a situation with “tragic consequences,” and the “individuals profiting from the serious vulnerability” of migrants.

Since early September, the court has tried 14 men over their involvement in what became the deadliest English Channel migrant crossing on record. They faced charges including involuntary homicide, involuntary injury, assisting the irregular entry, movement or stay of a foreign national within the territory of a state party to the protocol against the smuggling of migrants, endangering others and assisting the irregular entry, movement or stay of a foreign national in France as part of an organized group.

Thirteen of the defendants were handed prison sentences ranging from six months to the maximum of 10 years, many of which were suspended or to be served wearing an electronic bracelet, and one man was acquitted due to a lack of evidence. Six were found guilty of involuntary homicide.

Only one man was handcuffed and escorted out of the courtroom by police officers; victims’ family members testified that he was the “right-hand man” of the network’s leader. On Wednesday, the presiding judge said she was convinced by this, which was corroborated by phone records. She also condemned that he presented himself as a “simple migrant” during the trial, which was “very far from the actual reality.”

The court also rejected his request to reimburse roughly $1,700 in lawyer fees; during his testimony on Sept. 11, the court learned he had threatened five lawyers, which is why he didn’t have legal representation. He was sentenced to eight years behind bars.

The 113 plaintiffs were largely victims’ family members. Nine traveled from Erbil, in Iraqi Kurdistan, to testify Sept. 8 and 9. One father cried as he begged the court to locate his son’s body, “even if there’s only a finger left.”

On the night of Nov. 23, 2021, 33 migrants gathered on the shores of Calais in northern France to cross into the U.K. They had paid smugglers thousands of U.S. dollars for spots on a roughly 20-by-7-foot inflatable dinghy and were given life jackets that did not meet buoyancy standards for rough seas.

On Wednesday, the presiding judge said it was clear that the boat was overloaded, people were equipped with inadequate lifejackets and the motor was faulty.

A few hours into the journey, the boat began taking on water. Migrants made multiple distress calls to French and U.K. services that went unanswered, prompting a separate, ongoing investigation into French military personnel for failing to help people in danger.

The two survivors told the court the water was freezing, currents were strong and most aboard could not swim. They survived by clinging to debris. Mohammad I., one of the survivors, said he knew he had to keep moving so the cold would not stop his heart.

“We couldn’t save those drowning next to us, otherwise we’d drown with them,” he said on Sept. 8. “Everyone was a bit everywhere in the water.”

Roughly 12 hours after the initial distress calls, a fishing vessel spotted the bright orange lifejackets carrying lifeless bodies through the water.

text:
Human rights advocates asked a United Nations panel to intervene Wednesday to help end a new U.S. government practice of withholding from families and lawyers the whereabouts of thousands of detainees facing deportation.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement removed the names of detainees with final removal orders from its Online Detainee Locator System on Sept. 15 in an apparent effort to speed up their deportations. The change, which ICE did not announce and has not explained, applies to more than 16,000 of the nearly 69,000 detainees who are in ICE custody.

The move has interfered with detainees’ ability to challenge looming deportations by impeding access to their lawyers while devastating families who lost track of their loved ones, immigration lawyers say.

A coalition of more than 30 groups who advocate for noncitizens in the U.S. petitioned the U.N.’s Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances to declare the policy a violation of international law and to push for its end.

“A system with no transparency is a system with no accountability, and that should terrify all of us,” said Sarah Decker, an attorney at the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, one of the petition’s signatories. “Disappearing people into a network of remote detention sites, hiding their whereabouts, and cutting off their access to outside help is the definition of an enforced disappearance.”

Separately, on Wednesday, more than 45 House Democrats led by Reps. Luz Rivas and Veronica Escobar urged ICE to restore the names to the locator, calling the practice of concealing them “contrary to foundational principles of the American legal system.”

ICE’s parent agency denied Wednesday that its practices amount to disappearing people, saying all detainees “have opportunities to communicate with their family members and lawyers.”

“The appropriate process due to an illegal alien with final deportation orders is removal, plain and simple,” the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement. “That said, DHS has a stringent law enforcement assessment in place that abides by due process under the U.S. Constitution.”

Detainees can typically call relatives if they have money in their commissary accounts, while calls to their legal representatives are supposed to be free.

Approximately 1.4 million people living in the U.S. are subject to final orders of removal. That typically means an immigration judge has ruled they should be deported and the decision has been upheld on appeal or not appealed. They still have several legal options to challenge their detention and deportation. Federal judges have ruled thousands of times that detainees should be released or granted bond hearings.

The petition to the U.N. said the policy has already “obstructed legal counsel from accessing their clients in detention, preventing interventions to seek immigration relief, challenge unconstitutional detention, and block unlawful deportations.”

It cited examples of several detainees, including a mother and 7-year-old daughter who were challenging their detention at a Texas facility but lost access to their lawyers as they faced deportation to Venezuela. Only after a judge ordered ICE to disclose their whereabouts did the agency do so, about 18 hours later, and release them from custody, the petition said.

One man reported intense stress and that the “darkest thoughts imaginable went through” his mind after the whereabouts of his elderly disabled mother were abruptly removed from the system, according to the petition.

The petition said ICE’s online locator, launched in 2010, has become “an even more crucial tool” as President Donald Trump’s administration has carried out a sweeping campaign to arrest and deport people who are in the country illegally. It noted that the U.N. working group had lobbied for the locator’s creation and its 2024 expansion to include people detained by the Border Patrol.

The petition asked the U.N. group to urge ICE to publicly list all detainees’ locations within an hour of their arrest and give detainees’ lawyers 24 hours’ notice before a transfer. The U.N. group, which was formed in 1980, helps families locate loved ones who have reportedly been subjected to enforced disappearance by government agents. It has five members and is currently chaired by Grazyna Baranowska of Poland.

Welcome AddressTime: 9:45 AM – 10:00 AM EDT

Clay Shirky (New York University)

AI, Immigration, and EthicsTime: 10:00 AM – 10:15 AM EDT

Charlton Mcllwain (New York University)

Panel #1: How is AI being used for immigration policy and enforcement?Time: 10:30 AM – 12:00 PM EDT

This panel asks how AI systems are currently being used for immigration policy and enforcement. Together, the panelists will address the functionalities and use cases being developed and the data practices required for these technologies to proliferate. Discussions will center on the implications of this technology for immigration case adjudication. They will help us understand the major actors in this space, such as the leading technology companies and the influence of business interests in shaping immigration governance.

Featured Panelists:Saira Hussain (Electronic Frontier Foundation)

Katya Schwenk (The Lever)

Chinmayi Sharma (Fordham Law)

Steven Hubbard (American Immigration Council)

Jay Stanley (American Civil Liberties Union)

Moderated by Natasha Iskander (New York University)

Keynote: What even is AI, and why does the answer matter for immigration enforcement and governance?Time: 12:15 PM – 1:15 PM EDT – Lunch served

Keynote speaker: Meredith Broussard (New York University)

Our keynote will explore the essential question: what is AI, and how does it work? Speaker Meredith Broussard will illuminate different types of AI, such as natural language processing, machine learning, and agentic/embodied AI, and explore what we mean by “AI in governance.” She will address the social biases built into AI models and the historical context for AI’s growing use in immigration enforcement. This keynote sets AI in the context of other technologies that are used by the government, asking: how is AI different, and is it unique?

Introduced by De Angela L. Duff (New York University)

Panel #2: What does the use of AI in immigration policy application and enforcement mean for all of us?Time: 1:30 PM – 3:00 PM EDT

This panel addresses the use of AI in immigration policy and governance more broadly. Our panelists will illuminate how AI systems have pushed the government into new functions, with few opportunities for appeal. They will outline new governance possibilities for data-driven, AI-powered surveillance, the integration of massive, disparate datasets from public, private, and government sources, and algorithmic decision-making. They will address what these changes mean for political rights and protections, especially privacy and civil liberties. These technologies are redefining public life and social categories of inclusion and exclusion along lines of race, gender, sexuality, immigration status, and others. Our panelists will conclude by exploring how we can reshape the use of AI to support democratic governance and political rights.

Featured Panelists:Margaret Hu (William & Mary Law School)

Faiza Patel (NYU – Brennan Center)

Jacob Silverman. (Journalist)

Iván Chaar López (University of Texas at Austin)

Sarah Lamdan (American Library Association)

Moderated by Cristina Beltrán (New York University)

Panel #3: What are avenues for action and accountability?Time: 3:15 PM – 4:15 PM – Coffee served

The last panel of the day asks leading researchers to help the audience understand where we fit into this picture. How do we interrogate and challenge uses of AI that cause harm? How can we act to ensure that AI systems are used for good governance and in support of civil rights and democratic principles? Panelists will explore the new ethical concerns raised by research—database or field research—in contexts shaped by AI-enabled surveillance capabilities.

text:
New York, NY—Today, the Supreme Court sided with the Trump administration, allowing it to resume fast track deportations of immigrants to third-party countries other than their countries of origin, while the legal challenge to the policy continues. The Supreme Court also announced that it will hear oral arguments at the end of this year to determine its final ruling. The court’s order overturns lower courts’ findings that immigrants have a constitutional right to "meaningful notice" and a hearing to object if they fear torture or persecution in the designated third country.

Under third party deportation diplomatic agreements, the Trump administration has deported roughly 25,000 immigrants to more than two dozen third countries since January 2025.

Murad Awawdeh, President and CEO, New York Immigration Coalition:

“Every person who resides here deserves access to due process before being removed from the country they call home. By allowing the Trump administration to resume these third-party deportations, the Supreme Court has opened the door for people to be rapidly deported to countries they do not have any connection to–including personal or family ties–having to face language and cultural barriers, as well as possibly persecution or torture. No one should have to live with the fear that their loved one could be sent thousands of miles away to an unfamiliar country without a meaningful opportunity to have their day in court. A country that deports people without a hearing is not enforcing its laws. It is abandoning them. This ruling is another tool the federal government is using to expand its mass deportation agenda, putting more lives at risk and destabilizing our communities. The Trump administration must end this inhumane practice and stop treating people’s lives as disposable, and provide individuals in deportation proceedings—often facing life or death consequences— the right to counsel and due process. We will not accept a system where people's lives are treated as cargo.”

text:
When word of an internal Immigration and Customs Enforcement leadership call over the weekend leaked to media outlets, some Trump administration officials came to believe the agency planned to limit arrests of undocumented immigrants to those with criminal histories.

The perceived softening of the administration’s hardline stance to deport anyone in the country illegally set off President Donald Trump, who immediately sought to clear the record — telling a well-known correspondent at Fox News in a phone call that ICE would continue to arrest anyone in the country illegally, regardless of criminal history.

Behind the scenes, Trump also directed his anger toward Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, according to a source familiar with the incident and a source close to the White House.

While DHS, which oversees ICE, denies that any such directive was issued, the episode exposed the ongoing disconnect between the White House and the officials charged with carrying out Trump’s mass deportation campaign. And it comes weeks away from the midterm elections, as some Republicans have publicly and privately expressed unease over who the administration is taking into custody.

Immigration remains a key political issue for the White House ahead of the midterm elections, and administration officials have been sensitive to any potential changes in operations that appear to weaken the president’s approach to his mass deportation pledge.

Earlier this summer, Trump was furious over a pause on most vehicle stops conducted by ICE following fatal shootings in Texas and Maine. The decision to pause those stops, which Trump ultimately overturned, immediately received blowback from his political base, who believed it was a sign of the administration going soft on its immigration crackdown.

Mullin has repeatedly said that anyone in the country illegally may be eligible for removal. But the sources told CNN that he privately supports the shift away from what officials call “collateral arrests,” meaning people who may be in the vicinity of an operation or with a person on law enforcement’s radar.

The guidance verbally communicated on the weekend call with some ICE agents appeared to direct them to take a different approach to “collateral arrests” and instead focus on criminals, fueling confusion among the agents, according to three sources briefed on the call.

Mullin, a former GOP US senator from Oklahoma, took the helm of DHS just six months ago when Trump fired his predecessor, Kristi Noem.

While sources insisted there’s no indication that Mullin is at risk of losing his job, that episode reignited concerns among Homeland Security officials and sources close to the White House that Mullin isn’t in lockstep with the president.

“Mullin is definitely out of step with President Trump and the base on immigration,” one of the sources said.

In a statement to CNN, a Homeland Security spokesperson said: “We are all focused on delivering on the President’s mission to deport illegal aliens and are all the same page. Anyone who says otherwise is just trying to sow division and create an illusion of chaos.”

The spokesperson maintained that “no one is off the table,” adding that, “anyone in our country illegally will be arrested and deported.”

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement that Mullin “has helped deliver the most secure border in history and shattered ICE arrest records.”

“President Trump and Secretary Mullin will continue to carry out the agenda the American people voted for,” she added.

The administration’s arrest tactics and decision to increasingly arrest undocumented immigrants without criminal records has fueled criticism among some Republicans, most notably Florida Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, who represents a heavily Hispanic district. She broke with the president in a recent campaign ad ahead of the midterms.

In her ad, Salazar pointed to statistics she said show that 50% of the people detained by ICE in July “had no criminal record.”

An uptick in ICE activity in southwest Kansas that drew concerns among the agricultural industry also prompted a response from Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, who said in a statement last week that local law enforcement had not been “given advance notice or the level of cooperation we would expect from ICE’s enforcement and removal operations.”

“As a result, there have been mass disruptions to local communities and businesses,” he said, adding that he shared his concerns with DHS.

ICE picked up its immigration arrests over the summer. In August, ICE took around 51,000 people into custody, setting a new monthly high under the Trump administration. The previous high had been set just one month prior when the agency took more than 46,000 people into custody in July.

Since the start of the Trump administration, ICE has been under immense pressure from the White House to arrest hundreds of people daily and over time, cast a wider net of who’s eligible for arrest, beyond those who are public safety or national security threats.

In recent weeks, Mullin, who’s faced backlash from corners of the MAGA base for not being strong enough on immigration enforcement, has forcefully defended the administration’s crackdown, posting photos of deportation flights.

But multiple sources have told CNN that Mullin has had a hard time transitioning to his role. CNN previously reported that Mullin had expressed frustration with working under the close watch of the White House.

“Ultimately, Mullin is no longer a principal — he’s a staffer to the president,” one Trump adviser told CNN. “He’s had a hard time coming to terms with that, like many others before him.”

Mullin also saw his pick for director of ICE Lance Schroyer, a former Oklahoma state trooper, abruptly pulled by the White House after his nomination stalled in the Senate. Mullin had chosen Schroyer after his first proposed pick for the role caused friction with some White House officials.

text:
The US Supreme Court on Tuesday let US President Donald Trump's administration resume deporting migrants to countries other than their own without offering them the chance to show the harms they may face, bolstering a tool his administration has used for rapid expulsions as part of his immigration crackdown.

The court granted the Justice Department's emergency request to put on hold Boston-based US District Judge Brian Murphy's ruling that the Department of Homeland Security's policy to remove migrants to so-called third countries is unlawful. The court also agreed to hear arguments in the dispute in December, with a formal ruling on the policy to follow.

The court has a 6-3 conservative majority. Its three liberal justices dissented from the decision to let the deportations immediately resume pending the final outcome of the litigation.

Murphy's ruling came in a class-action lawsuit filed by immigrant rights groups on behalf of migrants seeking to prevent the US government from sending them to third countries without notice and a chance to assert the harms they could face.

More than 25,000 migrants have been deported to 29 countries under the policy implemented last year, according to a tally by human rights groups, with the vast majority going to Mexico.

The policy is one of a number of measures the administration has taken in its pursuit of Trump's goal of mass deportation. The Republican president has enforced a sweeping crackdown on immigration - among his top priorities - since returning to office last year.

The administration has carried out third-country deportations to politically unstable South Sudan, which the US State Department urges Americans to avoid due to the risks of crime, kidnapping, and armed conflict, as well as Uganda, Equatorial Guinea, Liberia, the Central African Republic, and other nations.

Department of Homeland Security General Counsel James Percival welcomed the court's decision.

"A bad day for criminal illegals and open-borders activists alike," Percival wrote on social media.

Trina Realmuto, a lawyer for the plaintiffs at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, said the court has "allowed the administration to resume sending people to third countries where they face persecution or torture. That is a devastating result for people who may be put on a plane before they ever have notice or an opportunity to raise a fear claim."

Judge rules US immigration policy against immigration law, due process protections

In February, Murphy ruled that the policy violates immigration law procedures and due process protections under the US Constitution's Fifth Amendment. Due process generally requires the government to provide notice and an opportunity for a hearing before taking certain adverse actions.

The Supreme Court, which has allowed a number of Trump's hardline immigration policies, previously sided with the administration in the legal challenge, suspending a preliminary order that Murphy issued earlier in the case halting the removals. In another win for the administration, the Supreme Court subsequently lifted limits the judge had imposed to protect a group of men from being sent to South Sudan.

The case began in 2025 after the Department of Homeland Security moved to step up deportations of migrants who cannot be returned to any country listed on their deportation orders.

The policy provided that migrants could be swiftly removed without notice to third countries that have provided credible diplomatic assurance that they will not persecute or torture the individuals. For countries that have not provided such assurance, deportees would be notified of their destination and US authorities would assess the likelihood of persecution or torture only if the individual raises such fear on their own.

In its emergency filing to the Supreme Court, the Justice Department said third-country deportations are "an essential tool to remove certain aliens, including some of the worst criminal aliens."

But both Murphy and critics of the administration said the policy is also targeting migrants who had been granted legal protection from being sent back to their home countries.

Deportees see sexual assault, unlawful transference, plaintiffs say

The policy has resulted in deportees being unlawfully transferred by third countries back to their home countries from which the US had already granted them protection, while others have been beaten, sexually assaulted, detained, or have disappeared, the plaintiffs said in a court filing.

The administration is ignoring "the significant harm resulting from deporting thousands of longtime US residents, many with no criminal history, to third countries without regard to the persecution or torture they face there," the plaintiffs said.

The Boston-based 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals upheld most of the judge's ruling on September 18.

The case has been hotly contested since it began, and included findings by Murphy that the administration "repeatedly violated, or attempted to violate" his orders. Murphy in 2025 found that the administration had violated another order he issued requiring additional steps before attempting to send a group of migrants to South Sudan.

text:
Management & Training Corporation, a Utah-based private prison firm, has signed a contract with Immigration and Customs Enforcement to operate a detention facility in Marana, according to a statement from the company on Wednesday afternoon.

The contract was signed on Sept. 29, 2026. MTC said it anticipates the facility will begin operating within two months. The statement described a facility with a 775-bed capacity and a staff of about 338 full-time employees.

In July 2025, MTC purchased the land parcel — a shuttered prison once operated by the same firm — from the Arizona Department of Administration. The purchase, along with murmurs of an imminent detention center, has drawn scrutiny and ire among residents and immigrant rights advocates, who have pointed to concerns over human rights and rising death rates in ICE detention facilities.

In February 2026, the Department of Homeland Security published a performance work statement on a federal database, outlining a potential agreement between ICE and MTC.

But for months, a contract was not signed. As recently as mid-September, AZPM inquired about the contract’s status.

“We don’t have any updates to provide at this time,” a company spokesperson said in a Sept. 17 email.

As the contract appeared dormant in the public eye, members of Pima Resist ICE (PRICE) said they observed regular activity at the site, such as “trucks that work for plumbing companies and just general contractors,” PRICE member Bennett Burke told AZPM.

“We don't have any official notice of anything, but the work is happening,” Burke said earlier this month. “So we know that they're proceeding with getting the facility ready.”

For months, PRICE has pushed back against the planned detention center, often urging the Marana Town Council to take the same stance. The council has repeatedly declined to pass a resolution opposing the facility.

“We aren’t done fighting this thing. Not by a long shot,” said Kristin Downing, another member of PRICE, in a statement Wednesday. “We have been talking with legal experts, doing research, building alliances, and exploring creative ways to make sure this camp never opens. We care too much about our community to just give up.”

The details of the contract remain unclear. The document did not appear in a public database of federal contracts during several searches Wednesday afternoon.

A years-long history in Arizona

Management & Training Corporation, or MTC, has a years-long history in Arizona.

The site of the detention center — an expanse of land near the Marana Regional Airport — was once a private prison operated by MTC through a contract with Arizona’s Department of Corrections.

The minimum security prison held approximately 500 male inmates. At the end of 2023, Gov. Katie Hobbs ended the state’s contract with MTC, citing financial reasons. That decision shuttered the facility.

In its statement announcing the new contract Wednesday, MTC cited its nearly 30-year history in Marana, adding that the company would focus on “operating the facility safely and professionally, meeting and exceeding ICE’s National Detention Standards (NDS), and providing compassionate care to the people entrusted to us.”

The firm, however, has received criticism in past years — including a state-led review under Republican leadership.

In 2015, Republican Gov. Doug Ducey terminated a separate agreement with MTC after riots broke out in a Kingman prison operated by the firm. A state review reported that the prison was understaffed, that inmates held hunger strikes and that employees were “poorly paid,” NPR and KJZZ reported at the time.

A recent investigation from The Intercept and LOOKOUT News reported that when MTC operated the Marana prison in 2022, the company failed to report sexual assault allegations.

Note: This story has been updated to include comments from PRICE. This is a developing story and will be updated as new information becomes available.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Representative Lou Correa (CA-46) today led 56 colleagues in demanding the Trump Administration guarantee quality legal services and humane treatment for unaccompanied immigrant children in a letter to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., and Attorney General Todd Blanche.

The letter follows reports of children as young as two years old showing up in immigration courts nationwide for fast-tracked hearings, many without an attorney. This change has been part of the Trump Administration’s cruel efforts to target immigrant children for removal and deny them legal immigration pathways.

“We write to demand answers regarding the fairness of the legal process and the quality of representation being provided to unaccompanied children under the new legal services contracts for Our Rescue and the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants (USCRI). Congress has shown clear intent through bipartisan passage of the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization that children deserve representation in legal proceedings. However, we have received reports that unaccompanied children are being provided with inadequate representation and that their cases are being moved into expedited judicial proceedings meant to limit the strength of their legal defense and increase deportations. We urge you to follow the law and give children the fair day in court they deserve by ensuring legal service providers do not just collect a paycheck, but vigorously represent those they are paid taxpayer dollars to serve, and that courts give adequate consideration to each child’s case,” the lawmakers write.

“Unaccompanied immigrant children are receiving substandard legal services at a time when the Trump Administration is already trying to prevent a fair hearing of their cases. The Department of Justice (DOJ) Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) has reportedly directed immigration judges to limit the length of continuances from months to three weeks, reducing the time children have to find an attorney and prepare for their case. In some jurisdictions, children are given only days of notice to appear in immigration court, which directly violates EOIR policy,” the lawmakers continued. “Judges who attempt to give more time in proceedings are reportedly at risk of being punished. While children are being given less time to prepare for proceedings, the Administration is training immigration judges to deny asylum claims, further stacking the odds against these kids, some of whom have been abused or abandoned and are survivors of violent crime.”

“Reports of inadequate representation and EOIR’s efforts to prevent children from having their case fully considered are unacceptable. We urge you to end the prolonged detention of children, give them adequate time to prepare their cases, stop pressuring judges to deny claims, and conduct oversight to ensure new legal services providers effectively represent their clients in exchange for our tax dollars,” the lawmakers concluded.

Specifically, the lawmakers requested answers to the following questions:

Has the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) or DOJ conducted oversight into the legal services that USCRI is providing for unaccompanied children? If so, has HHS or DOJ found any instances where legal representatives represented children virtually with cameras off or failed to speak during proceedings?

For each month of 2026, how many times have unaccompanied children appeared in immigration court without legal counsel?

Do Our Rescue and the USCRI have sufficient lawyers on staff who are barred in all states and can make filings for all unaccompanied children to whom they will be responsible for providing legal services?

In 2026, how many times has EOIR summoned a child to immigration court without giving the 10 days of notice required for immigration court appearances?

Have immigration judges been given any guidance since January 20, 2025, directing them to deny or change the way they review any type of petition, application, motion, or other filing or request for unaccompanied children? If so, please provide a record of this instruction.

Is there any policy, formal or informal, requiring or encouraging the conclusion of unaccompanied children's immigration proceedings by a certain date or timeframe? If so, please provide a copy of said policy.

In 2026, have any judges within EOIR been reprimanded, warned, or faced a consequence or warning of consequences for allotting children additional time in their legal proceedings?

This letter was signed by Representatives Yassamin Ansari, Becca Balint, Nanette Barragán, Suzanne Bonamici, Janelle Bynum, André Carson, Greg Casar, Joaquin Castro, Judy Chu, Gilbert Cisneros, Yvette Clarke, Jim Costa, Jasmine Crockett, Jason Crow, Madeleine Dean, Diana DeGette, Mark DeSaulnier, Maxine Dexter, Veronica Escobar, Lizzie Fletcher, Maxwell Frost, Robert Garcia, Sylvia Garcia, Daniel Goldman, Adelita Grijalva, Steven Horsford, Jonathan Jackson, Henry Johnson, Raja Krishnamoorthi, George Latimer, Zoe Lofgren, Stephen Lynch, Jennifer McClellan, Gwen Moore, Jerrold Nadler, Joe Neguse, Eleanor Norton, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Brittany Pettersen, Mark Pocan, Mike Quigley, Delia Ramirez, Emily Randall, Luz Rivas, Andrea Salinas, Mary Gay Scanlon, Janice Schakowsky, Lateefah Simon, Melanie Stansbury, Greg Stanton, Mark Takano, Rashida Tlaib, Norma Torres, Juan Vargas, Debbie Wasserman Schultz, and Frederica Wilson.

text:
A United States immigration judge has ruled the leader of Wisconsin’s largest mosque can be deported under a controversial law that United States President Donald Trump’s administration has used against non-citizens advocating for Palestinian rights.

Judge Jayme Salinardi ruled on Wednesday that Palestinian-born Salah Sarsour, president of the Islamic Society of Milwaukee, can be removed from the US based in part on a memo by Secretary of State Marco Rubio that “his actions undermine US foreign policy to combat antisemitism around the world”, according to his lawyers.

Recommended Stories

list of 4 items

list 1 of 4Trump admin asks top US court to reverse pro-Palestinian scholar’s release

list 2 of 4Palestinian Americans meet US lawmakers as Trump seeks $2.8bn for Israel

list 3 of 4US judge orders release of Palestinian rights advocate detained by ICE

list 4 of 4Rights groups, Milwaukee leaders slam ICE’s arrest of Palestinian advocate

end of list

Sarsour, who has lived in the US for more than three decades, called the ruling “deeply disappointing”.

“I will continue fighting to defend the right to free speech and to stay in the country I have called home for more than three decades,” he told The Associated Press news agency.

His lawyer, Patrick Taurel, strongly rejected the decision.

“I wish the world could see the evidence that we presented and hear the testimony that the court heard because the case we presented compels only one conclusion, which is that Salah is not deportable,” Taurel told reporters on Wednesday.

“He’s done nothing wrong. He should be given back his green card, frankly, with an apology for what’s being done to him.”

The ruling does not mean Sarsour will be immediately deported.

His lawyers have 60 days to argue that sending Sarsour back would put him at risk of torture, which could protect him from deportation under the Convention Against Torture. If they lose, they plan to appeal. Taurel said he can’t be deported while that appeal is pending and will remain in the US for the “foreseeable future”.

‘Extreme deference’

Sarsour was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in Milwaukee in March, nine months after Rubio issued a memo declaring him deportable on foreign policy grounds.

The June 2025 memo invoked a rarely-used US law that allows the Secretary of State to seek the deportation of non-citizens whose presence could have “potentially serious adverse foreign policy consequences.” The administration has used the same provision against pro-Palestinian activists Mahmoud Khalil and Mohsen Mahdawi.

Sarsour’s lawyers criticised the “extreme deference” Salinardi gave to Rubio’s memo. But Taurel said the judge believed his hands were tied by an earlier ruling in Khalil’s case, which found that a letter from the Secretary of State could be enough to make someone deportable on foreign policy grounds.

That meant Salinardi could not look behind Rubio’s decision to examine the evidence supporting it, Taurel said.

“If the Secretary of State says the person is deportable, it is game over,” he told reporters Wednesday.

The government did not win on all of its arguments.

Salinardi rejected its allegation that Sarsour had lied on his green card application. Taurel said the judge also rejected an allegation that Sarsour had falsely claimed to be a US citizen in order to vote.

Al Jazeera reached out to the State Department and the Department of Homeland Security but did not receive responses by the time of publication.

Decades-old convictions

Sarsour is separately fighting the Trump administration in federal court over his detention while his deportation case is ongoing.

A federal judge ordered his release from ICE custody in June after 81 days, questioning why decades-old convictions that US authorities had long known about suddenly justified detaining him. The judge found there was a “substantial” case that the government was retaliating against him for speaking out about Palestinian rights.

The Trump administration has appealed his release, arguing that Sarsour’s convictions in Israel make him a security threat. He was imprisoned in 1988 after confessing to throwing stones and a Molotov cocktail at Israeli military personnel, and was convicted again in 1995 over an attempt to hold weapons.

Sarsour denies the offences, and his lawyers say the confessions were forced through torture. His former lawyer, Jawad Boulos, testified in August that Sarsour was coerced into signing confessions and was not convicted of an offence tying him to a “terrorist” organisation.

Taurel criticised Salinardi for giving what he called “extreme deference” to Israeli government records submitted by ICE, which Sarsour’s lawyers argue were incomplete and relied on confessions obtained through torture.

“A great deal of evidence we presented was ignored,” Taurel said.

The evidence challenged Israel’s military court system, where he said secret evidence can be used and Palestinians can be denied access to lawyers for extended periods.

Luna Droubi, an attorney representing Sarsour, said the case raises broader questions about whether immigrants can speak freely on political issues without fear of being targeted by the government.

“Why raise these arrests now?” she said. “Do I have the right to speak out about issues that matter to me? What if I draw a political cartoon? Am I going to be arrested and detained because of that?”

‘The end of my life’

Sarsour said being deported to the occupied West Bank “means the end of my life”.

His lawyers argue his prior treatment in Israeli custody shows he could face torture if sent back. Taurel said Sarsour’s former lawyer testified that his case stood out because Sarsour told him that Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency, had taken him to hospital while in custody.

The judge also named Jordan as a possible destination. Sarsour travelled to the US on a Jordanian-issued document, but his lawyers say he is not a Jordanian citizen and has no right to live there. They believe he could ultimately be returned to the West Bank and Israeli custody if sent to Jordan.

title: Trapped on violent deportation flight - LA Times e-newspaper
description: On a tarmac in Texas, federal agents repeatedly ordered a group of shackled immigrants off a bus and onto an airplane that they had heard was ...
text:
On a tarmac in Texas, federal agents repeatedly ordered a group of shackled immigrants off a bus and onto an airplane that they had heard was destined for Africa.

Many complied, but some men refused. They had sought protection in the U.S. after fleeing repressive governments and asked to speak to lawyers before being deported to a faraway continent.

“Tell us where you’re taking us,” Kenis Adalberto López, a 44-year-old from Nicaragua, said he told immigration agents through tears. “I’d rather die here than in Africa.”

Eventually, an agent boarded the bus and fired pepper balls at the men, according to interviews with three of them. López, who was hit twice in the chest with projectiles, said he was strapped to a stretcher and carried onto the plane, where he was restrained for the roughly 24-hour journey to Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic.

More than 25,000 people have been expelled from the U.S. under a Trump administration program to deport asylum seekers and other migrants to “third countries” where they have no ties.

A federal appeals court ordered a pause on the program last week, saying the government failed to give migrants “a meaningful opportunity” to challenge their deportations to third countries. The Trump administration vowed to take the case to the Supreme Court, with Atty. Gen. Todd Blanche describing the program as “an entirely legal and invaluable tool to stem the tide of illegal immigration.”

The administration has routinely said that its enforcement operations are carried out in compliance with federal law and that detainees are treated humanely.

The Aug. 29 deportation of López and 42 others to Bangui highlights the sometimes violent tactics that officials have used to force detainees onto flights out of the U.S. — and the perils that await them once they land.

López and others recounted their journey in phone interviews from Africa.

The plane carried migrants from several countries, including Iran, Bangladesh and Afghanistan. Human rights lawyers say that many of them, including an Afghan man whose brothers worked with the U.S. military, had no criminal records and had been granted a special protection that barred them from being returned to their home countries because they had proved to a judge that they faced possible torture there.

Two of the men who resisted boarding the plane were kept in full-body restraint suits resembling straitjackets for much of the flight, according to witnesses.

All of the deportees were shackled at the ankles and wrists while in the air.

After stops in two other African countries, the plane touched down in the Central African Republic, one of the world’s poorest nations and the site of an ongoing civil war between Muslim and Christian rebels that has claimed tens of thousands of lives over the last 15 years. The primary languages are Sango and French.

The migrants were given shots for yellow fever and taken to a housing complex, where they remain today, monitored at all times by armed guards.

Bangui, which sits across a wide river from the Democratic Republic of Congo, is battling a recent cholera outbreak and faces water shortages and power outages.

Crime is rampant, with the U.S. government itself warning Americans not to visit the Central African Republic because of “unrest, crime, kidnapping, landmines, health issues and terrorism.”

Three flights carrying U.S. deportees have arrived there since June, according to human rights groups tracking the issue. Many complain that U.S. immigration agents confiscated their identity documents upon detention and never returned them, making it all but impossible to leave the country. Their immigration status in the Central African Republic is unclear.

Two men who arrived on a July 31 flight recounted being kidnapped on the street by armed men who they believe were police officers.

Yasmani Moreno said he and the other detainee each had to pay the equivalent of $100 to be released.

Moreno, 31, who arrived in Florida on a raft from Cuba in 2016, was initially allowed to stay in the U.S. under the “wet foot, dry foot” policy, which until 2017 let Cubans who reached U.S. soil remain in the country. His temporary permit expired before he obtained a green card.

He has documented his time in Africa extensively on TikTok, taking his followers for walks along Bangui’s muddy streets. “They sent me to a failed state,” he said in an interview.

After decades of coups and strife, government forces have sought to disband many militia groups there, sometimes with the help of mercenaries with the Wagner Group, a Russia-based military contractor accused of human rights abuses. International experts have denounced President Faustin-Archange Touadera’s repression of the opposition and push to eliminate term limits as worrisome turns toward autocracy.

For deportees who came to the U.S. after fleeing authoritarian countries, an unknown future in another undemocratic nation is frightening.

Luis Hernández, 38, escaped Nicaragua after he marched in 2018 pro-democracy protests that were violently suppressed by the left-wing Sandinista government. He asked for political asylum at the U.S. border. A judge denied his request but granted him protection from deportation under the international Convention Against Torture. For years, he led a quiet life working as a waiter in hotels in Washington, D.C.

In the past, people with such protection were generally allowed to stay and work in the U.S. indefinitely.

But in February, Hernández went to a regular immigration check-in and was detained. He was held in jails across the U.S., he said, until he was taken by bus to the tarmac in Texas on Aug. 28.

President Trump, in his push to expel 1 million people annually, has vastly expanded the pool of migrants eligible for deportation, with asylum seekers and people who a judge said may be tortured upon return now making up a growing share of detainees.

The U.S. has earmarked around half a billion dollars in aid to third countries who agree to take deportees, according to an investigation by the nonprofit journalism consortium Forbidden Stories, which found that in some cases, deportees sent to third countries were later returned against their will to their home nations.

“This is a deliberate attempt by the Trump administration to place refugees whom the U.S. government has determined need protection directly in harm’s way,” said Savi Arvey, director of policy for refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First.

Hernández said he was never notified that he was going to be sent to Africa — but that he and fellow deportees had heard rumors about flights there and suspected their fate when they saw the size of the plane they were being ordered to board. He said he was struck twice in the back and once in the knee with canisters containing pepper spray after he resisted boarding; pains from the blows persist.

After arriving in Bangui, he said, he went days without eating and sleeping, and suffered what he described as a mental breakdown.

“This is inhuman,” he said. “It’s psychological violence.”

He is worried in particular about ties between the Central African Republic and Russia, which is an ally of Nicaragua’s Sandinista government.

Sandinista operatives are suspected in a series of shootings, abductions and killings of Nicaraguan exiles in Costa Rica in recent years. Hernández wonders whether he is safe.

He has been following the news in the U.S. — including the recent appeals court ruling against the third country deportation program. His lawyer has urged him to look for another country that might grant him political asylum, but Hernández still holds out hope that the U.S. will welcome him back.

“There will be justice,” he said. “There’s still a democracy there.”

text:
Human rights advocates asked a United Nations panel to intervene Wednesday to help end a new U.S. government practice of withholding from families and lawyers the whereabouts of thousands of detainees facing deportation.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement removed the names of detainees with final removal orders from its Online Detainee Locator System on Sept. 15 in an apparent effort to speed up their deportations. The change, which ICE did not announce and has not explained, applies to more than 16,000 of the nearly 69,000 detainees who are in ICE custody.

The move has interfered with detainees' ability to challenge looming deportations by impeding access to their lawyers while devastating families who lost track of their loved ones, immigration lawyers say.

A coalition of more than 30 groups who advocate for noncitizens in the U.S. petitioned the U.N.’s Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances to declare the policy a violation of international law and to push for its end.

“A system with no transparency is a system with no accountability, and that should terrify all of us,” said Sarah Decker, an attorney at the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, one of the petition's signatories. “Disappearing people into a network of remote detention sites, hiding their whereabouts, and cutting off their access to outside help is the definition of an enforced disappearance."

Separately, on Wednesday, more than 45 House Democrats led by Reps. Luz Rivas and Veronica Escobar urged ICE to restore the names to the locator, calling the practice of concealing them “contrary to foundational principles of the American legal system.”

ICE's parent agency denied Wednesday that its practices amount to disappearing people, saying all detainees “have opportunities to communicate with their family members and lawyers.”

“The appropriate process due to an illegal alien with final deportation orders is removal, plain and simple,” the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement. “That said, DHS has a stringent law enforcement assessment in place that abides by due process under the U.S. Constitution.”

Detainees can typically call relatives if they have money in their commissary accounts, while calls to their legal representatives are supposed to be free.

Approximately 1.4 million people living in the U.S. are subject to final orders of removal. That typically means an immigration judge has ruled they should be deported and the decision has been upheld on appeal or not appealed. They still have several legal options to challenge their detention and deportation. Federal judges have ruled thousands of times that detainees should be released or granted bond hearings.

The petition to the U.N. said the policy has already “obstructed legal counsel from accessing their clients in detention, preventing interventions to seek immigration relief, challenge unconstitutional detention, and block unlawful deportations.”

It cited examples of several detainees, including a mother and 7-year-old daughter who were challenging their detention at a Texas facility but lost access to their lawyers as they faced deportation to Venezuela. Only after a judge ordered ICE to disclose their whereabouts did the agency do so, about 18 hours later, and release them from custody, the petition said.

One man reported intense stress and that the “darkest thoughts imaginable went through" his mind after the whereabouts of his elderly disabled mother were abruptly removed from the system, according to the petition.

The petition said ICE's online locator, launched in 2010, has become “an even more crucial tool” as President Donald Trump's administration has carried out a sweeping campaign to arrest and deport people who are in the country illegally. It noted that the U.N. working group had lobbied for the locator’s creation and its 2024 expansion to include people detained by the Border Patrol.

The petition asked the U.N. group to urge ICE to publicly list all detainees’ locations within an hour of their arrest and give detainees’ lawyers 24 hours’ notice before a transfer. The U.N. group, which was formed in 1980, helps families locate loved ones who have reportedly been subjected to enforced disappearance by government agents. It has five members and is currently chaired by Grazyna Baranowska of Poland.

title: Attorney General Ellison statement on DOJ complaint against Minnesota federal judges
description:
Today, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche announced that the Department of Justice has filed a judicial misconduct complaint against nearly all federal district judges in Minnesota.
This is a desperate and dangerous attack on American judicial independence.
Instead, over the past two years, federal officials have taken to social media to berate judges in Minnesota and around the country who have ruled against them.
Today’s attempt to disqualify nearly all of Minnesota’s active federal judges — all of whom observe the highest ethical standards — is a dramatic and dangerous escalation of the Trump Administration’s attacks on America’s judiciary.
Attacks on judicial independence are attacks on the rule of law, our democracy, and the people who safeguard it.
text:
Today, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche announced that the Department of Justice has filed a judicial misconduct complaint against nearly all federal district judges in Minnesota. This is a desperate and dangerous attack on American judicial independence.

The complaint is a direct attempt by the Trump administration to intimidate judges who have ruled against them in the past and an attempt to intimidate every judge against ruling against them in the future.

Our nation’s founders knew that an independent judiciary, free from political influence, coercion, or threats is an important bulwark against tyranny. It’s how they designed our Constitution. An independent judiciary remains a bedrock principle of our democracy today.

This complaint has nothing to do with judicial ethics and everything to do with political punishment. Blanche and Trump are trying to punish the judges who ruled against federal government actions during Operation Metro Surge — including the Administration’s undisputed non-compliance at the time with hundreds of court orders — even though sometimes the court ruled with the government. Remember that Trump promised a campaign of “reckoning and retribution” against Minnesotans during Metro Surge: federal agents terrorized, hurt, and killed Minnesotans and are still standing in the way of justice for the victims. Today’s complaint is more evidence Trump won’t let go of his campaign against Minnesota.

Intimidation and bullying are right out of the authoritarian playbook. Trump and his allies have bullied immigrants, refugees, and the trans community, and now they’re turning their attacks toward a co-equal branch of government.

text:
WASHINGTON: Human rights advocates asked a United Nations panel to intervene Wednesday to help end a new US government practice of withholding from families and lawyers the whereabouts of thousands of detainees facing deportation.

US Immigration and Customs Enforcement removed the names of detainees with final removal orders from its Online Detainee Locator System on Sept. 15 in an apparent effort to speed up their deportations. The change, which ICE did not announce and has not explained, applies to more than 16,000 of the nearly 69,000 detainees who are in ICE custody.

The move has interfered with detainees’ ability to challenge looming deportations by impeding access to their lawyers while devastating families who lost track of their loved ones, immigration lawyers say.

A coalition of more than 30 groups who advocate for noncitizens in the US petitioned the UN’s Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances to declare the policy a violation of international law and to push for its end.

“A system with no transparency is a system with no accountability, and that should terrify all of us,” said Sarah Decker, an attorney at the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, one of the petition’s signatories. “Disappearing people into a network of remote detention sites, hiding their whereabouts, and cutting off their access to outside help is the definition of an enforced disappearance.”

Separately, on Wednesday, more than 45 House Democrats led by Reps. Luz Rivas and Veronica Escobar urged ICE to restore the names to the locator, calling the practice of concealing them “contrary to foundational principles of the American legal system.”

ICE’s parent agency denied Wednesday that its practices amount to disappearing people, saying all detainees “have opportunities to communicate with their family members and lawyers.”

“The appropriate process due to an illegal alien with final deportation orders is removal, plain and simple,” the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement. “That said, DHS has a stringent law enforcement assessment in place that abides by due process under the US Constitution.”

Detainees can typically call relatives if they have money in their commissary accounts, while calls to their legal representatives are supposed to be free.

Approximately 1.4 million people living in the US are subject to final orders of removal. That typically means an immigration judge has ruled they should be deported and the decision has been upheld on appeal or not appealed. They still have several legal options to challenge their detention and deportation. Federal judges have ruled thousands of times that detainees should be released or granted bond hearings.

The petition to the UN said the policy has already “obstructed legal counsel from accessing their clients in detention, preventing interventions to seek immigration relief, challenge unconstitutional detention, and block unlawful deportations.”

It cited examples of several detainees, including a mother and 7-year-old daughter who were challenging their detention at a Texas facility but lost access to their lawyers as they faced deportation to Venezuela. Only after a judge ordered ICE to disclose their whereabouts did the agency do so, about 18 hours later, and release them from custody, the petition said.

One man reported intense stress and that the “darkest thoughts imaginable went through” his mind after the whereabouts of his elderly disabled mother were abruptly removed from the system, according to the petition.

The petition said ICE’s online locator, launched in 2010, has become “an even more crucial tool” as President Donald Trump’s administration has carried out a sweeping campaign to arrest and deport people who are in the country illegally. It noted that the UN working group had lobbied for the locator’s creation and its 2024 expansion to include people detained by the Border Patrol.

The petition asked the UN group to urge ICE to publicly list all detainees’ locations within an hour of their arrest and give detainees’ lawyers 24 hours’ notice before a transfer. The UN group, which was formed in 1980, helps families locate loved ones who have reportedly been subjected to enforced disappearance by government agents. It has five members and is currently chaired by Grazyna Baranowska of Poland.

text:
AUSTIN (KXAN) — The man shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in Austin on Sept. 20 will remain in custody after appearing in a federal courtroom Wednesday afternoon.

Wilber Rafael Garces Perez faces one criminal charge in connection to that shooting — assaulting, resisting, and impeding a federal officer. His attorney in the criminal case has declined to comment.

During Wednesday’s federal court hearing, a judge said Garces Perez will remain detained because he is a flight risk and not because he is a danger to the community.

The criminal hearing delays Garces Perez’s immigration hearing, which was also scheduled for Wednesday afternoon.

“This case today is not an isolated case,” Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, Garces Perez’ immigration attorney, said after the hearing. She pointed to other cases involving ICE in which the same federal criminal charge was applied and called it a “tool of retaliation.”

“I will say that this is a particular charge that is often used against protesters and resisters against the government,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said in a social media post earlier in the day.

During her remarks after the hearing, Lincoln-Goldfinch also repeated concerns about Garces Perez’ medical treatment and called for his release from detention. Garces Perez entered court Wednesday in a wheelchair, his left arm in a sling, according to a KXAN investigative reporter in the courtroom.

His immigration attorney did not answer questions from reporters.

title: How ICE crackdowns on African immigrants in NYC are leaving families in fear, and tears
description:
What’s ICE doing with immigrants on the third floor of 26 Federal Plaza?
Legal counselors representing immigrants told amNewYork that respondents are still attending their legally mandated court hearings on the 12th and 14th floors.
The third floor of 26 Federal Plaza is made up of offices belonging to several different agencies and rooms that have been transformed into makeshift courtrooms.
“What we are seeing in this administration is pure cruelty.” The emotional impact of detentions at Federal Plaza was again on full display outside the facility Wednesday.
Nearby, several African women — who also had been the subjects of ICE detention — welled up with tears as they looked on.
text:
According to immigrants who are the subjects of the Trump Administration’s latest rollout of ICE enforcement, and advocacy groups who are working to defend them, federal immigration agents have stepped up their detainment of those who hail from across West Africa.

Public Advocate Jumaane Williams deemed the crackdown racist.

“They told everybody about the worst of the worst; they told everybody it was just about legal versus illegal. They are now doing everything they can to change people’s legal status to not being here legally,” Williams said. “President Trump and his MAGA leaders seem to want to remove all Black and Brown people from this nation, and today he’s targeting Africans, particularly from West Africa.”

This comes as the Supreme Court said it is allowing the United States to deport detainees to Africa and what they described as “third-world countries,” even if the person they are deporting does not hail from those nations.

And while the uptick in federal activity has been felt on the streets across the five boroughs, arrests are still being made inside New York’s immigration court, according to those with knowledge of the situation.

What’s ICE doing with immigrants on the third floor of 26 Federal Plaza?

Legal counselors representing immigrants told amNewYork that respondents are still attending their legally mandated court hearings on the 12th and 14th floors. However, some immigrants who come to 26 Federal Plaza to answer court mandates for appearances are nonetheless sent to the facility’s third floor, where they are detained out of sight of any observers.

The third floor of 26 Federal Plaza is made up of offices belonging to several different agencies and rooms that have been transformed into makeshift courtrooms. What specifically happens on the floor, however, is not always known to those representing immigrants.

Williams himself attempted to gain access to the floor and was met with immediate resistance by the onsite security staff. They prevented him from walking through hallways, even though it is considered public space.

After a standoff for several minutes, a supervisor allowed Williams to inspect the hallways, provided he did not enter agency space.

“We actually made it to the third floor as well, which people haven’t been able to get access to. So, at first they said no, and then they allowed us in. We’re not sure why, but the cases that were being heard normally on the third floor were changed to another floor, but we were able to explore and see what’s there,” Williams said.

Meanwhile, the 12th floor saw an overflow of immigrants in what has become known as mega master hearings, with 100 or more unrepresented people together to speed up deportation cases. Families could be observed packed together in a room that did not have a physical judge present; instead, he appeared on a TV screen from Florida.

Many of those who attended ICE check-in on the first floor and the hearings on Sept. 30 were people of color with ties to Africa.

“There are too many people in there,” a security guard scoffed as he pushed his way through the huddled mass.

For Amadou Ly, a Senegal native who has faced deportation himself, the conditions at Federal Plaza and treatment of immigrants by the Trump White House are cruel — and that seems to be the point.

“We’re dealing with massive abuse, racism coming from this administration, unfair treatments, not even the most decent treatment of human beings. What we are seeing in this administration is pure cruelty,” Amadou Ly said, a Senegal native who has faced deportation himself. “What we are seeing in this administration is pure cruelty.”

The emotional impact of detentions at Federal Plaza was again on full display outside the facility Wednesday.

Tears for detained and deported mother

A young woman who only identified herself only as Madeline wept profusely as she shared that her mother, who was born in Gambia, was detained at a check-in on Sept. 22 after being in the country for more than two decades. Tears fell down her cheeks as she recalled arriving at the courthouse with her mother at just before 6 a.m. that day, then waited for hours.

“At around 12:30 she called me and told me that she would be staying in ICE detention, and that they will be sending her to Ghana. I never imagined to get back on the 5 train without my mother,” Madeline said. “During that time, she barely slept, she barely ate.”

As Madeline recounted her traumatic experience, her father also broke down and bawled uncontrollably — holding his face in his hands. Nearby, several African women — who also had been the subjects of ICE detention — welled up with tears as they looked on.

“She would describe that she would be shackled at her hands and her feet, like she was a criminal, and my mom’s been here for 23 years. She’s never done a single terrible, bad thing, and she has to be treated like she was a criminal,” Madeline added. “We’re gonna do everything we can to bring her back home with us.”
