title: Nurse charged with helping man in hospital escape from ICE custody - The Guardian
description:
An FBI agent’s declaration submitted in a federal court accuses Chloe Renae Freeman, 33, of “instigating or assisting escape”, a federal misdemeanor, by helping a patient leave an Ann Arbor hospital while in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody in May.
Freeman had voluntarily surrendered to the authorities and had her first hearing in federal court on Tuesday.
On 28 May, border patrol encountered an undocumented Mexican man in Ann Arbor during a “targeted immigration enforcement operation”, the FBI complaint says.
While at Trinity Health Ann Arbor hospital, where Freeman worked, medical staff noticed in his paperwork he was in ICE custody.
“Law enforcement have been unable to locate OBP since his escape from Trinity Health Ann Arbor Hospital,” the document adds.
text:
The federal government is charging a Michigan nurse accused of illegally helping an undocumented immigrant, who was being treated in a hospital, escape from immigration officials, court records unsealed this week show.

An FBI agent’s declaration submitted in a federal court accuses Chloe Renae Freeman, 33, of “instigating or assisting escape”, a federal misdemeanor, by helping a patient leave an Ann Arbor hospital while in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody in May. The patient, an undocumented immigrant from Mexico, had been arrested about two hours earlier by Customs and Border Protection (CBP) border patrol agents.

Freeman, who worked at the hospital at the time, told hospital investigators she did not agree with federal immigration officials “separating people from their families” and that she “was going to set him free”, the FBI complaint says. The undocumented man had still not been caught by the time she was charged in August.

This is one of the latest examples of people facing charges for anti-ICE actions, as the agency and its aggressive anti-immigrant crackdown grow widely unpopular.

In some cases, charges against protesters and anti-ICE advocates have fallen apart under scrutiny. But in others, the Trump administration has been successful in prosecuting activists.

Freeman had voluntarily surrendered to the authorities and had her first hearing in federal court on Tuesday. She was released on a $10,000 bond. Attorneys representing Freeman told the Guardian they were not making any public statements at the time.

On 28 May, border patrol encountered an undocumented Mexican man in Ann Arbor during a “targeted immigration enforcement operation”, the FBI complaint says. The man, identified only as “OBP” in the court records, had been previously removed from the US in 2022 and appears to have re-entered the country without permission, according to the authorities, which is a federal infraction.

When agents attempted to arrest OBP, he took off running, tripped over a curb and hit his face on the pavement, the complaint says. Agents arrested OBP, noticed his injuries and called for an ambulance. EMS workers recommended he be taken to a hospital to treat his injuries.

While at Trinity Health Ann Arbor hospital, where Freeman worked, medical staff noticed in his paperwork he was in ICE custody. They took him to receive a CT scan for his injuries. After the CT scan, the FBI said Freeman entered the CT scan room, removed the patient’s intravenous drip and guided him to the ambulance entrance, from which he fled.

An image included in the court records shows security camera images of OBP leaving through the ambulance bay doors, with a bandaged and bloody face.

The FBI says Freeman’s actions were “knowingly and willfully” taken to help OBP in “escaping the hospital without permission or authority”, the court document says.

“Law enforcement have been unable to locate OBP since his escape from Trinity Health Ann Arbor Hospital,” the document adds.

In June, hospital investigators interviewed Freeman, who admitted to letting OBP leave the hospital. She told the investigators that she did not believe in ICE “separating people from their families” and admitted that, due to his injuries, he “could have died”, the FBI complaint says.

It is unclear if the hospital investigators approached the FBI with their evidence or the extent of the collaboration between the two.

In a statement to Reuters, Trinity ​Health said ⁠Freeman no longer worked for the hospital. Trinity Health did not respond to a request from the Guardian about the extent of its work with the FBI in this case.

Separately, on Wednesday, more than 45 House Democrats led by Reps. Luz Rivas and Veronica Escobar urged ICE to restore the names to the locator, calling the practice of concealing them “contrary to foundational principles of the American legal system.”

ICE’s parent agency denied Wednesday that its practices amount to disappearing people, saying all detainees “have opportunities to communicate with their family members and lawyers.”

“The appropriate process due to an illegal alien with final deportation orders is removal, plain and simple,” the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement. “That said, DHS has a stringent law enforcement assessment in place that abides by due process under the U.S. Constitution.”

Detainees can typically call relatives if they have money in their commissary accounts, while calls to their legal representatives are supposed to be free.

Approximately 1.4 million people living in the U.S. are subject to final orders of removal. That typically means an immigration judge has ruled they should be deported and the decision has been upheld on appeal or not appealed. They still have several legal options to challenge their detention and deportation. Federal judges have ruled thousands of times that detainees should be released or granted bond hearings.

It cited examples of several detainees, including a mother and 7-year-old daughter who were challenging their detention at a Texas facility but lost access to their lawyers as they faced deportation to Venezuela. Only after a judge ordered ICE to disclose their whereabouts did the agency do so, about 18 hours later, and release them from custody, the petition said.

One man reported intense stress and that the “darkest thoughts imaginable went through” his mind after the whereabouts of his elderly disabled mother were abruptly removed from the system, according to the petition.

The petition said ICE’s online locator, launched in 2010, has become “an even more crucial tool” as President Donald Trump’s administration has carried out a sweeping campaign to arrest and deport people who are in the country illegally. It noted that the U.N. working group had lobbied for the locator’s creation and its 2024 expansion to include people detained by the Border Patrol.

The petition asked the U.N. group to urge ICE to publicly list all detainees’ locations within an hour of their arrest and give detainees’ lawyers 24 hours’ notice before a transfer. The U.N. group, which was formed in 1980, helps families locate loved ones who have reportedly been subjected to enforced disappearance by government agents. It has five members and is currently chaired by Grazyna Baranowska of Poland.

title: Venezuelan man shot by ICE in Texas charged in federal court - NewsNation
description:
Wilber Garces Perez was charged in federal court and faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted.
The criminal complaint alleges Garces Perez was pulled over by ICE officers and provided them with his driver’s license.
Garces Perez is accused of attempting to hit an ICE officer with his vehicle, which led the officer to fire his gun.
He said that an ICE officer approached his window and that he provided the officer with his driver’s license.
The ICE officer who shot Garces Perez has not been publicly identified but has been placed on administrative leave per ICE policy.
text:
(NewsNation) — The Venezuelan man who was shot by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers in Texas this month has been charged with resisting and interfering with a federal law enforcement officer, the Department of Justice announced Tuesday.

Wilber Garces Perez was charged in federal court and faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted. He is scheduled to return to court Friday for a detention hearing. A spokesperson for his attorney told NewsNation that they only learned of the charges after Garces Perez was not present at a pre-scheduled meeting with his attorneys.

The criminal complaint alleges Garces Perez was pulled over by ICE officers and provided them with his driver’s license. Federal prosecutors said the traffic stop was initiated after ICE officers confirmed that Garces Perez had been given a final order of removal by an immigration judge and had not left the United States.

Garces Perez is accused of ignoring officers’ orders to put his vehicle in park and step out of the car. The criminal complaint says that body camera footage shows that after officers gave him further instructions in Spanish, Garces Perez closed his window and struck one of the officers in the torso with his driver’s-side rearview mirror while attempting to leave the scene.

Court documents show that ICE officers chased Garces Perez’s car with their emergency lights and sirens on and that Garces Perez led officers on a high-speed chase through residential and commercial areas of Austin.

Garces Perez is accused of attempting to hit an ICE officer with his vehicle, which led the officer to fire his gun.

Account of Garces Perez’s shooting disputed

The allegations greatly differ from the version of events provided after the shooting by Garces Perez’s attorney. Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch said last week that her client’s car was sideswiped twice by an unmarked ICE vehicle and that after being hit once, Garces Perez did a U-Turn under a highway overpass unaware that the vehicle that struck his vehicle was hit.

She said that Garces Perez’s vehicle was sideswiped again before he was shot by federal officers while attempting to leave the scene. Garces Perez was driving for DoorDash at the time of the shooting, his attorney said.

Lincoln-Goldfinch also disputes that her client is in the United States illegally and says he entered by using the CBP-One app and failed to appear in court earlier this year after the notice was sent to the wrong address.

In an interview with investigators at a Texas ICE detention facility, Garces Perez said that an ICE vehicle cut him off and parked diagonally in front of his car, which he said caused a collision between the two vehicles.

He said that an ICE officer approached his window and that he provided the officer with his driver’s license. He then asked the officer if he could park his car so his wife could come pick up the car as Garces Perez knew he would be arrested, the criminal complaint says.

The officer said not to move the car, Garces Perez said, and again ordered him to get out of the car, which Garces admits to disregarding.

Garces Perez told investigators he drove off, which led to a short chase, which ended when an ICE SUV struck his car, which spun around after being hit, court documents show. Garces says he then remembers an ICE officer firing his gun through the back window of his car and says he was hit in the back by the gunshot. Garces says after being shot, he opened the door to his car and took the keys out of the ignition.

Garces Perez says he was taken to a hospital by ambulance. Lincoln-Goldfinch has said a bullet was still lodged in her client’s back when he was taken to the ICE facility and that he did not have feeling in the left side of his body for a time after the shooting took place.

Were ICE officers wearing body-worn cameras during Garces Perez’s shooting?

Lincoln-Goldfinch has questioned whether ICE officers were wearing body-worn cameras. Published reports indicate that the officer who shot Garces Perez was either not wearing a camera or did not have it powered on.

The criminal complaint states that the ICE officer who shot Garces Perez did not have a body-worn camera, according to his partner who admitted in the criminal complaint that he turned off his body camera “at some point of the chase. The ICE officer who shot Garces Perez has not been publicly identified but has been placed on administrative leave per ICE policy.

Austin Police released dashcam footage from the vehicle of an off-duty detective last week. That footage captures part of the vehicle chase and the sound of three gunshots but does not capture video footage of when Garces Perez was shot.

A judge recently ruled that Garces Perez cannot be deported pending an upcoming immigration court hearing.

A spokesperson for Lincoln-Goldfinch told NewsNation that Garces Perez still has a bullet lodged in his back and that doctors say he remains in grave danger because of it. When his attorneys were able to visit him Tuesday, Garces Perez was in considerable pain, dizzy and needed pain medication, which his attorneys say he has not been provided.

text:
President Trump admitted that he struggles to strike the right balance on immigration during a Hispanic Heritage Month event at the White House on Wednesday.

“Frankly, it’s the hardest job that I’ve had,” Trump said. “They’ll say you’re too tough or you’re too soft. Get tougher, get softer. No matter what you do, it’s always tough.”

“We’ve been very strong,” he continued, claiming that over the last 17 months, no one has been able to enter the U.S. illegally.

In August, over 12,000 people crossed the Southwest border, according to Customs Border Protection.

In the same remarks, Trump urged Hispanic and Latino voters to head to the polls in November.

“You’re an unbelievable, special group of people. You’ve been with me from the beginning,” he said.

The president’s comments come as polling shows Republicans struggling with the voting bloc, which boosted Trump during the 2024 presidential election. Signs of disapproval among Hispanic and Latino voters are particularly noticeable in Texas and Florida.

According to a May survey from UnidosUS, 20 percent of Hispanic voters in Florida who supported Trump in 2024 said they would not repeat their vote. Meanwhile, a September Cook Political Report and TelevisaUnivision poll found that 18 percent of Latinos in Texas who voted for Trump said they no longer back him.

Earlier this month, Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.), who is up for reelection, spoke directly to Trump in an ad in front of the White House, criticizing his stance on immigration.

“The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today,” said Salazar in the new clip.

“You can be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism,” the Republican continued. “I’m not talking about giving them amnesty. I’m talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land.”

This story was updated at 5:02 p.m.

text:
The Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR), the nation’s largest Muslim civil rights and advocacy organization, today said that all members of Congress should sponsor the NO BAN Act and that courts should take notice after the official White House rapid response account promoted a 96 percent reduction in legal immigration from Muslim-majority nations.

CAIR noted that the explicitly anti-Muslim language undermines the Trump administration’s longstanding denials of discriminatory intent in litigation surrounding immigration restrictions.

The White House’s Rapid Response 47 account posted: “Legal Immigration from Majority-Muslim Nations Was Cut 96% Since 2024.” The post highlights a Cato Institute analysis finding that monthly immigrant visa issuances and refugee admissions for nationals of 45 Muslim-majority countries fell from 21,096 in December 2024 to 808 in February 2026. These figures measure nationality, rather than each individual’s religion.

CAIR said the White House’s decision to promote this reduction specifically by reference to the Muslim population confirms the discriminatory goals behind the administration’s escalating travel bans and restrictions on lawful immigration, including the expanded Muslim and African travel ban that took effect January 1, 2026.

SEE: CAIR Condemns Expanded Muslim and African Travel Ban Targeting American Families and Palestinians

In a statement, CAIR Government Affairs Department Director Robert S. McCaw said:

“By openly celebrating the exclusion of legal immigrants from Muslim-majority nations, the White House is admitting the bigoted motivation behind its immigration decisions despite years of denials under oath in courtroom litigation.

“During the first and current Trump administration, government lawyers have denied the discriminatory purpose of the Muslim and African travel bans. The administration cannot continue to credibly claim religious neutrality while presenting exclusion associated with Muslim nations as a measure of success.

“Behind these numbers are spouses separated from their partners, children separated from their parents, and refugees seeking safety. These are human beings pursuing lawful immigration pathways. Their faith and national origin should never make them targets of collective punishment.

“Congress must investigate the implementation and consequences of these restrictions, demand the underlying decision-making records, and advance the NO BAN Act. Courts reviewing the legality of the administration’s immigration policies should consider this official statement and reevaluate whether anti-Muslim animus has unconstitutionally motivated those policies.”

CAIR said the latest White House post must be understood against the administration’s continuing restrictions on lawful immigration, family reunification, asylum and political expression. Working backward from its most recent statements, CAIR highlighted the following:

September 2026: New barriers to legal immigration and warrantless arrests: CAIR-California issued guidance on a new public charge rule taking effect September 18 that could affect visa and green card applicants. That same day, CAIR-CA welcomed a federal injunction limiting certain warrantless immigration arrests in Southern California and condemned the administration’s practice of detaining people before justifying their arrest.

August 2026: Immigration enforcement used against protected speech: On August 29, CAIR welcomed a federal ruling protecting noncitizen students from immigration retaliation for constitutionally protected expression, including criticism of Israel’s genocide in Gaza and advocacy for Palestinian rights.

June 2026: Immigration application freezes affecting 39 countries: On June 5, CAIR welcomed a federal ruling striking down an administration policy that effectively froze asylum, work permit, green card and citizenship applications for people from 39 countries, many of them Muslim-majority nations. CAIR urged compliance with the ruling and restoration of normal processing.

January 2026: Suspension of immigrant visas for 75 countries: CAIR condemned the announced suspension of immigrant visa processing, effective January 21, emphasizing its separation of American families and disproportionate harm to communities of color, including people from Muslim-majority nations. The State Department subsequently reported that the pause ended August 21 under a court order.

January 2026: Expanded Muslim and African travel ban: Effective January 1, the administration expanded its travel restrictions to 39 countries and people using Palestinian Authority-issued or endorsed travel documents. The expansion added Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger, South Sudan and Syria to the fully restricted list, moved Laos and Sierra Leone from partial to full restrictions, and eliminated categorical exemptions for immediate family members of U.S. citizens. CAIR condemned the expansion when it was announced in December, emphasizing its collective punishment of Muslim, African and Black communities and its separation of American families.

December 2025: Nationwide asylum freeze and renewed scrutiny: CAIR condemned a USCIS directive freezing pending asylum applications nationwide, halting immigration applications for nationals of 19 targeted countries, and ordering renewed scrutiny of previously approved immigration benefits. CAIR called for congressional investigation and passage of the NO BAN Act.

June 2025: Restoration of the travel ban: CAIR condemned renewed restrictions on 19 countries and warned that vague ideological screening could be abused to exclude immigrants because of their religious identity or political activism.

CAIR’s opposition dates to January 30, 2017, when it filed Sarsour v. Trump, among the first lawsuits challenging the original Muslim ban.

The administration’s denials are documented in its own statements. In a January 29, 2017, White House statement, Trump insisted that the policy was not about religion. In its 2018 Supreme Court brief in Trump v. Hawaii, the administration argued that the proclamation was religion-neutral and did not target people based on their religion. CAIR said the White House’s latest religious framing exposes the discriminatory agenda it has challenged throughout both administrations and severely undermines those longstanding defenses.

CAIR called on the administration to abandon discriminatory immigration restrictions, comply with court orders, and restore fair, individualized processing of affected immigration applications.

description:
Over the weekend of February 23, 2025, the federal government added over 700,000 ICE warrants (sometimes also known as ICE administrative warrants) into the NCIC database.

ICE warrants are not the same as ICE detainers.
This has led to a number of states and local law enforcement agencies to pass policies like the Washington State Police.

text:
The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) is a computerized system of criminal and missing person information that has been operated by the FBI since the late1960s. NCIC is meant for rapid access by state and local police during the course of their routine police enforcement. Historically, civil violations, such as immigration violations, were not added to NCIC. However, over the years, Congress authorized their entry. Over the weekend of February 23, 2025, the federal government added over 700,000 ICE warrants (sometimes also known as ICE administrative warrants) into the NCIC database.

It is important to note that an “ICE warrant” is not a real, warrant in that it is not reviewed by a judge or any neutral adjudicator to determine if it is based on probable cause. ICE warrants are not criminal warrants for criminal charges; they are civil administrative warrants for civil violations. Police do not have legal authority to arrest individuals based on an ICE warrant alone. ICE warrants are not the same as ICE detainers.

HPD’s entanglement with ICE goes beyond what state law requires, and they must draw a distinction between civil and criminal warrants. ICE warrants have caused confusion and resulted in police unlawfully detaining or arresting individuals based on these ICE warrants under the mistaken belief that they are criminal warrants or that local police had authority to arrest individuals solely for civil immigration violations. This has led to a number of states and local law enforcement agencies to pass policies like the Washington State Police. In most cases involving criminal warrants, if there are outstanding criminal warrants on a person in the NCIC database, police may arrest them on that criminal basis alone. However, most police do not have legal authority to arrest on the basis of ICE warrants. Thus, prolonging traffic stops to hold someone in order to wait for ICE to execute the arrest can risk liability for an unlawful seizure under the Fourth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution.

Local law enforcement and ICE entanglement hurt our communities and further drive the wedge of mistrust. We urge our representatives to hold HPD and other City agencies accountable for their entanglement with ICE. We urge HPD and the City of Houston to end existing agreements that dedicate our valuable city resources to ICE.

SB 4 (2017) requires local law enforcement to comply with valid ICE detainer requests5 and prohibits any Texas town, county or higher education institution–hereafter referred to as local entities–from limiting their assistance to ICE or U.S. Customs and Border Protection. SB 4 prohibits local entities from having policies against asking about immigration status or limiting assistance in immigration enforcement. While it is legal for Texas law enforcement to inquire about immigration status during the course of enforcing Texas criminal laws, it is not required. SB 4 does not give local police the authority to perform immigration enforcement duties. That authority generally requires an agreement with ICE under Section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) and is limited by the U.S. Constitution.

Currently, Harris County does not have a 287(g) agreement but that will change once SB 8 goes into effect on January 1, 2026 and requires the sheriff of each county that operates a jail or contracts with a private vendor to operate a jail to request and enter into a 287(g) agreement. However, it is important to note that SB 8 only applies to the sheriff and does not apply to the Houston Police Department (HPD).

NCIC is a system that has been used by all law enforcement agencies around the country, the Houston Police Department (HPD) is no exception. However, HPD’s NCIC policy exceeds what SB 4 (2017) prescribes; critical advocacy could help reduce HPD’s role. At least since 2020, if the HPD officer comes across an ICE hit (or ICE warrant) in the database, the officer shall call ICE law enforcement service center (LESC). According to the February 26, 2025 email from Chief Thomas Hardin to HPD command staff, if ICE LESC offers a “reasonable amount of time” for HPD to wait for them to meet the officer at the scene, then waiting is considered acceptable. If ICE does not offer to meet the officer at the scene, the officer will select the option that does not involve transporting the noncitizen, such as collecting enough information to facilitate an arrest later on.

As detailed above, SB 4 (2017) only requires that local law enforcement comply with valid ICE detainer requests and prohibits local entities from having policies limiting assistance in immigration enforcement but does not require them. The current HPD policy requires HPD to call ICE LESC as soon as they see an ICE hit (or ICE warrant), regardless of the situation. This has led to HPD calling ICE after conducting traffic stops8, on a domestic violence survivor trying to report her abuse and a mother and child stranded at Hobby Airport, to name a few examples.

HPD’s entanglement with ICE is a violation and betrayal of community trust. Despite Mayor Whitmire denying HPD’s entanglement with ICE, HPD has been going above and beyond what state law requires for years. The addition of 700,000 ICE warrants in the NCIC system has highlighted the deep level of entanglement between ICE and HPD that goes against what local law enforcement has told our communities for years. According to the 2025 Kinder Institute’s Houston area survey, 72% of respondents disagreed that Houston would be better off if all noncitizens were deported. A majority of Houstonians do not want to see their neighbors uprooted from their communities because it is the culture and diversity that makes our city stronger. In fact, 1 in 4 residents cited diversity as the best thing about Houston. Therefore, in the spirit of what Houston stands for, we urge our representatives to hold HPD and other City agencies accountable for their entanglement with ICE. We urge HPD and the City of Houston to end existing agreements that dedicate our valuable city resources to ICE.

title: Federal Court Strikes Down State Department's 75-Country Immigrant Visa Ban
authors: Alla   Taher, Alla Taher, Katie P. Jacob
description:
Under the policy, consular officers were instructed to continue interviewing immigrant visa applicants and conducting eligibility reviews.
The policy impacted thousands of family-based and employment-based immigrant visa applicants who were pursuing permanent residence through U.S. consulates abroad.
The INA requires consular officers to evaluate each immigrant visa applicant individually and determine eligibility based on the applicant’s unique circumstances.
By directing consular officers to automatically deny visas based on nationality, the Secretary improperly controlled adjudications that Congress reserved for consular officers.
The decision is a favorable development for applicants from the 75 affected countries because the DOS can no longer rely on the nationality-based immigrant visa ban when adjudicating immigrant visa cases.
text:
Key Takeaways:

The court’s decision in CLINIC v. Rubio represents a major victory for affected families and employers by restoring the requirement that immigrant visa applications be adjudicated on an individualized basis rather than denied because of nationality alone. The ruling reopens a pathway for many family-sponsored and employment-based immigrants whose cases were stalled or denied under the policy. At the same time, applicants should remain cautious. The decision does not guarantee visa approval, does not eliminate all immigration-related country restrictions, and may be subject to further appellate review and delays by the DOS. Individuals with pending or previously refused immigrant visa cases should consult an experienced immigration attorney and proactively prepare for resumed processing and seek guidance regarding any other restrictions that may continue to apply.

Recently, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York issued a significant decision in Catholic Legal Immigration Network, Inc. v. Rubio, No. 1:26-cv-00858 (S.D.N.Y. Aug. 21, 2026), striking down the U.S. Department of State’s (DOS) policy that suspended immigrant visa issuance for nationals of 75 countries. The court found that the policy violated the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) and exceeded the Secretary of State’s authority. As a result, the court vacated the policy and set aside visa refusals that were based solely on the now-invalid ban. The DOS has appealed the decision.

While this decision restores access to immigrant visa processing for many affected applicants, it is important to understand that it does not apply to nonimmigrant visas nor eliminate all country-based immigration restrictions. Separate travel and entry restrictions remain in place for certain nationalities and may continue to affect an individual’s ability to obtain a visa or enter the United States.

Following the court’s decision, multiple news outlets reported that visa interviews were being cancelled worldwide to allow consular officers to receive new training on Public Charge. Although new training is being provided, the DOS has not publicly updated the FAM Section on public charge.

Background

On January 14, 2026, the DOS announced that it would suspend immigrant visa issuance to nationals of 75 countries, effective January 21, 2026. The government justified the policy on the basis that immigrants from those countries posed a heightened risk of becoming a “public charge” and relying on government benefits.

Under the policy, consular officers were instructed to continue interviewing immigrant visa applicants and conducting eligibility reviews. However, if an applicant was otherwise eligible for an immigrant visa and no other inadmissibility ground applied, officers were directed to refuse the application under INA § 221(g) solely because of the applicant’s nationality. Under INA § 221(g), Consular officers may deny a visa if the consular officer did not have all of the information required to conclude that applicant is eligible to receive a visa.

The policy impacted thousands of family-based and employment-based immigrant visa applicants who were pursuing permanent residence through U.S. consulates abroad.

What Did the Court Decide?

The court concluded that the policy was unlawful for several reasons. Specifically, the court found that:

The policy discriminated based on nationality. The INA prohibits discrimination in the issuance of immigrant visas based on nationality. The court held that the Department of State’s blanket refusal policy violated this prohibition because otherwise qualified applicants were denied immigrant visas solely due to their country of citizenship.

The policy ignored Congress’ requirement for individualized adjudications. The INA requires consular officers to evaluate each immigrant visa applicant individually and determine eligibility based on the applicant’s unique circumstances. The court found that the policy replaced this case-by-case analysis with a categorical nationality-based ban.

The Secretary of State exceeded his authority. The court emphasized that Congress granted consular officers, not the Secretary of State, the authority to decide whether individual immigrant visas should be issued or refused. By directing consular officers to automatically deny visas based on nationality, the Secretary improperly controlled adjudications that Congress reserved for consular officers.

In addition to vacating the policy itself, the court ordered that immigrant visa refusals based solely on the policy be set aside and returned for further adjudication. The court did not order visa approval but required the government to reconsider affected applications without relying on the unlawful policy.

What Does This Mean for Applicants?

The decision is a favorable development for applicants from the 75 affected countries because the DOS can no longer rely on the nationality-based immigrant visa ban when adjudicating immigrant visa cases.

However, applicants should be aware of several important limitations:

Immigrant visa eligibility must still be established. The ruling does not guarantee visa issuance. Applicants must still satisfy all applicable immigrant visa requirements, including public charge considerations, financial sponsorship requirements, medical examinations, security clearances and all other grounds of admissibility.

Consular processing delays may continue. Many consulates accumulated significant backlogs while the policy was in effect. Even though the policy has been vacated, visa issuance may not immediately return to normal processing times. Applicants should anticipate delays as consular posts work through pending cases and reconsider previously refused applications.

The government filed an appeal. On September 10, 2026, the U.S. government officially filed a notice of appeal. The appellate court denied the government’s request to pause the lower court’s decision striking down the policy during the pendency of the appeal. While the policy is currently vacated, further litigation could affect implementation of the ruling. Applicants should monitor developments closely.

Separate travel and entry restrictions may still apply. The court’s decision addressed only the DOS’s 75-country immigrant visa suspension policy. It did not invalidate separate presidential travel restrictions affecting certain nationalities. Individuals from countries subject to full or partial travel bans may continue to face limitations on visa issuance or entry despite the court’s ruling.

Recommended Next Steps for Applicants

Individuals affected by the former policy should consider the following actions:

Review your case status. Applicants whose immigrant visas were refused under INA §221(g) because of the 75-country policy should monitor their case status closely for updates from the applicable U.S. embassy or consulate.

Retain documentation. Keep copies of refusal notices, correspondence from the consulate, interview records and any evidence submitted in support of the visa application. These documents may be important as cases are reopened and reconsidered.

Update supporting evidence. Applicants should ensure that financial documents, affidavits of support, employment records, police certificates and other supporting documentation remain current and valid in anticipation of renewed processing.

Be prepared for further requests. Consular officers may request updated information or additional supporting evidence before finalizing adjudication of previously refused cases.

Consider travel ban implications. Applicants from countries currently subject to separate travel restrictions should evaluate whether those restrictions may independently affect their eligibility or ability to enter the United States.

text:
On a cloudy Saturday in March 2025, a federal judge in Washington, D.C., called an emergency hearing over the fate of more than 100 Venezuelans. The U.S. government had invoked the Alien Enemies Act against them, a wartime law used only three times before in U.S. history.

The Department of Homeland Security was rushing to fly the men out of the country — to a notoriously brutal prison in El Salvador — even though they hadn’t had any opportunity to challenge their removal. They never got their day in court. Still, they were loaded onto planes and strapped into their seats with their wrists, waists, and ankles in restraints. As they waited on the tarmac, every second counted.

Attorneys from the ACLU, on behalf of the Venezuelan men, and the Department of Justice, on behalf of the Trump administration, squared up for a legal fight. There was no time to resolve it in a courtroom, so they met on a 5 p.m. Zoom conference. Just over an hour later, the judge made a decision. “Any plane containing these folks that is gonna take off or is in the air,” he said, “needs to be returned to the United States.” However that’s accomplished, the judge added, whether that meant turning around a plane or not disembarking anyone on the plane. He also delivered a message directly to the Department of Justice lawyers: The Trump administration needed to comply, immediately.

But that’s not what happened. The planes didn’t return, and the government deplaned the men at the Center of Confinement for Terrorism (CECOT), a prison in El Salvador known for its documented human rights abuses.

That was the beginning of J.G.G. v. Trump, a case the ACLU filed that cloudy March 15th, 2025 and the very first case we delved into on the ACLU’s new judicial history podcast, “Let the Record Show.” We started here because we recognized that history was being made, in real time.

And since that episode dropped, ACLU attorneys have gone to court twice as a result of this issue. Keep reading to find out what happened on September 25 and September 29, 2026, in two cases challenging the Trump administration’s use of the Alien Enemies Act — a wartime law being used during peacetime to speed up deportations without due process.

In a packed court room on September 29, all 11 active judges of the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals heard intense arguments over whether Trump officials will face consequences for openly defying a federal judge. The focus of this hearing: accountability. During the proceedings, Deputy Director of the ACLU Immigrants’ Rights Project Lee Gelernt, representatives from the Department of Justice (DOJ), and the full court debated whether the district court could continue its inquiry into which Trump administration officials should be referred for criminal contempt prosecution for violating the court’s order.

“The government’s trying to shut down the inquiry by the district court to find out who made the decisions to defy the order,” Gelernt said. “We are hoping the court of appeals rules in our favor.”

On March 15, the district court ordered that the government not deplane any of the ACLU’s clients at CECOT. At that time, the government was stonewalling the court, and not providing information about the flights that were winging their way to El Salvador. Hours later, in the middle of the night, the government deplaned the men despite the court’s order. The district court has undertaken a limited criminal contempt inquiry to determine whether any Trump administration officials should be referred for criminal contempt prosecution for their actions in violating the court’s order. The administration has continued its stonewalling, providing only cursory declarations that do not make clear which officials were responsible for the violation of the order. Accordingly, the district court ordered two DOJ attorneys on the case on March 15, including one former DOJ attorney who provided whistleblower evidence on the violation of the court’s order, to testify. The government has sought to shut down that testimony and prevent the district court’s inquiry to determine who should be referred for prosecution.

In J.G.G. v. Trump, we challenge President Donald Trump’s unlawful invocation of the Alien Enemies Act, a centuries-old wartime act, during peacetime, to accelerate mass deportations. We are representing a class of individuals, more than 100 Venezuelan men, who were removed under this directive on March 15, 2025 to CECOT. The Trump administration alleged they were part of a notorious Venezuelan gang without providing them with any due process or opportunity to contest this allegation. Last June, a federal judge ruled that the removal under the Alien Enemies Act on March 15 was unlawful and ordered the Trump administration to provide the individuals due process to challenge their deportations under the act in court. Yet, Trump officials sent planes to El Salvador anyway. This case focuses on accountability — specifically, whether Trump officials will face consequences for openly defying a federal judge.

This week, the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals faced a direct test of executive accountability in two high-stakes J.G.G. v. Trump hearings. The American Civil Liberties Union and ACLU of D.C. are counsel in this case.

On September 25, a panel of D.C. appellate judges heard arguments on whether the men sent to CECOT without due process are entitled to finally get hearings to have an opportunity to respond to the government’s claims that they are gang members and to challenge their removal under the Alien Enemies Act. Gelernt said the Trump administration has admitted that it violated the plaintiffs’ constitutional rights but is resisting at every turn providing them with the due process the government denied them.

“They concede we rushed them out, gave them no due process,” Gelernt said. “It can’t be the end of the game. That would be such an untenable rule for this court to adopt.”

The district court held that the Trump administration violated the men’s due process rights by sending them to CECOT with no opportunity to challenge their designation as members of the gang under the Alien Enemies Act before being whisked out of the country and deplaned at CECOT in the dead of night. The court ordered the administration to provide information on how it would return those who wished to the United States and ordered that each of the men could file pleadings challenging their designation under the Alien Enemies Act. The government appealed this order and outrageously argues that because it took the men to El Salvador they have no ability to challenge the government’s violation of their rights.

AP: Watchdog Says Trump Can't Cancel More Than $800M In Spending

President Donald Trump is not permitted to withhold beyond the end of the fiscal year ending Wednesday more than $800 million in spending approved by Congress. That’s according to a review from the Government Accountability Office that was sent to federal lawmakers and Vice President JD Vance on Tuesday. The president announced his intention on Friday night to impound more than $800 million from 11 appropriations accounts, using a rare and contested power to axe funding for immigrant services and diversity-focused initiatives. (Freking, 9/29)

KFF Health News: US Poised To Boot Legal Immigrants From Medicaid, Including Refugees And Sex-Trafficking Victims

Hundreds of thousands of immigrants with legal status are at risk of losing government health coverage starting Oct. 1, state data shows, signaling that the impact of Medicaid changes in President Donald Trump’s signature legislation from 2025 may be greater than anticipated. Many lawfully present immigrants will be among the first people to lose Medicaid coverage under congressional Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which is expected to cut spending by more than $900 billion through 2034 for the state-federal health program for people with low incomes or disabilities. The law will strip many more immigrants of their Affordable Care Act plan subsidies and Medicare coverage next year. (Galewitz, Jones and Boyd-Barrett, 9/30)

More on the immigration crisis —

The Washington Post: Supreme Court Allows ‘Third Country’ Deportations To Resume For Now

The Trump administration can resume deporting certain migrants to countries where they are not citizens for the time being, while the justices hear arguments and make a final ruling on the policy, a divided Supreme Court ruled Tuesday. The ruling is a temporary victory for a centerpiece of President Donald Trump’s mass deportation agenda and sets up a major Supreme Court argument in December over the controversial policy. (Mark and Jouvenal, 9/29)

Prosecutors say Wilber Garces Perez struck an agent with his car’s mirror before another agent shot him. ... President Donald Trump has revived a policy change from his first term that gives immigration agents broad authority to deny green cards and visas to applicants who have received public benefits — or whose families have. David Lat: Welcome to the Original Jurisdiction podcast. I’m your host, David Lat, author of a Substack newsletter about law and the legal profession also named Original Jurisdiction, which you can read and subscribe to at davidlat dot substack dot com. You’re listening to the 106th episode of this podcast, recorded on Wednesday, September 23.

My guest today is Jaime Santos, co-chair of the Compensation and Benefits Litigation Practice at Proskauer Rose and one of the nation’s leading appellate and ERISA litigators. We began our conversation by covering Jaime’s impressive and inspiring career path, which took her from a trailer park in a tiny town in Indiana to Harvard Law School, followed by two federal clerkships and partnership at two top law firms. We then discussed how she built her practice in appellate and ERISA litigation, her recent move from Goodwin Procter to Proskauer, and her thoughts on the game of musical chairs now unfolding in the Supreme Court and appellate bar. We concluded by talking about her most meaningful matters over the years, including her victory before the high court in Wilkinson v. Garland, as well as the most interesting cases in the Supreme Court’s upcoming Term and in the world of ERISA and employee-benefits litigation. Without further ado, here’s my conversation with Jaime Santos.

Jaime, thank you so much for joining me.

Jaime Santos: Thank you. I’m excited to be here.

DL: Tell us about your background and upbringing. Where did you grow up?

JS: I grew up in the Midwest, in this tiny town in Indiana called Rensselaer—basically in the middle of a cornfield. I was raised by a single mom with one sibling, and we grew up in a trailer park. When I was 14, we moved to St. Louis, Missouri—the inner city, which is the opposite of a rural Indiana cornfield. My aunt, who lived in St. Louis at the time, basically told my mom, “You cannot raise these children in Indiana with only corn and white people. Move to St. Louis. We will help out, and we’ll get these kids through high school and make sure they have a good future.”

DL: I wouldn’t have guessed that you were from the Midwest because you went to college out on the West Coast and law school out on the East Coast. Do you have any lawyers in the family?

JS: No lawyers in the family. My mom, before I was born, worked in the South Chicago steel mills, and then, when I was growing up in Indiana, she was a bookkeeper for a small printing company. My dad left when I was a year old. So I don’t even know that I met any lawyers until after undergrad.

It was funny: I went to the University of San Diego mostly because I wanted to get as far away from home as possible. When I was applying to schools, I got this beautiful glossy magazine—this is how we used to apply to undergrad—and it had beautiful pictures of the ocean. I applied, immediately got in, and got a full scholarship, so I didn’t apply anywhere else. I thought, “Well, this is the objective: get into college and have someone else pay for it.” And I spent four years there.

DL: What did you major in when you were there?

JS: I majored in ethnic studies, sociology, and Spanish.

DL: And what were you thinking in terms of your career at the time?

JS: I didn’t really know. I thought maybe I wanted to be a professor or maybe I wanted to work for nonprofits. I didn’t do debate or anything like that. I was really involved in student government, the multicultural center, and student leadership. To help pay for things, I also worked a ton through undergrad: I was a sandwich delivery person and a telemarketer, and I worked at the registrar.

I did have this one professor—my favorite professor, Dr. Rafik Mohamed—who taught a class called Sociology of Law. At the very beginning of the class, he taught us, just for a few minutes, how people sometimes write case briefs—the notes that law students keep to track cases and what they mean. We went through the class, and at the end of the semester, I went to his office and said, “Hey, that thing you taught us at the beginning—I decided to do that with every case we read.” I showed him all the notes I’d put together and said, “I’ve noticed a bunch of patterns across cases.” He said, “You’re a weirdo who does this for fun. You definitely need to go to law school.”

I didn’t at the time. I worked for four years after undergrad—as an event planner at a nonprofit, then at a law firm. But eventually I realized he was right, and I really wanted to use my brain. And event planning was fun, but it’s just not a very brainy activity. So I studied really hard for the LSAT, got into Harvard, and ended up going there about four years after I graduated from undergrad.

DL: When you were at HLS, did you have an idea of what type of law you wanted to practice?

JS: Going in, I definitely didn’t, because I was so excited just to be there. Harvard was the one place, when I was growing up, that anyone in my family would have known—other schools, we didn’t know as well. I was the first in my family to go to college; my mom and dad didn’t go, and neither did my grandparents.

I was so excited to go that I completely threw myself into everything; I studied crazy hard. I was afraid I was going to be the dumbest person at Harvard, surrounded by all these fancy people who’d gone to Ivy League undergrads. So I studied nonstop, at least the first two years.

I had more fun my third year. I got onto Law Review, I RA’d for a bunch of different professors, and I took really hard classes. Dan Meltzer had this super hard Fed Courts class—it was a five-credit class that felt like a 20-credit class—and I studied so hard that I literally sprained my neck. I had to get treatment because I sprained my neck studying too hard.

Coming out of that, I thought maybe I wanted to do labor and employment work. But when I was clerking—first on the Central District of California, then on the Ninth Circuit—I realized pretty quickly that I didn’t actually care about subject matter. I just liked complicated issues that were really hard.

Going into the clerkships, I thought, “I probably want to do labor or employment work.” Coming out of them, I thought, “I just want to do nerd stuff.”

DL: Which did you do first, the Ninth Circuit clerkship or the Central District clerkship?

JS: The Central District clerkship, though I actually got my Ninth Circuit clerkship first. I interviewed with Judge Raymond Fisher—I think it was probably in the fall right before my 3L year—and after I got that clerkship, he helped me talk to some district judges as well. Then I went through the normal interview timing process for district court clerkships at the time, which was just the year before graduation. Now it’s apparently the year you’re born—but back then, it was more human.

DL: Yes, I totally agree, and it’s really unfortunate how the timing has shaken out. But it’s interesting that you went to the district court right after law school, because I actually think a district court clerkship is, in many ways, the harder job, and a little overwhelming if you go straight from law school, whereas a circuit clerkship is more like a transition from law school to the practical world. And so that first clerkship must have been a demanding experience.

JS: It was. I clerked for Judge George King, who was then the chief judge of the Central District of California, and he was a particularly demanding judge to work for. He was really smart and really great, and I learned a ton. But we were working 80- to 100-hour weeks, every week, the entire year. It was very demanding.

For Judge Fisher, I think part of why he liked clerks who had clerked on the district court first was that it broke them in—or at least gave them a much better understanding of what district courts were doing, because he liked to defer to district courts on things they did better, and not defer on things that were really classic appellate issues. And I was absolutely a better Ninth Circuit clerk because I had been through the district court clerkship and understood what the dockets looked like and the incredible caseload and what trials looked like and how everything gets resolved.

DL: I totally agree. I think clerks who’ve clerked for a district court before a circuit court are probably less inclined to recommend reversal in everything, because they know how tough that job is and respect the discretion district judges have over so many areas. So I’m sure it made you a better clerk.

JS: I hope so. I don’t know that Judge Fisher would say I was the best clerk; I would often get in trouble for trying to come up with new arguments no one had proposed. One time I wrote a very long memo about Heck v. Humphrey and how the whole case failed. And I remember he wrote at the top of my bench memo something like, “This looks great. Did anyone argue it?” And I said, “No, Judge….” And he said, “Okay, let’s deal with what the parties argued.”

DL: Party presentation: it’s a thing. So you probably felt right at home once you got into practice.

JS: Absolutely. After my clerkship, I joined Goodwin Procter. The timing was funny: I finished my clerkship when I gave birth to twins, who were born a month early—only about seven business days before the end of my clerkship. I felt very bad about that, like I’d abandoned Judge Fisher.

So I finished my clerkship, gave birth to twins, and then twelve weeks later started at Goodwin. It was funny, because Willy Jay—who’s now at Paul Weiss—had just started there maybe the year before. I wasn’t hired by him or into the appellate group at all; I was just hired into litigation generally. I had a mentor at the firm who helped me weasel my way into the appellate group, basically by trying to make myself completely indispensable on any appeal.

When I started, Willy had just hired two recent Supreme Court clerks who weren’t allowed to work on Supreme Court matters for a couple of years. They didn’t really have much of an appellate group otherwise. So once I’d weaseled my way in and shown that I had a strong work ethic and would do literally anything I was asked to do, Willy started putting me on his Supreme Court matters. I also had—at the time, and still have—a raging case of imposter syndrome. I think of it as an asset, even though a lot of people see it as a weakness. It made me really good at my job because it made me question what I was doing, in constructive ways: I made sure that my arguments were airtight, that I researched more, and that I worked harder than other people.

Once I’d shown my value, I got to do more appellate work. I had a turning point around 2015. I worked with Willy on Teva v. Sandoz, a patent case, and I’d also argued two Ninth Circuit pro bono appeals. That work, taken together, left me completely hooked on appellate work, and I knew that was what I wanted to focus on. After the Teva argument, I told Willy that it had almost made me want to apply for a Supreme Court clerkship. He said, “What are you talking about? Why did you never apply?” I said, “I didn’t clerk for a feeder judge, and I just thought I wouldn’t have a chance.” He said, “You should definitely apply.”

So I applied for clerkships, and I got an interview with Justice Sonia Sotomayor. I didn’t end up getting the clerkship, but I spent the last month of my maternity leave with my youngest child basically prepping for that interview. I read the last three years of Supreme Court opinions, I read every opinion Justice Sotomayor had ever written, and I spent a month reflecting on what I wanted to do and where I wanted to go.

When I didn’t get the clerkship, I asked my firm if I could move down to D.C., because I wanted to immerse myself in the appellate world and learn from Willy and build our D.C. appellate practice, if he’d have me. The firm was incredibly supportive; they said, “Absolutely.” I moved a few months later.

Once I got down there, I was facing a bit of a conundrum: I tend to be a Type A, ambitious person, and I really wanted to be the most successful appellate lawyer I could be. But I knew I didn’t have the credentials that a lot of your former guests have—folks like Lisa Blatt, Paul Clement, Easha Anand, and Willy as well. But I really wanted to be good at this and get to a very high level.

So I thought, “You’re going to have to find a different way, Jaime. It’s not the normal path. Supreme Court to OSG [Office of the Solicitor General] isn’t going to work for you, and you’re going to have to find another way to get there.” I spent the next five-plus years trying, on the one hand, to get really good at honing my appellate craft and learning as much as I could, and, on the other, trying to figure out how to raise my profile and expand my network so I could succeed in the long term. You can only go so far being smart and hardworking. In D.C., that doesn’t actually get you very far, and it doesn’t get you hired.

I started doing a lot of public speaking, at law schools and conferences, and talked about anything: diversity in the legal profession, what it’s like to be a working mom, appellate practice. I got the chance to work with a group of current and former law clerks to advocate on issues of judicial misconduct in the federal courts, and then ended up working with a bunch of judiciaries across the country on their own judicial misconduct procedures, and that gave me the chance to testify before the Senate Judiciary Committee and the Judicial Conference. I helped start a podcast. I ended up serving as secretary of the Inn of Court in D.C., which is where the 200 biggest appellate nerds meet once a month during the Supreme Court Term for cocktails and panels. I thought, “This is a ton of work, but it’ll give me the chance to know everyone.” So I did all of these things as my side gig, while also trying to learn to be a really good appellate lawyer.

DL: What you just described is exactly what lawyers who want to build a practice need to be doing—because as you say, and I know it’s a cliché, being smart and hardworking is table stakes. You need to stand out in some other way.

So you were very modest when you said you “started a podcast.” Tell us what podcast that was.

JS: Back in the day, pre-pandemic, I helped start Strict Scrutiny. I was on it for the first year, then left, and it has continued to grow.

DL: It’s now one of the largest, most successful, and most influential legal podcasts—or podcasts, period, anywhere. What led you to leave after a year?

JS: There were a number of different factors. It was never going to be a long-term option for me, in part because when I do something important, I put a lot of work into it. I was spending 15 to 20 hours a week on the podcast, which was awesome. I loved it. I got to know everything about the Court, and I got to talk every week with three other brilliant women. But long-term, there was just no way—unless I stopped sleeping entirely—that I could keep doing that. So that was a piece of it.

The other piece of it is that it’s hard to do what Strict Scrutiny became and also be an effective advocate. Especially toward the end of my tenure, I felt like the tone was a little different than what I was necessarily comfortable with. I love edgy commentary, but if you’re trying to advocate before the Supreme Court, being on a podcast that sometimes takes a mocking tone toward the justices or the advocates isn’t a great idea. It’s also just not my style as much. So I thought that I could do smart, interesting commentary on the Supreme Court in other venues, and it might be time to give it a rest, while continuing to support the people who do that work.

DL: I have a couple of thoughts. First, I’m not surprised that you spent that much time on the podcast. People need to know that we try to make these things look relatively easy, but it takes a lot of work to prepare for a podcast. When I have guests, I’ve researched them, I’ve read their writing, I’ve listened to oral arguments—I’ve done all sorts of things. And for a news-driven podcast like Strict Scrutiny, Leah Litman, Kate Shaw, and Melissa Murray are really busting their tails to follow the news of the day.

On your point about being outspoken or candid, being a law professor is good for that kind of work, because (a) they have tenure—they can afford to be outspoken and don’t have to worry about clients or judges being upset—and (b) law professors work hard, but they have a lot of flexibility. You have clients, and you’re a working parent. So I don’t know how you’d find another 15 or 20 hours a week—unless you stopped sleeping, as you said. So I totally understand that.

You were working hard and dealing with imposter syndrome, and it clearly worked: you wound up being, alongside Willy Jay, the co-head of appellate at Goodwin. How long did you spend at Goodwin? You were there for a good long stretch.

JS: Yes—13 years. I think the last two or three years I was co-chair of the practice. Willy had gone on to become co-chair of the non-IP litigation group at Goodwin generally, and when he moved into that role, I moved into the co-chair role, along with my former colleague Kevin Martin, who’s in Massachusetts. I loved that role. Leadership is just in my DNA—getting the chance to lead the group, help expand it, and instill a sense of business development and proactiveness in everyone. I got to hire people and help promote people, and the group there is really phenomenal. It was a great place to spend 13 years.

DL: You recently made a move. This was certainly in the news, and once again, you have a leadership role too. Maybe you can tell us about that.

JS: Yes. I recently joined Proskauer Rose, straddling the litigation department and the employee benefits practice.

I definitely wasn’t looking to leave Goodwin. I really loved my colleagues, and my practice was growing there. Proskauer approached me through a friend who’s also a recruiter—shout-out to Karen Vladeck, whose lesser-known husband is Steve Vladeck. I’ve known her and Steve since I was on the Harvard Law Review and was the supervising editor for his book review; it’s funny how things come full circle.

So Proskauer approached me. The firm has this really incredible benefits platform, and an important part of my practice on the appellate side has always been ERISA litigation; I made that an intentional part of my practice. Their benefits practice and their benefits relationships are really conducive to the ERISA piece, and they wanted to invest heavily in that space. They also wanted to invest more broadly in their litigation practice. They’ve been building their trial practice, including folks who’ve joined on the antitrust side. My colleague Bart Williams joined from Munger about ten years ago and really turbocharged their trial practice.

So it seemed like a really great match for the two pieces of my practice I’d been building, and it was a super intensive process. I’ve heard of people switching firms in a month or so, and I don’t know how that would work. I spent three or four months interviewing, I visited three different offices, and I probably interviewed with 30 partners. Part of that is the firm wanting to make sure it’s recruiting people who culturally fit, but it was also very much me wanting to get a real feel for the place—because if I was going to leave this nerdy group of people I adore at Goodwin, I needed to feel sure of it.

And so I ended up coming to Proskauer, and I have been here for about a month.

DL: I have a couple of thoughts. First, you picked a great platform. Given your focus on ERISA, employee benefits, and executive compensation, Proskauer is really tops in that substantive area. I’m not surprised you were steered in the right direction by Karen, who’s one of the best recruiters in the industry—and a former law firm partner herself, so she knows the ins and outs.

I’m curious how you developed this additional expertise beyond the Supreme Court and appellate work. How did you come by the ERISA and employee-benefits focus?

JS: When I mentioned earlier that I didn’t have the normal path available to me and had to find a new way to do this, it was around the same time I was trying to figure it all out. I like being a generalist appellate lawyer, because I get bored doing the same thing too much. But on the appellate side, in terms of strategically building a practice, it’s really helpful to have one or two niche areas you know really well; you can market yourself, and you can speak on them.

I remember sitting in my D.C. office thinking, “What do I want my niche to be?” I thought about patent work; there’s a lot of work there. But there were a ton of, for lack of a better term, fancy gray-haired men with lots of credentials who were already the go-to lawyers in the space. Willy is one of them, Seth Waxman another—and no one’s going to hire me over Seth Waxman for a patent appeal. I thought about antitrust; I really like antitrust cases, but the dynamic was the same there. And bankruptcy—Roy Englert is amazing, the bankruptcy appellate god. I liked product-liability work. But Goodwin had largely wound down its product-liability practice, so that wasn’t going to be a good match.

I was going through the specialties, and I came to ERISA. I had done some ERISA cases, and I really liked them—because there’s a combination of administrative law, statutory interpretation, and some common law. It’s also very complicated, and everyone else hates it. So then I thought, “Who on the ERISA defense side is the appellate person?” And there wasn’t anyone; there was literally no one who was the overwhelming ERISA appellate person. On the plaintiffs’ side, there certainly were lawyers like David Frederick, Peter Stris, and Matt Wessler. But they do that work on the plaintiffs’ side, not on the defense side. And I thought, “This is an area where I can really carve out a place, be really good, and get to argue the appeals I lead.”

It turned out to be great for me in the long term, because it’s the one area where I feel I don’t have to fight over arguments or field the question, “Should she be the one who argues?” Even after I’d argued in the Supreme Court and argued en banc in the Sixth Circuit, in other areas, like patent, I’d have clients say, “I think someone with more experience, who’s done more Federal Circuit appeals, might be better.” That doesn’t happen on the ERISA side, because there isn’t someone more experienced—some gray-haired man who’s better suited. I’m the person, and I really like these cases. It was a strategic move that’s been great for my practice and a lot of fun.
