So I just want to highlight the wisdom of your approach. I spoke to a very successful lawyer at the top of their particular niche, and this person told me that when advising law students or young lawyers on choosing a practice, their advice is this. First, find something you’re genuinely interested in; don’t go into something just because it’s hot or trendy. Next, ask yourself whether there’s already a go-to person in that field—someone like Roy Englert or Seth Waxman. And then, if there’s no one who is that person, go be that person. So I guess you went and became that person for your field.

Let me now ask you about another topic. You’re an appellate and Supreme Court lawyer who moved in 2026, so join the club. It seems like pretty much every appellate and Supreme Court litigator moved in 2026. I won’t go through all of them, lest I leave somebody out—but what is up with this?

JS: It’s a very fair question, and I think there are a bunch of things going on. Some people are probably just chasing money. There’s a crazy amount of money kicking around, based on what I’ve heard about what some firms are willing to pay for an appellate practice.

For others, it’s more complicated. There are firms that have been undergoing a massive amount of change over the last ten years, increasing their transactional practice and shrinking their litigation practice. For litigators, and appellate litigators in particular, that can be really problematic. It can create bigger conflicts landscapes when you have big tech practices, especially if you’re representing smaller or mid-cap companies, since that can mean you can’t handle matters for Fortune 100 companies.

And with more of a focus on transactional practice, there’s less high-stakes litigation—and without high-stakes litigation, it’s really hard to have a successful appellate practice, unless you’re Paul Clement and people just pick up the phone and call you. It’s Paul, and Lisa Blatt, and Elizabeth Prelogar, and that’s basically it; there are probably a couple of others, but for the rest of us mortals, it doesn’t work that way. So as firms have changed their strategy, some appellate lawyers have taken a hard look at their practices and asked, “Is this really the right platform for me, or might I thrive somewhere else?”

And maybe the other piece is that if you look back 10 to 15 years, that was when you started to see litigation practices think, “I need an appellate practice to support my litigation practice—I’m losing pitches because we don’t have a good litigator here.” So a lot of people joined appellate practices 10 to 15 years ago, including Willy, and they might just want a change now. When you’ve been at the same place for a long time, you might just want a new experience. If you enjoy building a practice, you can start to feel antsy being part of one that’s already built—and that’s also a good reason to try something new.

DL: Looking back over the course of your career as a Supreme Court, appellate, and ERISA and benefits litigator, is there a particular matter you’re most proud of? I have one guess in my head, but I’ll let you tell us.

JS: I’ll give two—one appellate, one ERISA. The appellate one is probably obvious: I argued Wilkinson v. Garland in the Supreme Court a couple of years ago, on behalf of an immigrant, Situ Wilkinson, who was seeking relief from deportation under the cancellation-of-removal provision of the INA [Immigration and Nationality Act]. He was arguing that his removal would cause serious harm to his minor son, a U.S. citizen, and that he should therefore be allowed to stay in the United States. The Third Circuit had held there was no jurisdiction to review the immigration agency’s decision. We convinced the Supreme Court to take up the case, and it reversed.

There were a couple of reasons it was meaningful. The obvious one is that it was amazing to be entrusted by Situ to argue a case where his life and his family were on the line. You’re probably aware of this, but there are so many budgetary pressures in law firm practice that sometimes it feels like you’re just trying to get words on paper while spending as little time as possible. Getting to litigate a case the way I really wanted to—chasing down every thread, going down every rabbit hole, reading every case on the subject—is just a fun way to litigate, and I don’t get to do it that often.

It was also very meaningful because my family was there, and my mom came out from St. Louis to watch me argue. I talk to my husband and kids about my work, but I don’t really talk to my growing-up family about my work that much. I think part of it is that when I was growing up as a poor kid, people didn’t really talk about their jobs; you usually didn’t enjoy your job that much. It just wasn’t part of the culture I grew up in. And my work is complicated, technical, and not particularly intuitive, so I don’t talk to my mom much about what I do. But she could come out to the Supreme Court and completely understand the gravity of what I was doing, and having her there was a real point of pride.

Two of my three kids came. (One said, “That sounds too boring, Mommy, I’d rather go to school,” and went to school instead of watching me argue.) One of my kids got in trouble at the Court for trying to lie down on my husband’s lap, and she was told that wasn’t allowed. I remember thinking to myself, “You don’t wake up the justices when they fall asleep—why Emily?” So that was very meaningful to me.

The other reason it was meaningful is that I was proud to have gotten this coalition of justices. You have to count to five, and in an immigration case, that can be hard. But we got all three of the justices appointed by President Trump, plus Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor, to combine on this majority opinion. It goes to show that if you find the right case, make the right arguments, and do it with care, you can prevail. And I made sure to involve immigration advocates at every stage of briefing and at every moot. I don’t think it’s fair or just or right to take a case up to the Supreme Court that you have no chance of winning on behalf of a marginalized population, just to get an argument. I would never do that. I think it’s problematic, and I know some members of the bar do it, and I’m completely against it. But this was a case we really thought we had a chance at winning. We could make a good textual argument, we had good precedent, and we thought we could build a coalition. And we did, and it created good precedent nationwide.

DL: And what was the trial court matter?

JS: I’m going to anonymize it a bit, because it’s a case that’s still pending, but it’s an ERISA case—part of a series of cases that have gone almost 100% against ERISA defendants. There are something like 70 or 80 cases in this genre, and on almost every issue raised, courts have ruled in favor of ERISA plaintiffs. I see that pretty often in ERISA cases: you get one decision, and then another district court thinks, “I hate ERISA cases… This judge said this, I’ll go along with it.” It gathers steam, and everyone just keeps citing the original case.

There was an associate at my prior firm, Isabel Marin, who is awesome, and she and I basically crafted these arguments—really just administrative law and standing arguments that no one had started briefing when we started working on these cases. We went into court and told the judge, “We know that 25 courts have ruled against us, but these are really good arguments. Most of them weren’t raised, and if they were, they were poorly briefed; you can see it in the decisions, which say things like, ‘This issue was raised, but barely briefed.’ Please just take an independent look at this.”

We won an across-the-board decision, with the judge going against a wall of adverse authority: 100% of courts had gone the other way on Article III standing. I felt like it was a situation where the quality of the advocacy actually made a difference. Sometimes you don’t feel like it matters, but this time it really felt like it did. And even though it was an ERISA victory, it felt just like a normal appellate, ad-law, constitutional victory.

DL: That’s a great example. So much of lawyering comes down to creativity and to seeing arguments that haven’t been raised before.

I can also understand how amazing it must have been to have your mother in the audience when you argued Wilkinson v. Garland. It probably wasn’t easy for her as a single mom, and I got a bit of a chill or shiver as you were just telling me about how meaningful it must have been for her to watch her daughter argue before the highest court in the land.

Speaking of the highest court in the land, we’re recording this shortly before the start of the upcoming Supreme Court Term. Just an hour ago, I finished presenting on a CLE panel previewing the Term. For listeners who don’t follow the Court as closely as we do, what would you identify as some of the biggest cases or cases worth following?

JS: There aren’t a lot of high-profile cases that have been granted yet for this Term, but I always say that in September, and then the Court goes and grants a billion cases that give me heartburn. I think the Court is also leaving room in its docket for election cases this fall, in case they come up.

Probably the biggest case I’m keeping an eye on is the Suncor Energy case, which is about whether litigants can use state tort law to sue companies that have contributed to climate change. It’s interesting because, from my read, the defendant below was really trying to rely on general federal preemption principles—the idea that federal law, whether common law or statutory, supersedes state tort law. But the Supreme Court right now really does not like anything that starts with the word “implied”: implied private right of action, implied preemption, implied remedies—it’s a no-go. So the defendant has had to shift the argument toward a more constitutional, separation-of-powers argument, and it’ll be interesting to see how the justices come out on this and how principled the decision is. That’s one I’m keeping an eye on.

Another one—I call it the “Blockbuster Video bandanas case,” which isn’t what it actually is—it’s a case about the Video Privacy Protection Act, the statute passed many years ago so that Blockbuster couldn’t secretly reveal that George Clooney really liked binge-watching Teletubbies. It kept companies from disclosing people’s video-watching history, but the statute is written broadly enough that it could plausibly cover any transaction for any goods or services by a company that puts videos online. Think Home Depot self-help videos—my husband watches those all the time. Does this VPPA statute mean Home Depot can’t disclose that he bought a humidifier last year? I don’t know. The plaintiff says, “Yes—look at the statute, those words are on the page.” The defendant says, “What are you talking about? That’s not what the statute was meant to do.”

I think this is another case where the Court’s commitment to textualism versus contextualism is really going to be tested. I kind of believe the Court is textualist until it is not, and then you get this purposivism that masquerades as contextualism. Or maybe it’s just a better way of taking a look at the bigger picture, while still operating under a textualist method. But in both of these cases, I’ll be curious to see how principled the decision is.

DL: I totally agree with those picks—those are two of the most interesting cases. My husband Zach is the executive editor of SCOTUSblog, and he and I have gone back and forth on Suncor, because as a policy matter, you can understand why…

JS: It’s crazy, there’s no way…

DL: … you don’t want state or local officials being able to go after national or multinational companies. I understand that. But what’s the hook? As you mentioned, the Court doesn’t like anything “implied.” So what’s the concrete textual hook for ruling in favor of the companies? I don’t know; we’ll see. It’ll be interesting.

And on the VPPA case, this is the statute that was passed around the time of the Robert Bork nomination, when someone leaked his video-rental history—which had nothing scandalous in it, but people didn’t like the fact that it had been leaked. Doesn’t this case involve the plaintiff being served ads based on their viewing? We’re all served ads based on what we watch; it’s just a fact of modern life. So that’s an interesting one too.

JS: Yeah, it’s a question of how you deal with a statute that clearly wasn’t aimed at this, using this textualist approach the Court is taking. I could easily see a decision where the Court says, “Those words are on the page. Congress can amend it.” That also seems kind of insane as a policy matter, but maybe that’s just a policy issue.

DL: Are there any cases that you would mention or identify as sleeper cases, some important cases that are on the docket for the Court but maybe not getting the buzz they deserve?

JS: So there are two cases. One is a case my former colleague, Will Evans, who’s amazing and wonderful, is arguing: Montoya Palacios v. Liggins. It’s about EAJA fees—Equal Access to Justice Act fees, which a prevailing plaintiff who sues and wins against the government can generally recover, as long as it’s not a tort case and as long as certain standards are met.

Does EAJA apply in habeas cases? They’re technically civil cases, but they don’t always feel very civil all the time. This is a really important case right now, given all of the immigration raids the administration has been conducting—habeas has been the only avenue for relief in many cases. Even the government has said, in some instances, “You can only do this through habeas; you can’t bring a class action, you can’t bring an APA lawsuit.” Many of the groups doing this work are civil-rights organizations, nonprofits, or solo practitioners—teeny tiny little practices. So if they can’t recover EAJA fees when they win, even when the government wasn’t justified in its actions, it’ll be really hard for them to take on this work.

And the availability of EAJA fees affects what the government does in the first instance. When our client, Situ Wilkinson, was in immigration detention—he’d been there for years—we filed a habeas action to try to get him a bond hearing, which he’d been denied. The government, when we filed, agreed to release him as long as we agreed not to seek EAJA fees. I don’t know that he would’ve gotten out if there hadn’t been that risk of EAJA fees; why not just keep litigating? So it affects primary conduct, and it’s certainly important to the work immigration lawyers are doing.

DL: And then you mentioned there was maybe one other matter you wanted to highlight.

JS: Yes—there’s an ERISA case, obviously, which is the most important case of the Term. Luke McCloud, my friend from law school, is arguing it: Andersen v. Intel. It’s about what an ERISA plaintiff needs to show, when challenging an investment-plan lineup in a retirement plan, to state a viable claim. It’ll probably bore a generalist audience, but the Supreme Court granted cert in a similar case a few years ago, Hughes v. Northwestern University, and kind of punted on this issue. So I’ll be curious whether the Court digs in this time.

My experience with ERISA cases at the Supreme Court is that it usually writes very short, unanimous opinions that don’t really say that much. Maybe the justices are bored, or maybe they’re just worried about getting that area of law wrong. I’ll be curious whether they actually dig in, or just issue another very short, nine-page unanimous opinion from Justice Sotomayor.

DL: Well, it’s funny, I feel like ERISA is almost like a sleeper topic. It’s vitally important, but it doesn’t get as much attention as I think it deserves. And full disclosure, I’m something of an ERISA nerd myself. For those of you who aren’t familiar, it’s the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974. I took ERISA in law school, I later worked with my professor as a research assistant on his ERISA casebook, and my father-in-law is a pension actuary—so I actually have this weird interest in ERISA.

So I’m curious—I’ve had more than 100 guests on this podcast, including a number of Supreme Court and appellate advocates, but you’re actually the first ERISA and employee-benefits lawyer I’ve had on. Besides what’s happening at the Supreme Court, what’s an issue that’s really on the minds of ERISA lawyers right now? It doesn’t have to be something on appeal. What’s an issue in the trenches that some of your clients are concerned about?

JS: Historically, over the last 15 or 20 years, most ERISA litigation—the class action litigation I focus on—has been on the retirement-plan side. And there’s been a recent push toward health-plan litigation. I think that creates an enormous amount of risk for employers who sponsor health plans, because those plans are incredibly complicated. They often involve hundreds of millions of dollars—a lot of it employer money, since employers are often heavily subsidizing health plans—and a lot of people don’t understand them at all. So a plaintiff, or a plaintiff’s lawyer, can come in and wreak a lot of havoc without really understanding how things operate, and make things look very factually complicated. I’ve seen a number of health-plan class actions over the last couple of years starting to wind their way through the courts.

On the ERISA appellate side in particular, the areas most interesting to appellate courts, and especially the Supreme Court, are a bit like patent law—where you find something that’s ERISA, but not too ERISA. Think of where ERISA intersects with Article III standing or with class actions. There’s a bunch of issues percolating about the standing of plan participants who claim there was some violation of ERISA but can’t show they would have been in any different position even if ERISA had been complied with.

There’s also an issue winding through the courts about whether you can certify a mandatory, no-opt-out class of ERISA plan participants who are seeking money. For basically 15 years, courts almost uniformly said, “Yes, absolutely, a non-opt-out class is fine.” The Fourth Circuit recently said, “Wait—no, that’s a Rule 23(b)(3) class. You can’t do that.” It was the first court to go against this wall of authority, and I’ve already seen that issue pending in one other circuit.

So those are the kinds of issues I think can reach the Supreme Court despite being ERISA cases.

DL: Do you think that that last issue is going to result in a split perhaps?

JS: Absolutely. I think it’s only a matter of time.

DL: Interesting—well, I hope you’re the one to argue it.

So, turning to my speed round, these are four questions, and they are the same for all my guests. My first question is, what do you like the least about the law? And this can be the practice of law, or law as an abstract system.

JS: It’s probably somewhere in between the two: I really dislike the purity test that exists right now on both the conservative and progressive sides of the legal world. I’ve gotten a lot of flak from the progressive movement for… I have a lot of friends who are conservative lawyers or judges, and I sometimes have views that diverge from the left side of the political spectrum. I think that’s a good thing; it’s good to maintain relationships with people who feel differently from you. But I think there’s a sense right now that if you don’t violently agree with everyone in your ideological tribe, you’re a fraudster or a sellout.

I’ll give just one example of this. I remember when the SEC v. Jarkesy case came out a Term or two ago, and it was about whether the SEC could do in-house adjudication of claims for civil penalties instead of going to court. And I remember reading through the majority opinion, and I called a friend of mine and I said, “Okay, so quick question. I’m a progressive, so I know I’m supposed to hate this, but why? Don’t progressives like due process? Don’t we like access to courts? Do we really like immigrants being subject to in-house adjudication where the Department of Justice and DHS are the judge, jury, and prosecutor? Absolutely not. And so why would we like it for the SEC?”

So I feel like that kind of thinking can paint you as a pariah, and I don’t like that—and I know it happens on the conservative side, too. And I just wish we could be a little bit more open-minded and listen a little bit more.

DL: I totally agree with you there; you’re preaching to the choir. My second question is, what would you be if you were not a lawyer?

JS: So I would like to say an adventure tour guide, because I mentioned I’m an adrenaline junkie. When we go to Disney World with the kids, I’m the roller-coaster parent; my husband is the hold-the-bags parent. But realistically, I probably am too risk-averse for that. So maybe a baker? I really love baking. I like the precision. I like the creativity. I like that you immediately know if you have succeeded or failed, instead of having to wait a year for an opinion after argument. So maybe a baker.

DL: I’m with you on the baking. I like the precision. I do not have the judgment or discretion to be a cook and say, “Oh, I’ll throw in a little more of this or that.” With baking, if you follow the recipe, it works.

JS: Exactly, exactly.

DL: My third question is, how much sleep do you get each night?

JS: Currently, I probably average about six to seven hours a night, which is not too bad. It has gotten better. My first four years out of law school, I was averaging probably two to four hours, which is awful, but part of this was I had newborn twins who did not sleep, and I was practicing, and that was really tough, and I had demanding clerkships.

But more recently, I really need more sleep. As I get older, I really, really, really need more sleep. One thing I’ve noticed is that the time I go to sleep matters sometimes more than the amount of sleep I get. So if I go to sleep at 1:00 a.m., my sleep is trash; it doesn’t matter how much I try to get. If I go to sleep earlier, I’m in a much better situation.

Before argument, I prioritize sleep over everything, because I definitely notice that I am sharper and I can use my brain more efficiently when I have better sleep. So the two nights before argument, I always try to get at least eight hours of sleep, and my Friday night fun is to try to go to bed at 9:00 p.m.—that’s my favorite thing ever.

DL: Well, getting good sleep before an oral argument is good advice, and that brings me to my last question: any final words of wisdom, such as career advice or life advice for my listeners?

JS: Sure—so maybe two, but I might come up with a third by the end. The first is to be kind. I think this is going to sound too Pollyannish, but kindness for me is one of the most underrated characteristics that people have. And for my part—especially living in D.C., where everyone is smart and hardworking—I am so much more impressed by people who treat each other well than by someone who is super smart. And I’m talking about being kind to everyone—not just the people above you, but judges, their clerks, the staff, the leaders of your group, the IT people, the TSA agents—saying thank you, just being kind. If you are kind to people, they will have your back, they will be loyal to you, and when you make a mistake or say something stupid, like I do all of the time, they will forgive you and be understanding. So number one, be kind; that’s my governing principle.

The number two piece of advice is to try to focus more on raising other people up than yourself. There are so many people, in D.C. especially, who are just always focused on promoting themselves. And in my experience, if you focus on promoting other people and what they are doing—whether it’s making your client look good, making your colleague look good, making a junior lawyer look good, making a friend look good—you’ll be happier, other people will do better, and then the universe just kind of has a way of making sure it works out from a karma perspective. So try to help other people instead of yourself.

And then maybe a third one is, “There’s always a way.” There’s a way to do what you want to do, and you just have to find that way. I remember saying, after I did not get the clerkship with Justice Sotomayor, “Okay, this door is closed, so I have to do a little light breaking and entering and find a crawl space or break a window.” There’s always a way to do what you want to do. It might not be immediately apparent, but I try to find a way. If I have a bad day or a bad argument or get a bad decision, I let myself have 24 hours to sulk, and then I have to get myself up and figure out what to do. So take your 24 hours and then get your butt up and start figuring out another option.

DL: Well, you have definitely found a way to have a fascinating and really inspiring career. Jaime, thank you so much for joining me.

JS: Thank you. It was really fun.

text:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Wednesday took the remarkable step of seeking to censure both a former and sitting federal judge in Minnesota after the pair spoke to The New York Times about the Trump administration’s immigration surge in the state.

The two judges are Patrick Schiltz, an appointee of former President George W. Bush, and John Tunheim, an appointee of former President Clinton.

The complaint also asked the Judicial Council of the 8th Circuit to initiate an investigation into other “anonymous” judges who spoke to the outlet.

The reference is confusing, as the article named several judges on the bench who spoke to the Times on the record, including an appointee of President Trump. However, many of their comments did not directly touch on cases.

One of those comments, from Trump-appointed Judge Nancy Brasel, noted judges “are allowed to speak out about judicial independence.”

The story noted that judges were critical of how the Trump administration operated as it conducted immigration raids across the Twin Cities. Two U.S. citizens were killed during interactions with immigration agents, and the aggressive enforcement prompted bipartisan criticism, leading the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to shift to quieter tactics.

Schiltz previously noted that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) had defied 96 orders from 74 judges.

The DOJ argued in the filing that the two judges “have flagrantly violated the Code of Judicial Conduct with their improper and unethical comments.”

“Judges are ethically prohibited from commenting publicly on cases pending in any court and making political or policy statements concerning matters that are or have been before them,” the DOJ wrote, adding that the “canon” applies to media interviews.

“These judges should be ordered to recuse from any matters involving DHS because the public reasonably questions their impartiality in cases involving immigration. Moreover, the Eighth Circuit should initiate an investigation by the Judicial Counsel into the improper conduct by judges in the District of Minnesota who ‘covet publicity’ rather than adhering to the rule of law by adjudicating cases or controversies.”

A spokesperson for the U.S. District Court in Minnesota said judges were well within the bounds of ethics guidelines.

“As legal-ethics experts have confirmed, our judges were acting well within the ethical rules that apply to federal judges in speaking to the New York Times. Indeed, in February of this year, the Committee on Codes of Conduct issued an advisory opinion to emphasize that federal judges may ‘speak[] and writ[e] on core judiciary matters such as advocacy for the rule of law and judicial independence.’ Our judges acted within this capacity,” spokesperson Rebeccah Parks stated in an email.

Schlitz told the Times that on court orders “most, if not all, of the noncompliance was due to incompetence” and also said that level of defiance “just never happens.”

Tunheim also made brief remarks to the Times, saying that the widespread arrests did not focus on those with a criminal record.

“They weren’t arresting, in my view, people who were dangerous criminals on the street,” said Tunheim.

The DOJ argued that Tunheim’s remarks “while less verbose” were “equally unethical.”

“Opining that the Administration was not arresting illegal aliens who were ‘dangerous criminals’ is factually inaccurate and unvarnished political commentary,” the DOJ wrote.

Legal boards that govern the judiciary in recent years have affirmed the ability of judges to make some public comments.

An advisory opinion from the Judicial Conference’s Committee on Codes of Conduct affirms that the ethics code abided by judges allows them to advocate for the rule of law and defend the independence of the courts, including to seek increased judicial security and funding.

The opinion goes further to say that, in some circumstances, judges may stand up for their peers against unjust attacks.

“Although this Commentary addresses persecution specifically, the Committee believes the Code and its previous advisory opinions leave room, in at least some circumstances, for the measured defense of judicial colleagues from illegitimate forms of criticism and attacks that risk undermining judicial independence or the rule of law, whether or not they rise to the level of persecution,” the opinion states.

text:
An immigration judge has ruled that the president of Wisconsin’s largest mosque can be deported under a controversial, cold-war era law the Trump administration has sought to wield against foreign nationals who have been outspoken about Palestinian rights.

Salah Sarsour, a US permanent resident for nearly three decades, was detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement in March. He was released after a federal judge found he had probably been detained in retaliation of his advocacy for Palestinian rights, which the federal judge said would render his detention unlawful.

Despite that ruling, the administration pressed forward and fast-tracked Sarsour’s immigration case – a separate legal track – and on Tuesday night an immigration judge ruled he is “removable”.

Judge Jayme Salinardi, who was brought in from out of state to oversee the case, announced he would be retiring shortly after issuing the decision.

In a statement, Sarsour’s attorneys called the ruling “a setback for free speech rights”.

“The case we presented compels only one conclusion, which is that Salah is not deportable, he has done nothing wrong,” Patrick Taurel, one of Sarsour’s attorneys, said during a press conference shortly after the hearing. “He should be given back his green card with an apology for what’s been done to him.”

The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but claimed before that Sarsour was “suspected of funding terror organizations and lying on immigration forms”. He has denied both claims.

In a statement issued shortly after his arrest, the DHS cited Sarsour’s decades-old military court convictions in Israel for, it said, “throwing a Molotov cocktail at the homes of Israeli armed forces and illegally attempting to possess weapons and ammunition”.

Sarsour said those accusations stemmed from an arrest as a teenager by Israeli soldiers in 1989, during the first intifada. He also says he was forced, under torture and threat of rape, to sign documents in Hebrew without understanding them.

He ultimately spent two years in an Israeli prison after being convicted in a military court system that has a conviction rate of over 96% for Palestinians. Sarsour was again detained by Israeli authorities for nearly three months when he last visited Palestine in 1995.

His lawyers detailed those facts over four immigration court hearings, during which they noted that the government had for years known about Sarsour’s arrests in Israel.

In addition to his involvement with several local organizations, Sarsour is a board member of American Muslims for Palestine (AMP), a national advocacy group that Trump administration officials have accused of countering US foreign policy interests.

“They’re retaliating against him for speaking out about Palestinian human rights,” said Luna Droubi, another attorney. “That should terrify all of us.”

“It’s a principle of this country that people should feel that they can speak freely, and that’s being eradicated”.

In a statement, Sarsour, who has six children and nine grandchildren, all US citizens, called the decision “deeply disappointing” but vowed to “continue fighting”.

“We have a mission: let’s continue to make our voice clear, to protect the first amendment, to support justice,” he told the Guardian in July. “I’ll continue with that message whether I’m inside or outside.”

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Department of Homeland Security has tapped $20 million to pay for the campaign-style ads glorifying President Donald Trump that have drawn widespread criticism from Republicans and Democrats as a blatant misuse of taxpayer dollars that likely runs afoul of anti-propaganda law.

In a letter Tuesday to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, two top Democratic senators said that the money is being drawn from Trump's so-called "One Big Beautiful Bill" and was supposed to go for U.S. Customs and Border Protection.

"We should not have to remind you that using government funding to create or air political ads like the ones that have been running over the last few days is illegal and a shockingly corrupt misuse of taxpayer dollars," wrote Sen. Patty Murray of Washington, the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, and Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut, the ranking Democrat on the subcommittee that handles Homeland Security funding.

The senators, in their letter to Mullin, demanded answers within the next 48 hours about "how this president is literally stealing their tax dollars to air campaign ads celebrating himself."

They asked the secretary if the department plans to use additional federal funds to air these ads or create new ones, and if so to share contracting information with the Congress. They also asked Mullin if he had spoken to Trump about using the taxpayer funds for the ads.

The political uproar over Trump's hagiographic ads, which started running last week during popular TV shows, including college and National Football League programming, has not abated as critics on the left and right raise alarms about the use of taxpayer funds, particularly so close to the midterm elections.

The White House has defended the advertisements, which disclose that they are funded by the U.S. government, as public service announcements.

Ad spend is up to $2.5m as criticism and legal scrutiny grow

The unusual commercials, which echo the GOP's midterm election slogans, against imagery of Trump's tenure in office — one with a "Love me, Love me" song refrain in the background — appear to violate a law against congressionally appropriated funds being used for propaganda. Experts also have said the ads, which are airing on network and cable TV and streaming, differ from other administrations' PSAs because they aren't designed to help Americans access any specific program.

Over the weekend, a new ad promoting the president resembles a black-and-white video from his own 2024 campaign that shows Trump walking down a hallway as his voice can be heard warning of a "final battle" against "globalists" and "warmongers." It ends with Trump staring straight into the camera lens with the "Paid for by the U.S. Government" message printed.

WATCH: Tamara Keith and Amy Walter on taxpayer funds used for TV ads promoting Trump

Sen. Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, compared Trump's ads to those used by authoritarian former leader Viktor Orban of Hungary. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a Republican from South Dakota, said it "shouldn't be paid for with taxpayer dollars."

Data from the outside firm AdImpact shows more than $2.5 million was spent on the three ads over the past seven days. The actual amount spent could be significantly more, depending on whether networks classified the ads as political.

The senators said that DHS has committed $20 million to the campaign.

A person who was unauthorized to discuss the situation and granted anonymity confirmed the findings, which were first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

Trump's ads use taxpayer dollars, likely skirting the law

The unusual ad campaign comes as Republicans face an increasingly volatile midterm election season with their control of the House and Senate — and Trump's future agenda — all at risk.

Voters say they are struggling with high prices of gas and groceries, and are concerned about the lengthy U.S. war against Iran, now in its seventh month. Democrats are gearing up for vast oversight of Trump and his administration if they seize power, and impeachment is not off the table.

House Democrats said Trump's director of the Office of Management and Budget, Russ Vought, moved the money from Homeland Security to the ad campaign on Sept. 19.

The Homeland Security funds are part of a whopping $175 billion Congress gave the department in the "Big, Beautiful, Bill" as part of his immigration enforcement and deportation agenda. Democrats voted against that package, which Trump signed into law last summer, in part because of its steep cuts to Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, known as SNAP.

Rep. Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, and Rep. Henry Cuellar of Texas, the ranking Democrat on the Homeland Security subcommittee, said that after gutting $1 trillion from Medicaid and social services and "more than quadrupling funding for mass deportations, it turns out the Trump administration used Republicans' One Big Beautiful Bill to pay for President Trump's political ads."

They said when Democrats regain control, they "will work to uncover and reverse misuses of taxpayer money like this and hold those who abused their power accountable."

What's also striking about the administration's use of taxpayer dollars for the ads is that Trump's own political campaign committee MAGA Inc. is sitting on hundreds of millions of dollars of funding that could be used during the midterm season. Groups aligned with MAGA Inc. have started shelling out funds for the House and Senate races.

The administration has defended the use of the taxpayer dollars for the ads and shown no signs of changing course.

text:
This story was reported and written by VPM News.

It started with something Paul Fleisher could see from the road on his commute: planes.

But these weren’t the commercial jets most people associate with the Richmond International Airport. They were parked on the far end of the airport, away from the main terminal.

Fleisher, who lives in Henrico County, started noticing them — and white prison transfer buses — more often on his way to his workout at the YMCA, or when he went to check out books at the Sandston Public Library.

Eventually, he connected the flights to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

“From what I understand, one of the strategies that ICE is using is to shuffle people around from place to place. It makes it hard for their family members to know where they are — or if not impossible,” Fleisher said.

ICE operates a network of chartered flights working with private airlines like the ones Fleisher observed — GlobalX and Eastern Air Express — not just to deport people from the United States, but to move people in its custody between local detention centers and the Alexandria Staging Facility in Louisiana, a major hub for ICE’s air operations.

ICE did not respond to emailed questions.

The 78-year-old retiree started documenting the flights by taking photos and submitting them to a local Facebook page, RVA ICE-SCREAM, to raise awareness.

“I’d like to know who these folks are who are being flown somewhere. I’d like to know where they’re going,” Fleisher told VPM News on Sept. 11. I’d like to know how this permission to do these flights locally here at the Richmond airport came about.”

For people in ICE custody, these flights can mean more than simply being moved from one place to another.

They impact family visitation, legal counsel and illustrate how quickly someone can move through the system — as was the case for former Richmond resident Ricardo Martinez Cantanero last summer.

According to a letter he wrote, after being detained at Southwood Apartments, he was moved through local ICE facilities before being brought to RIC — where he first boarded a GlobalX plane that landed in Texas, then at ICE’s Alexandria Staging Facility, before finally landing in his home county of Honduras. The entire process took three days.

Fleisher said he believes he has a moral obligation to speak up, as many in Greater Richmond may not know this is happening locally.

“First of all, our country is a nation of immigrants. My grandparents came from Eastern Europe. No person — no human being — should be treated the way that these undocumented immigrants are being treated,” Fleisher said. “So when you see an injustice, you have the obligation to speak up.”

More than 100 flights already this year

Human Rights First’s ICE Flight Monitor, which tracks immigration enforcement flights using publicly available aviation data and other sources, has documented a growing number of flights involving Richmond International Airport. This issue was first reported by the Henrico Citizen in 2025.

The organization counted 128 enforcement flights departing from RIC in 2025. Through July of this year, it counted 104.

Troy Bell, spokesperson for the Capital Region Airport Commission (which owns and operates RIC), said flights with people detained have passed through RIC for several years, but noted that these flights have increased “substantially” since early 2025. When asked for a flight count, Bell told VPM News the airport does not maintain a flight count for any chartered operations.

The ICE Flight Monitor also documented dozens of domestic “shuffle” flights this summer — flights being used to move people in ICE custody between detention centers and other locations.

According to Human Rights First’s August report, in the month of July, 1,363 shuffle flights operated across 61 cities, the highest number recorded since at least 2020.

Flights departed from Richmond three to four times per week in July, according to the report.

But Bell told VPM News that the commission has no direct agreement with the Department of Homeland Security or US Immigration and Customs Enforcement pertaining to these flights. Nor, he said, does it have “the legal right to either authorize or refuse DHS/ICE flights.”

Approval for these flights comes from the air traffic control tower at RIC, which is in charge of approving operations on the airfield — including takeoffs and landings.

The Richmond tower is operated by the Federal Aviation Administration. Because RIC regularly accepts federal funding, it is subject to FAA “grant assurances,” which are requirements airports agree to follow in exchange for funding.

Recent changes to the FAA’s Airport Compliance Manual reinforce Grant Assurance #27, which requires federally obligated airports to: “… make airport facilities available to the United States for use by Government aircraft ‘at all times’ and in common with other aircraft.”

“RIC may not ban ICE flights or request a reroute to another airport, as the FAA has exclusive sovereignty over U.S. navigable airspace,” Bell said.

The FAA did not respond to a list of questions from VPM News, including the agency’s role in determining that an aircraft chartered by the Department of Homeland Security or ICE would use RIC as part of its operations.

Bell noted that these flights don’t utilize the airport’s commercial gates or terminals. He also confirmed that fixed-base operators, like Richmond Jet Center, handle the ground marshalling of these government charter flights and provide fuel.

When asked if the airport commission receives any revenue associated with these flights, Bell said operators like RJC pay fixed rent — with or without handling government charters.

Per Richmond BizSense, Richmond Jet Center finalized a 5-year contract and facility upgrade terms with RIC in May 2025. According to terms of the lease, RJC pays the airport an annual rent of $582,000.

RJC did not respond to questions from VPM News.

Calls to end ICE flights

Over 100 people gathered on a Saturday in September alongside Airport Drive to protest the airport’s position.

Fleisher — a lifelong activist who demonstrated as a teenager to desegregate his local movie theatre in Harford County, Maryland, and later was an antiwar activist during the Vietnam War — helped organize the protest alongside RVA Indivisible. To him, the gathering allowed others with concerns a chance to speak out in a more visible way.

Holding signs that read “END SHUFFLE FLIGHTS” and “STOP ICE FLIGHTS,” demonstrators said the protest was not simply a call to stop the flights, but a demand for greater transparency on how this is allowed to happen at RIC.

Bill Muth, a Richmond resident, said so much of what the Department of Homeland Security is doing happens under a veil of secrecy. He said demonstrating is his way to make visible what DHS is “desperately trying to keep invisible.”

“We’re learning so much about how Richmond International Airport is integral to the shipment of innocent people out of this country or to other detention centers, and it’s just not normal, and it’s just not okay,” Muth said.

For others, participating in the protest is about showing solidarity.

Janet Eddy, an organizer with the Central Virginia Indivisible chapter, said that she wants the immigrant community to know they are not alone.

“Part of the reason I come out here is because whenever an immigrant comes by in their car, I hope they can hold this image as they listen to people say horrible things that aren’t true about them,” Eddy said.

As for Fleisher, he described the protest as a success and hopes that it will be a first step forward, although he admits he’s not sure what comes next.

“Maybe talking to local leaders. Maybe talking to the airport commission. Maybe identifying the flight carriers that are flying in and out of here, and if we can find some way to put some economic pressure on them — to do that,” Fleisher said at the protest.

CHICAGO (AP) — The U.S. can deport the leader of Wisconsin’s largest mosque — an outspoken advocate of Palestinian rights — on the grounds that he is a threat to national security, an immigration judge ruled on Sept. 30.

Salah Sarsour was detained in Milwaukee in March by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers. A federal judge ordered Sarsour’s release in June, saying he raised a “substantial” claim that the Trump administration was targeting him for speaking out against Israel and advocating for Palestinian rights.

Sarsour called the ruling “deeply disappointing,” but said he intends to appeal.

“I will continue fighting to defend the right to free speech and to stay in the country I have called home for more than three decades,” Sarsour said in a statement.

Government attorneys say Sarsour’s decades-old convictions in Israel make him a threat to national security and accuse him of lying on his green card application and falsely claiming citizenship to vote. Judge Jayme Salinardi, with the Chicago Immigration Court, found him removable on foreign policy grounds but tossed out the government’s claim that Sarsour lied to immigration authorities.

The Department of Homeland Security has not responded to an emailed request for comment on the decision.

Sarsour says his life will be at risk if he is deported to the West Bank

Sarsour, who was born in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, was imprisoned in Israel in 1988 after being convicted of throwing stones at Israeli military personnel. DHS has said he was also convicted of throwing a Molotov cocktail. His defense team says he was accused of that but not convicted. In 1995, he was convicted of attempting to possess weapons. Sarsour denies committing those crimes and his attorneys say he was tortured and coerced into confessing in both instances.

Sarsour, the president of the Islamic Society of Milwaukee, does not have a criminal record in the U.S., where he has lived since 1993. His attorneys say the U.S. government has known about Sarsour’s convictions in Israel since he arrived.

Deportation to the West Bank “means the end of my life,” Sarsour told The Associated Press on Sept. 29.

One of his attorneys, Patrick Taurel, said Sarsour’s treatment by Israeli authorities is “probably a good indicator of what awaits him” if he is deported.

At a status hearing on Sept. 30, Taurel pressed the judge to specify that Sarsour can only be deported to Israel or the Palestinian territories. Jordan, a country to which Sarsour has no connection, is listed as a possible destination on the order of removal.

Sarsour was instructed by immigration officers to list Jordan as his home country on an immigration form because his preferred entry — “Palestine” — is not a fully independent, unified state. But he “has no right to reside in Jordan,” Taurel said.

Salinardi declined, saying that can be addressed on appeal.

If sent to Jordan, Sarsour “would just be immediately handed off to Israel,” Taurel said during a news conference on Sept. 30.

Attorney says Sarsour will fight deportation

Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a memo in June 2025 invoking a rarely used immigration provision saying Sarsour could be deported on the same grounds as Mahmoud Khalil and Mohsen Mahdawi, both advocates for Palestinian rights whom the Trump administration has tried to expel, according to court documents.

Salinardi found Rubio’s letter singling out Sarsour as a foreign policy risk was “presumptive and sufficient evidence” that the government can remove him, Taurel said Sept. 30, reading from the judge’s decision. The judge gave “extreme deference” to Rubio and to Israel, which has “collaborated” with DHS in the effort to deport Sarsour, the attorney said.

Taurel has said Sarsour will need to demonstrate that he could be tortured again if he were deported, calling it a “very high bar” that he believes his team “can meet in this case.”

A notice of appeal is due within 30 days, and Sarsour has 60 days to file an application for relief. The government cannot deport Sarsour until he has exhausted all available legal avenues. Salinardi, who did not schedule a new hearing, announced he is retiring and that Judge Craig Defoe will oversee the case going forward.

Sarsour says he was tortured and coerced into confessions

Jawad Boulos, who represented Sarsour when he was convicted in Israel, testified in August that Sarsour was coerced into confessing and that he wasn’t convicted of any charge tying him to a terrorist organization. He said Sarsour was tortured by Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency.

The Department of Homeland Security challenged Boulos about the torture allegations, questioning how he could know it was true.

Sarsour’s defense team has repeatedly asked why the government waited until 2026 to detain him, saying it has known of his imprisonment in Israel for decades.

Experts on forced confessions and the treatment of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli prisons also testified in Sarsour’s defense. Israeli military courts have faced repeated scrutiny over allegations of limited due process and the high conviction rate of Palestinians. Israel rejects the claims.

In June, U.S. District Judge James Patrick Hanlon ordered Sarsour released from ICE custody saying he could have a case arguing the U.S. government detained him in retaliation for protected speech. Further, Hanlon said, government attorneys had not explained why Sarsour was suddenly considered a threat after decades as a lawful permanent resident.

The Trump administration has appealed Hanlon’s ruling.

Sarsour, who has Type 2 diabetes, lost more than 30 pounds while detained by ICE, and his blood sugar levels were checked only once a month, putting him at risk of organ failure or death, his attorneys said.

An investigation by KFF Health News and The Associated Press found that hundreds of detainees in at least 33 states have filed federal lawsuits with similar allegations of medical neglect.

Trump admin denies app removals are retaliation The Trump administration has asked the court to dismiss Aaron’s lawsuit, claiming that Apple independently chose to moderate that content, despite comments from agency officials suggesting otherwise.

text:
Apple continues to face backlash for removing ICE-tracking apps like ICEBlock from the App Store, a drastic step that seemed to be triggered by Trump administration claims that the apps endangered officers.

According to US Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), Apple has no evidence to support claims that apps raised safety concerns. Instead, the lawmaker accused Apple of using immigrant deaths with no connection to the apps to justify censoring Americans who have the right to record ICE activity.

It appears that Apple is “working with the government to violate its customers’ First Amendment rights to record and report on the activities of their own government,” Raskin said in a letter to Apple sent Monday, CNN reported.

Raskin had been hounding Apple for answers for months. In July, Apple finally explained to Raskin that ICEBlock was removed, along with other apps, after a fatal shooting left two detainees dead at a Dallas ICE office, CNN reported.

As an earlier CNN report explained, the shooter in that case, Joshua Jahn, fired bullets indiscriminately into the ICE facility before dying of a self-inflicted gunshot. Jahn left notes saying that he “hoped his actions would give ICE agents real terror of being gunned down.”

At that time, the US attorney for the Northern District of Texas, Nancy Larson, highlighted the “tragic irony” that it was a detainee who was killed during the attacks, CNN’s report said. But the Department of Homeland Security, along with FBI director Kash Patel, has since claimed that the incident showed agents were being targeted. DHS also frequently cites an internal October 2025 statistic claiming that ICE officers face an 8,000 percent increase in death threats. The agency will not release data to let independent parties verify that claim.

Additionally, Patel has said that the Texas shooter “searched for apps that tracked ICE agents’ locations.” But Raskin pushed back on that claim, too, telling Apple that there is “no evidence” that the shooter used ICE-tracking apps. And even if he did, “he did not need a tracking app to locate the fixed position of a government building” and “is reported to have found the address using an app that comes standard on Apple devices,” Raskin’s letter said.

“There appears to be no direct connection between the Dallas incident and the apps you removed,” Raskin said.

Apple pressured to share DHS communications

To ensure that no Americans’ core speech rights are violated by removals unconstitutionally ordered by the government, Raskin has asked Apple to “send a full list of the apps it removed following concerns from the Justice Department” so that it will finally be possible to “conduct an independent review of those removal decisions.”

Federal officials have insisted that Apple acted on its own.

However, in a lawsuit accusing the Trump administration officials of censoring watchdogs, ICEBlock creator Joshua Aaron told the court that officials publicly bragged about getting the app removed. And in Apple’s July letter to Raskin—which was signed by Timothy Powderly, Apple’s senior director of government affairs—the iPhone maker seemed to confirm this. Powderly specifically cited agency reports of a “significant increase in ICE activity and threats against ICE” as triggering the follow-up review of ICE-tracking apps.

Apple claimed it was acting to protect both officers and detainees, ultimately deciding that sharing “precise location information about ICE officers (and, as a result, other individuals who may be in proximity to ICE agents, such as protestors or detainees)” provides “a potential roadmap for targeted violence and creating a significant risk of harm.”

The company “does not take decisions about removing apps from the App Store lightly, but acts when it must—especially when there are serious concerns that an app is creating safety risks,” Powderly said.

Raskin remains dubious that records will show the apps posed any risks. On Bluesky, Aaron did not comment directly on CNN’s report, but he did boost an ICEBlock post that thanked Raskin for continuing to press Apple to explain the removals.

“Apple’s sticking to their story even though everyone can see this was jawboning plain as day,” ICEBlock’s post said.

Trump admin denies app removals are retaliation

The Trump administration has asked the court to dismiss Aaron’s lawsuit, claiming that Apple independently chose to moderate that content, despite comments from agency officials suggesting otherwise.

It doesn’t matter that former officials like Pam Bondi publicly took credit for removing ICEBlock from the App Store, boasting that she made the “demand” and “Apple did so.” Those comments were merely officials expressing opinions about Apple’s promotion of supposedly dangerous apps, they argued. They’re hoping the court will agree that Aaron has not uncovered evidence of communications that can be “reasonably understood to convey a threat of adverse government action” against Apple “if Apple chose not to remove ICEBlock from the App Store.”

But in an August ruling, the Second Circuit recently upheld that courts broadly recognize “a First Amendment right to record law enforcement activity in public,” Aaron argued in a recent filing that could influence how the case is decided at this stage. In his opposition to the government’s motion to dismiss, Aaron maintained that the record showed that the government was acting to censor Americans.

As he argued:

The then-Attorney General told the nation she demanded removal of the app, Apple reversed a decision it previously reached after a thorough five-week legal review citing only “information provided to Apple by law enforcement,” and the then-Attorney General characterized Apple’s response as “compliance.”

If the case proceeds, which Aaron expects it will, discovery would likely reveal the actual communications between government officials and Apple leadership, which so far have remained hidden. Only then can a court sufficiently determine if “a threat of adverse government action” triggered app removals, Aaron argued.

Raskin told Apple that he thinks the removal decisions won’t fly under the First Amendment.

“Monitoring the actions of federal immigration authorities who have been deployed to (users’) neighborhoods… is a core First Amendment right and not a crime,” Raskin said.

text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE: September 30, 2026

CONTACT: press@acaciajustice.org

WASHINGTON –Today, the Acacia Center for Justice released a new report, “Freeing Children, Reuniting Families: The Power of Habeas Advocacy,” documenting a troubling increase in the number of unaccompanied children spending months in federal custody despite having parents, relatives, and other caregivers ready to care for them. The report also finds a dramatic rise in habeas corpus petitions filed on behalf of children and highlights the growing role of the Children’s Due Process Project (CDPP) in securing children’s release and reunification with family.

The report reveals that since the beginning of the second Trump administration, there has been a 3,500% increase in habeas filings on behalf of unaccompanied children compared to filings during the entire previous administration from 2021 through 2024. At the same time, children who historically spent approximately 30 days in Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) custody before reunification are now spending more than 170 days in custody on average, prolonging family separation and delaying access to stability and support.

“The report shows that children are increasingly turning to habeas in order to be released from federal custody,” said Jill Williams, Principal Research and Evaluation Manager and the lead author of the report. “These are not cases where children lack sponsors or caregivers. Instead, government-created delays, repeated vetting requirements, and procedural barriers are keeping children separated from their families for what amounts to nearly a full school year for the average child in the US. What we see in the data is that petitions are overwhelmingly successful at compelling children’s release, raising questions as to why they are experiencing prolonged detention in the first place.”

Referrals to the Children’s Due Process Project have continued to climb since the report’s study period ended, underscoring the growing need for legal intervention on behalf of detained children.

While the report documents a growing crisis, it also highlights an emerging legal response.

Through the Children’s Due Process Project, Acacia and its partners, the Immigration & Human Rights Clinic at Loyola University Chicago School of Law, The Door, and National Center for Youth Law (NCYL), are connecting detained children with experienced pro bono counsel to challenge unlawful and prolonged detention. Early results demonstrate both the urgent need for representation and the legal community’s willingness to respond. Nearly 60% of referred cases have already been matched with pro bono attorneys; more than one-third remain in active placement, and approximately one-third of referrals have already resulted in successful outcomes for detained children.

One of the first children represented through the project spent 186 days in government custody before a habeas petition was filed on his behalf. Just ten days after filing, he was released and reunited with his father.

“Behind every statistic is a child waiting to return home,” Jessica Viramontes, Co-Manager of the Children’s Due Process Project, “This case demonstrates what the report shows nationally: when children gain access to experienced legal advocates and federal courts, release is almost guaranteed to follow, and demonstrates why the government’s current procedures are unnecessary.”

According to the report, the increase in prolonged custody is driven not by an absence of suitable caregivers but by increasingly burdensome reunification processes.

“This is family separation dressed up as paperwork,” said Kel White, Associate Director of Public Education and Training at Acacia.

The findings come amid broader concerns about where newly detained children are being sent. Recent reporting found that more and more children the government detains in Texas, while advocates and members of Congress have also raised concerns about efforts to expand child detention capacity in Louisiana. These developments raise significant questions about children’s access to family, legal counsel, medical care and due process protections.

text:
As the government continues to bomb civilians in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific, this decision ordering in camera review of the memo is a crucial win for transparency and accountability

September 30, 2026, New York — Today, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York rejected several of the Trump administration’s key rationales for withholding an Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) opinion that it is using to justify its ongoing extrajudicial boat strike campaign, which has murdered 234 people. The court also ordered the government to provide additional details about who has seen the memo and how they have used it, and to turn the memo over to the court so the judge can determine whether it should be released publicly. The judge gave the government until October 14 to comply with his order.

The court found that the administration has adopted the memo as its “working law,” noting that “the assembled record compellingly supports the finding that DOD—the agency that asserts disclosure authority over the Memo—has treated the Memo as its effective law and policy governing the boat strikes.” However, the court also ordered the administration to provide it with further information so that it may rule on whether the memo is protected as a closely held presidential advice document.

This decision comes months after the American Civil Liberties Union, the New York Civil Liberties Union, and the Center for Constitutional Rights sued to force disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA).

“The public deserves to know how our government is justifying the cold-blooded murder of hundreds of civilians. Today’s order is a huge step in the right direction of ensuring that the government does not get to summarily execute people based on secret law,” said Jeffrey Stein, staff attorney with the ACLU’s National Security Project.

The still-secret memo reportedly blesses the ongoing strikes as lawful acts in an alleged “armed conflict” with unspecified “drug cartels,” and also purports to immunize personnel who authorize or take part in these unlawful strikes from future criminal prosecution for what would otherwise be considered homicide.

“No president can arbitrarily assassinate people from the sky based on their sole say-so,” said Center for Constitutional Rights Legal Director Baher Azmy. “If the OLC opinion seeks to dress up the obvious illegality of these serial murders in legalese to provide Trump cover, the public needs to see that analysis and ultimately hold accountable all those who facilitate murder in the United States’ name.”

The court held that the Department of Defense has expressly adopted the legal reasoning in the OLC memo as binding on the agency, which means that the memo cannot be maintained as “secret law.” Among other conclusions, the ruling rejected the government’s claim that it could withhold the OLC memo from the public as privileged under the deliberative process and attorney-client privileges.

In addition to this FOIA lawsuit, the ACLU and the Center for Constitutional Rights have also filed a lawsuit on behalf of two families from Trinidad & Tobago who are seeking redress after a U.S. boat strike killed their loved ones.

For more information, see here and here.

title: Clinton-Era Laws Passed 30 Years Ago Enabled Trump's Anti-Immigrant Agenda. | Truthout
authors: Zack Kligler, Laura Hernández, Shireen Akram-Boshar, Sharon Zhang, Mike Ludwig, Victoria Valenzuela, Chris Walker, Julia Conley, Amy Goodman, Alex Nguyen
description:
We must finally confront and uproot the core of the U.S.’s anti-immigrant underbelly, which is largely reflected in the racially motivated notion of criminalization.
The numbers show just how much these laws have supercharged the mass incarceration and deportation of immigrants over the past 30 years.
In 1995, 50,924 people were deported and fewer than 7,500 people were held in immigration detention.
Once mandatory detention created the demand, private prison companies cashed in and played an integral role in building what is now the world’s largest immigration detention system.
Today, the ’96 laws continue to be key tools the Trump administration uses to carry out its immigration agenda.
text:
The more the American public sees of President Donald Trump’s hardline, anti-immigrant policies in action — the deaths, military-style invasions of neighborhoods, and mass detention and deportations — the more his approval on the issue drops.

If this trend sounds familiar, it’s because a similar wave of disapproval played out in Trump’s first term. Despite that backlash, Trump returned to office embracing even more extreme measures.

We must finally confront and uproot the core of the U.S.’s anti-immigrant underbelly, which is largely reflected in the racially motivated notion of criminalization.

Trump was not the first politician to exploit the concept of criminality, and he certainly won’t be the last. Criminalizing narratives are deeply planted in the American psyche, and they have commonly acted as the vessel through which white supremacist rhetoric and policy are ingrained into our culture and laws.

In the late 1980’s, criminalization went mainstream in the form of racist dog whistles, particularly those hinging on vile anti-Blackness deployed by politicians seeking to activate white voters. In the decades since, conservative and liberal leaders alike more purposefully extended this criminality framework to immigration — so much so that it’s now perhaps the primary driver of the public immigration debate.

Consider how Americans of all political stripes are often presented with the binary choice of supporting the “right” type of immigrant. In this oversimplification, immigrants fall into categories like “good” or “bad,” “legal” or “illegal,” “deserving” or “undeserving.”

Trump did not invent these narratives. They’ve underpinned both major parties’ politics of immigration for several decades, despite their basis in fiction and fear-mongering rather than evidence and compassion, or the fact these narratives are weaponized against non-white immigrants who for centuries have disproportionately faced restrictive and punitive policies for the act of seeking relief in this country.

But Trump’s partisan opposition, despite its massive opportunities in the face of unpopular, hardline policies, has repeatedly failed to capture the public’s long-term support on immigration. Too often, Democrats repackage the same old criminalizing narratives — often in softer terms, but always in line with the oversimplified good-or-bad thinking. This lack of imagination is reflected in the nearly annual bipartisan votes to increase funding for federal enforcement agencies like Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection, as well as Democratic leaders’ messaging and policies.

Take, for example, former President Barack Obama’s push to deport “felons, not families”; Joe Biden squandering his mandate to reverse the cruelty of Trump’s first term by continuing many Trump policies, like Title 42 and the backing of for-profit immigrant detention; or Kamala Harris, in her presidential bid, focusing much of her immigration rhetoric on “securing” the border.

It’s a toxic cycle: The public rightfully disapproves of the atrocities of anti-immigrant policies; in response, liberals roll out unimaginative plans hinged on outdated narratives; and finally, in the vacuum created by the lack of any tangible, pro-immigrant vision, the right recaptures the public’s attention with fear mongering and a sensationalist focus on crime and the border.

To break this cycle, we must imagine a pro-immigrant future in which our communities, not politicians and pundits, get to define safety.

We can start with recognizing that the modern-day legal basis for the criminalization of immigrants largely rests on a pair of anti-immigrant bills signed into law by Bill Clinton 30 years ago. Building upon the U.S. legacy of racialized immigration control, the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act (IIRIRA) and the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act (AEDPA) further entrenched mass incarceration and laid the blueprint for the detention and deportation machine we have today.

These laws drastically expanded the government’s ability to automatically detain and deport people without due process and without consideration for their current circumstances.

IIRIRA, in particular, dramatically expanded who can be deported, made detention mandatory, created fast-track deportations, and stripped immigration judges of much of their discretion.

The numbers show just how much these laws have supercharged the mass incarceration and deportation of immigrants over the past 30 years. In 1995, 50,924 people were deported and fewer than 7,500 people were held in immigration detention. By 1997, the number of people deported more than doubled to 114,432, and by 2001, 20,500 people were held in detention. Thirty years later, the devastation has only climbed higher, with nearly 330,000 people deported in 2025 and roughly 70,000 people in ICE detention today.

Once mandatory detention created the demand, private prison companies cashed in and played an integral role in building what is now the world’s largest immigration detention system. Today, approximately 90 percent of people detained in ICE custody are held in prisons owned or operated by private corporations.

The bills also provided the blueprint to turbocharge detention and deportation by further entangling the criminal legal and immigration systems. In what is known as the prison-to-ICE pipeline, immigrants are subject to double punishment; many face the loss of their freedom twice for the same conviction. Because ICE can arrest people as they’re released from prison (despite that individual serving their time and completing their sentence) many are re-incarcerated on the very day they would otherwise go home to their families.

This double standard disproportionately punishes Black people and reinforces systemic racism by propagating existing racial disparities — like those found in conviction rates and policing practices like profiling — into the immigration system.

Today, the ’96 laws continue to be key tools the Trump administration uses to carry out its immigration agenda. As the administration’s enforcement net widens to target and arrest political dissidents, families, and even U.S. citizens, we must recognize the role criminalizing narratives have played in leading us to our present slide into authoritarianism. Criminalization is the primary justification used to make these cruel policies all the more entrenched and widespread.

Here lies the danger of not fighting the root of the problem: When we concede fundamental rights like due process for some, we begin to concede those rights for all. When we fight only for those immigrants who have not yet been labeled “criminal,” we’ll find ourselves unprepared when authoritarians inevitably stamp that label on more and more of us.

Enough with the exclusions.

All people are worthy of human dignity, due process, and the right to live in safety, no matter where we were born. Those who have been previously ensnared in the U.S. carceral system — including those who have committed harm in their past — are not disposable. They’re people, often with full lives established in the U.S., who are worthy of redemption and second chances like anyone else.

To build toward this vision, we must rally around bold proposals that affirm these values. We must reject the toxic “good immigrant/bad immigrant” narrative once and for all and champion a vision in which freedom, human rights, and basic human dignity are the floor for our demands, not merely concessions or carveouts for some.

Legislatively, we must repeal laws like the IIRIRA and AEDPA bills of 1996, and their modern-day counterparts like the Laken Riley Act, which expands mandatory detention. The New Way Forward Act offers a concrete start to fixing much of the damage of the ‘96 laws. And at the border, it won’t be enough to restore the U.S. asylum system to its pre-Trump state. Instead, we must decriminalize the act of seeking safety or economic security.

At the state and local level, communities can chip away at the interconnected carceral and deportation dragnet by fighting for legislation that blocks local law enforcement’s collaboration with ICE, including the transfer of people from local jails and prisons to the agency.

Ultimately, to turn the tide, it’s going to take all of us. In each of our lives, we must resist the urge — at work, the dinner table, online, and in our opposition to Trumpism — to tie one’s worth and humanity to however they’ve been labeled. In fighting for everyone, we’ll advance our struggle for fairness, justice, and family unity. And we’ll just so happen to build a winning coalition along the way.
