title: Constitution Day Speaker Explores Rights of Immigrants - News - Stockton University
description:
Das delivered Stockton’s annual Constitution Day lecture, “Rights, Resistance, and the Deportation Machine.
They are constitutional questions.
Das used the story of her longtime client and immigrant rights advocate Ravi Ragbir to illustrate how constitutional protections intersect with immigration enforcement.
Das urged the audience to view constitutional rights not simply as principles contained in a document, but as protections that depend on people asserting and defending them.
Prior to the keynote lecture, Das met with Political Science students for a question-and-answer session on the Constitution and immigration policy.
text:
Galloway, N.J. – Constitutional rights can provide critical protections for immigrants facing detention and deportation, but those protections depend on people willing to affirm and defend them, immigration law scholar Alina Das told a Stockton University audience Sept. 29.

Das delivered Stockton’s annual Constitution Day lecture, “Rights, Resistance, and the Deportation Machine. She is a Professor of Law and James Weldon Johnson Professor at NYU School of Law, where she is co-director of the Immigrant Rights Clinic.

“Constitution Day gives us an opportunity to do something universities should do especially well: ask difficult questions, examine ideas carefully, listen to different perspectives, and deepen our understanding of the rights and responsibilities that shape our democracy,” said Joe Bertolino, Stockton University president.

“Tonight’s conversation takes us directly into questions that have been part of the American constitutional story for generations: questions about immigration, citizenship, government authority, individual rights, due process and the meaning of equal protection under the law,” Bertolino said. “These are legal questions. They are constitutional questions. But they are also deeply human questions because laws and policies ultimately affect people, families and communities.”

Das has defended immigrants facing detention and deportation, including movement leaders. Her work focuses on the intersection of immigration and criminal law through litigation and advocacy. A widely published scholar cited by the U.S. Supreme Court, she is also the author of "No Justice in the Shadows: How America Criminalizes Immigrants " (2020).

Das used the story of her longtime client and immigrant rights advocate Ravi Ragbir to illustrate how constitutional protections intersect with immigration enforcement. Ragbir, a lawful permanent resident who had served a sentence for a federal fraud conviction, later spent nearly two years in immigration detention while fighting deportation. After his release, he became an advocate for other immigrants facing detention and deportation.

Das represented Ragbir through continued attempts at deportation after he was detained again by immigration authorities in 2018. His legal team argued the government had targeted him because of his outspoken advocacy for immigrant rights, raising First Amendment questions about the government’s power to punish speech.

“No matter what the speech is, our government should not have the power to weaponize the immigration system in order to censor viewpoints or to control public debate,” Das said. “The beauty of the First Amendment is it protects not only our right to speak, but our right to listen. For the public to hear all sides of the debate and decide for ourselves what we believe is right or wrong.”

Ragbir’s case ultimately involved another power established by the Constitution: the presidential pardon. President Joe Biden granted Ragbir a full and unconditional pardon in January 2025, removing the criminal conviction that was the basis of his deportation proceedings.

Das urged the audience to view constitutional rights not simply as principles contained in a document, but as protections that depend on people asserting and defending them. “The Constitution holds great promise for immigrants in this country. But it is ultimately up to all of us to protect and advance those rights,” she said.

For two decades, Stockton has commemorated the signing of the United States Constitution with a keynote address each fall featuring prominent legal scholars, practitioners or journalists.

Prior to the keynote lecture, Das met with Political Science students for a question-and-answer session on the Constitution and immigration policy.

Stockton’s event is sponsored by the William J. Hughes Center for Public Policy, the Stockton University Foundation, University Advancement and the Office of the Provost.

--Story by Stacey Clapp; Photos by Abbigail Erbacher

text:
Key federal agencies failed to provide any records to back up President Donald Trump’s allegations that tens of thousands of noncitizens are registered to vote in various blue states, a nonpartisan government watchdog said in a new lawsuit.

Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, or CREW, told a federal court in Washington, D.C., that the administration is violating an open records law by failing to hand over information on its methodology and data sources on the matter.

Trump claimed without evidence during a primetime address to the nation in July that 278,000 noncitizens were registered to vote in federal elections. The unfounded allegation is part of a pattern of Trump spreading misinformation about voting fraud since losing the 2020 presidential race as he pushes Congress to pass onerous new restrictions on voting.

CREW filed several Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests asking how the administration determined that 278,000 figure.

The same day as Trump’s speech, the Department of Homeland Security released a statement asserting 250,000 noncitizens are registered in states like California, Nevada, New Jersey and Pennsylvania. Secretary Markwayne Mullin then sent letters to state election officials warning them about the alleged noncitizens on their rolls.

The lawsuit demands the Department of Homeland Security turn over records showing how it calculated that figure.

“DHS has declined to disclose its methodology despite election officials in at least three of the four states demanding it,” CREW wrote in its filing. “Without a transparent methodology, independent experts assert the administration’s figures cannot be evaluated and should not be credited.”

American Oversight, another government watchdog, also sued DHS for not responding to its own FOIA requests on noncitizen voting records in a separate lawsuit filed Wednesday.

The administration faces several lawsuits accusing federal agencies of defying FOIA requests or court orders for information regarding its plans for the midterm elections, including any records related to the potential seizure of ballots or deployment of federal agents to the polls.

So far, the administration’s efforts to find widespread noncitizen voting have turned up squat.

In Nevada, DHS initially told state officials there were as many as 15,903 potential noncitizens illegally registered to vote. That number then fell to 185. Just last week, Nevada election officials said the 185 individuals flagged are in fact all citizens.

In Pennsylvania, DHS admitted in late August that it didn’t have “high confidence” in its previous assertion that more than 14,000 noncitizens were on the voter rolls.

CREW said in its lawsuit that states “had no way to verify DHS’s claims” on noncitizen voters as “the agency failed to provide any underlying data or methodology.”

Not only that, but CREW said it’s “not clear how DHS could have compiled these statistics through legal means.”

The Department of Justice is 0-25 in its attempts to force states to surrender voter files containing sensitive information, including driver’s license numbers and Social Security data. Yet, CREW said the letters DHS sent to state election officials “indicate it matched registrants on precisely those fields.”

The watchdog also questioned whether the administration violated a federal court order that blocked DHS from using its flawed Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) system to remove voters from registration rolls. “DHS was prohibited from using the modified SAVE system until the Supreme Court stayed the order on September 25, 2026,” the group wrote.

“The public needs these records now in order to evaluate the truth of DHS’s claims, respond appropriately, and restore confidence in the election process ahead of the midterm elections,” the watchdog said.

text:
FAIR had shown third-country removals comply with binding regulations

WASHINGTON—Yesterday, the U.S. Supreme Court suspended a lower-court injunction stopping the ongoing removal of a class of dangerous alien criminals to nations other than their home countries. The injunction’s suspension allows the aliens to go on being removed while the case proceeds. The Federation for American Immigration Reform (FAIR) had filed an emergency brief in the Court the day before urging that result.

The aliens—who have been convicted of such crimes as child sexual assault, sexual abuse of the mentally disabled, and murder—claimed that if they were removed to their home countries, they would face torture. But when federal officials asked them if they would consent to being removed to nations such as South Sudan—countries that have agreed to take them—instead, they said yes. Nevertheless, the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts enjoined their removal as inconsistent with this country’s treaty obligations under the Convention Against Torture (CAT), and the First Circuit affirmed.

As FAIR showed in its brief, however, the appellate court failed to show how the removals were inconsistent with CAT. Instead, it rewrote and added to the regulations under which such removals are carried out—which implement CAT as directed by Congress and therefore have the force of law—by claiming that the regulations require individualized diplomatic assurances that a given alien will not be tortured. Actually, the regulations require “credible” diplomatic assurances to that effect, which might be blanket assurances that no aliens of a given description will be tortured, and make no mention of extra, individualized assurances about particular aliens so covered.

“There was no real issue of torture in this case,” said Christopher J. Hajec, deputy general counsel of FAIR. “These aliens are being sent to countries that have no motive to torture them, and have given America assurances that they won’t. These removals are obviously legal, and we are pleased the Supreme Court has cut off the contrived delaying tactics of the lower courts by suspending the injunction.”

The case is DHS v. D.V.D., et al., No. 26A406 (Supreme Court).

title: DACA: Immigration Reform, Human Rights and the American Story - Tufts University
description:
In the United States (and in the so-called liberal West), immigrant communities are consistently characterized as sources of crime, disease, cultural and social decay.
DACA residents have come to understand themselves as part of an innumerable population of undocumented residents in the US.
The Mexican diaspora to the United States was targeted in the 1930’s at the height of the Great Depression.
DACA residents expose persistent questions in the USA of what constitutes statehood/citizenship.
Unfortunately, they were unaware that the American immigration system and political structure would deny them this DREAM.
text:
By: Niklas Robinson

President Barack Obama (2008-16) signed the executive order establishing the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program on 15 June 2012. These “Dreamers” included approximately 1.2 million people who arrived in the United States at a young age, without permanent residency. He further amended immigration policy in 2014 to include undocumented immigrants with children who were permanent residents or citizens, benefiting an additional 3.7 million residents. The program required applicants to renew their status every three years and pay accompanying fees. Residents under these immigration laws did not face deportation and could apply for work permits. This immigration policy signaled positive movement by the executive branch on immigration and exempted 6.7 million people from deportation. As of 2016, 74 percent of immigrants in the US hold permanent legal status as permanent residents, refugees, or asylum seekers. DACA and the Obama era immigration policies protected some undocumented people from repatriation; however, they did not end the historical trend of US immigration authorities continuing to deport migrant populations by the millions. In fact, under the Obama administration, over 5 million people were deported to their home countries. Regardless of who sits in the Oval Office, persecution of immigrants is a bipartisan issue. In the United States (and in the so-called liberal West), immigrant communities are consistently characterized as sources of crime, disease, cultural and social decay. Nativist reactions are not simply a historical anomaly resulting from discrete political crises; they are a recurring historical pattern.

The 2012 and 2014 executive orders signaled an attempt by the American government to resolve the unfinished “Dream Act” (Development, Relief, and Education for Alien Minors Act), first introduced in Congress on 1 August 2001 by Senators Dick Durbin and Orrin Hatch. This bipartisan bill was scheduled for debate in the House on October 12, 2001, but for obvious reasons did not reach the congressional floor. Failing to pass the DREAM Act, and the focus on the “War on Terror” by the Bush administration, resulted in continued anxiety among undocumented migrants in the US, returning them to a liminal status. In these shadows, they have existed for centuries. The historical context of these laws can be read through modern American politics, but it also reflects the last 150 years of immigration to the United States.

In Pedagogy of the Oppressed, Paulo Freire analyzes the openings authoritarian systems exploit to seize power. Similarly, recurrent anti-immigration strains in American history have provided openings for authoritarian impulses across the 19th-21st centuries. Nativists, “Know Nothings,” Immigration restriction leagues, eugenicists, and today, Christian nationalists and replacement theorists decry the presence of immigrants as corroding the “true” American body politic, culture, and society (Erika Lee, America for Americans). The experience of DACA residents in the USA resonates with Freire’s analysis of conscientização and the possibility of a descent into inaction, fanaticism, or critical action (Paulo Freire, Pedagogy of the Oppressed). DACA residents have come to understand themselves as part of an innumerable population of undocumented residents in the US. They realized they could not apply for a university, work permits, or passports. But DACA residents do not simply view themselves as trapped in a hegemonic state system where workers and minorities are relegated to the lower rungs of society by a ruling elite that conspires to consolidate political and economic power and achieve supremacy over the passive, ignorant masses. Instead, they are aware they live as almost stateless actors, and now demand recognition and resolution of their status from politicians, employers, educators, and civil society at large. They do not need to “admit their fear of freedom openly” as Freire writes, because they have lived in a liminal space since their arrival as infants (Paulo Freire, Pedagogy of the Oppressed). DACA students are aware and active agents in liberating themselves from the shadows of statelessness.

Placed in the context of the history of the immigrant experience in the Americas, DACA represents the latest manifestation of xenophobic policies that have, from the very inception of the American republic, been consistently inhumane, unjust, and systematic. In the 20th century, during the Mexican Revolution, some estimates show almost 1 million Mexicans moving to the US to escape the horrific violence that shattered that nation. The Mexican diaspora to the United States was targeted in the 1930’s at the height of the Great Depression. In the 1930’s, that great lion of American liberalism, Franklin Roosevelt, oversaw the repatriation of over 1.5 million “Mexicans,” 60% of whom were US citizens. The administration quickly reversed course during World War 2, when demand for cheap labor led to the establishment of the Bracero program. Fast forward to the 1990s, Bill Clinton signed the 1994 IRCA Act, largely in concert with the resurgence of nativist policies across the country, epitomized by the failed Proposition 187 in California. At the end of the 20th century, American politicians attempted to work (amid the blood sport that was becoming American politics, led by the Newt Gingrich Contract with America) to “solve” the “migrant” problem (Levitsky, Ziblatt. How Democracies Die). Those debates culminated in the DREAM Act of 2001. It never passed.

Every nation forges and reinforces its identity through specific historical memories and narratives. The fragments used to entrench those narratives are chosen specifically to reinforce the “exceptionalism” of each particular modern nation. The US’ historical narrative has been particularly adept at marginalizing competing narratives to reinforce the “exceptional” character of its birth and development from a colony to the last remaining superpower. The assumption that “objective” history explains national origins and a progressive destiny is naive. Democracy’s shallow roots are under increasing threat from the aggressive xenophobic racism seemingly enveloping the “liberal” West. Yet the experience of DACA students at places like Delaware State University, an historically Black College and University (HBCU), can, in some way, alleviate the apocalyptic anxieties we have about authoritarianism’s triumph over democratic systems. DSU is the ideal institution to welcome these “Dreamers” because of its historical role in providing opportunities for Freedmen and their descendants.

The DACA question links multiple elements of the American historical narrative. DACA residents expose persistent questions in the USA of what constitutes statehood/citizenship. Theodore Roosevelt’s notion of “True Americanism,” emerged during the Progressive Era, continues to ask, “Who is fit to be an American? What people are ‘fit’ to be part of this liberal republic? Until only recently, those questions have been intentionally ignored. Slavery, segregation, white supremacy, genocide, and misogyny rarely appear in textbooks or lectures in American public schools. Perhaps briefly, slavery is addressed in a US history class as an episode that has long since been remedied. American imperialism also rarely enters the public discourse on American exceptionalism. Cubans, Puerto Ricans, and Filipinos are forgotten but usually erased when considering the idea of American identity. Southeastern Europeans and immigrants from the Global South did not fit the vision of citizenship formulated from the racist 19th-century ideas of William Graham Sumner, Cecil Rhodes, the seemingly progressive Franklin Roosevelt, or Donald Trump. Nor do the millions of migrants from Monterrey, Nuevo Leon, Oaxaca and Chiapas.

DACA enrollees represent over 120 countries and territories and reflect the multi-ethnic/national composition of the United States. According to the United States Citizenship and Immigration Service (USCIS, formerly INS), of the approximately 1.2 million DACA recipients, about 88% are natives of Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador. The reprieve DACA provides them in no way masks the utter violation of the human right of free movement that these young people suffer under. Their choices, stark and entirely unjust, include returning to a native country where they often know no one, or staying in the United States in the limbo that is DACA, receding into shadow. Yet another way exists, forged by DACA students (among others), one that demands justice, recognition, and liberty.

That this is a matter of human rights, is beyond question. The UN Declaration of Human Rights articulates the fundamental ideas that govern people’s movement. Written after WW2, in light of the death of over 70 million humans, many of whom were murdered because of their ethnicity, religion, and immigration status. In articles 13-15, the declaration articulates the right of free movement, freedom from persecution, and protection from arbitrary revocation of citizenship.

Xenophobia and scapegoating immigrants for perceived (real or not) political, social, and economic ills are well documented. Historically, immigrants in the US have been persecuted based on race, ethnicity, religious, and political beliefs. Less discussed are the repatriations of Mexican Americans between 1930-32, where under the FDR administration over one to two million Mexicans (60% US citizens) were “deported” to Mexico because they were considered central causes of the Depression (Francisco Balderrama and Raymond Rodríguez. Decade of Betrayal). America’s historical narrative avoids this discussion. DACA demonstrates clear continuities with this historical trend of American xenophobia. Many residents have matriculated from American public schools, where they were imbued with the Horatio Alger myth: that through self-determination and will, they could achieve anything. Unfortunately, they were unaware that the American immigration system and political structure would deny them this DREAM. It seems as if the lessons of history continue to be dulled by the cacophonous confusion of policymakers, where the choices Dreamers face are life in the shadows or deportation. Statehood seems the least likely of outcomes.

text:
SAN JOSE, Calif. (CN) — A group of diversity visa applicants asked a federal judge during a hearing Tuesday to extend the government’s deadline for processing applications.

Senior U.S. District Judge Edward Davila previously issued a preliminary injunction to temporarily force the State Department to restart processing the applications after the applicants challenged two government policies that had placed indefinite holds on green card applications and adjustment of diversity visa status. He also granted in part class certification of subclasses for individuals whose diversity visas were on hold.

But on Tuesday, Davila wondered how he could order the government to continue processing diversity visas after Sept. 30, the end of the fiscal year, and also generally the end of the government’s obligation to process diversity visas for 2026 under the Immigration and Nationality Act.

“Tell me the legal basis to extend the relief you are asking for,” he told plaintiffs’ attorney Curtis Morrison.

Morrison asked Davila for emergency supplemental relief for thousands of diversity visa applicants, and for U.S. consulates around the world to continue to adjudicate and issue up to 40,000 unused diversity visas. He argued Davila could find the government in contempt of court for not complying with his preliminary injunction.

“There has not been resumption of ordinary visa adjudications,” Morrison said. “It’s a Catch-22, if they are not invited to an interview they can’t attend an interview, so that is very frustrating for the plaintiffs.”

Morrison noted that while many of his thousands of plaintiffs have received relief, either in the form of rescheduled interviews, visa adjudications or issued visas, class members who had their visas on indefinite hold, or had their interviews canceled, had yet to see relief.

“The audacity of defendants to not schedule new interviews at all,” said Morrison to the court. “And I thought what is causing that? The defendants have interpreted the court’s order as applications to those who already had interviews scheduled.”

Davila said he was disappointed the government failed to follow the court’s order diligently, saying it frustrated the process by delaying adjudications due to retraining and sending cables to consulates about the new directives several days after the court’s order.

The judge said he felt giving the government a quota to fulfill would expand the court’s order beyond his legal authority to do so. But he asked if extending the diversity visa application processing period for the next 11 days — approximately the amount of time the government delayed restarting processing applications — was a measurable and appropriate action.

Department of Justice attorney Nag Young Chu said that Davila’s suggested remedy was likely against statutory law and that the government “substantially” complied with the court’s order.

“Because this such relief, it’s never been done before, I don’t logistically know how it would happen at the agency,” Chu said.

Furthermore, the attorney said, consulars stop processing new applications before the fiscal deadline and prioritize “security checks to explain certain deficiencies," adding that each consulate allocates its resources differently.

According to Davila, based on status reports supplied by the government three days a week since his Aug. 28 preliminary injunction, 3,814 visas have been processed.

Under the diversity immigrant visa program, the Department of State holds a lottery in which it randomly selects noncitizens from countries with historically low rates of U.S. immigration for the opportunity to apply for a green card. If an applicant is in the U.S. under a different visa at the time of selection, they must a submit form with Immigration Services to adjust their status to permanent resident.

Selection to the program does not guarantee a visa, just the ability to apply for one. Generally, the Department of State selects up to 55,000 immigrants to start the application process for each fiscal year.

In December 2025, the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the State Department issued the two policies that placed indefinite holds on green card applications and adjustment of diversity visa status.

And in February, the State Department issued a notice indefinitely pausing visa approval for 75 countries, requiring consular officers to refuse all immigrant visa applicants until the agency develops new guidance for them to assess if an applicant might become dependent on public assistance once in the U.S.

Davila said he would take the plaintiffs’ motion for supplemental relief under submission but did not indicate if he would publish an order before Sept. 30.

text:
The Supreme Court this week granted a Department of Justice (DOJ) application to stay an order issued by Judge Brian Murphy of the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts (D. Mass.) in D.V.D. v. U.S. DHS, which the First Circuit affirmed in large part on September 18. The order blocked “third country” removal policies implemented by ICE under Trump II — and ironically, this was the third time the justices agreed to stay orders in this case. The Court also agreed to review the matter, and while there are major issues in this case, the basic ones are straightforward.

“Recalcitrant Countries”, “Statutory Withholding”, and CAT

Generally, DHS deports aliens under final removal orders to their countries of nationality, citizenship, birth, or residence, but Congress also specifically permits DHS to remove aliens to other, “third” countries, including ones not designated in removal orders.

Aliens are usually only sent to third countries in one of two situations: (1) their countries of removal are “recalcitrant”, meaning they refuse to accept their deported nationals; or (2) the aliens have been granted a limited form of protection, either “statutory withholding” of removal under section 241(b)(3) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) or protection under the Convention Against Torture (CAT).

Only DOJ adjudicators (immigration judges and Board of Immigration Appeals members) can grant aliens statutory withholding or CAT, and to grant those protections, they must first order the alien removed and then issue an order barring DHS from removing the alien to a specified country or countries. Thus, those protection orders do not bar removal to any other country that will accept the alien.

As the regulation governing statutory withholding states: “Nothing in this section ... shall prevent [DHS] from removing an alien to a third country other than the country to which removal has been withheld or deferred.” The CAT regulation goes further, providing DHS can even send beneficiaries of that protection to countries from which removal was withheld or deferred if the State Department (DOS) receives assurances the aliens won’t be tortured there.

Unlike asylum and statutory withholding, CAT isn’t expressly provided for in the INA. While the United States signed the convention in April 1988 and ratified it in October 1994, that U.S. ratification was not “self-executing” and required congressional legislation to make it effective.

That legislation was section 2242 of the Foreign Affairs Reform and Restructuring Act of 1998 (FARRA), which made it U.S. policy “not to expel, extradite, or otherwise effect the involuntary removal of any person to a country where there are substantial grounds for believing that the person would be in danger of being subjected to torture”.

FARRA did not expressly explain how that policy was to be implemented, however, leaving it up to the “appropriate” executive-branch agencies to enact regulations to enforce CAT protections.

Under those regulations, there are two different forms of CAT protection DOJ can grant: “withholding of removal” and “deferral of removal”.

The latter is a more restrictive protection available to applicants for protection who are barred from receiving statutory withholding under section 241(b)(3)(B) of the INA (including because they are persecutors, have been convicted of a particularly serious crime, or pose a danger to the national security of the United States).

DHS’s Authority to Remove Aliens to Third Countries

Section 241(b) of the INA, “Countries to which aliens may be removed”, underscores how complex it is to remove aliens from this country, because Congress therein addresses nearly every removal scenario.

By statute, different “country of removal” rules apply depending on whether the alien was stopped while “arriving at the United States” — in which case the primary country of removal is the place where the alien boarded the plane or vessel that brought him to the United States, except if it is contiguous unless the alien is a native, national, citizen, or resident of that contiguous place — and every other case, when the alien can designate a country of removal.

Those “other aliens” can only designate contiguous places if they are natives, nationals, residents, etc., and DHS can disregard an alien’s designation if the alien fails to designate a country “promptly” (most asylum, statutory withholding, and CAT applicants don’t make a designation), or if the country won’t take the alien, or if DHS determines sending the alien to that country “is prejudicial to the United States”.

Regardless, the INA expressly permits DHS to remove an alien to a third country if that country will take the alien and removal to a specified or designated country is “impracticable, inadvisable, or impossible”.

As DOJ notes in its latest application to the Supreme Court: “Congress did not set forth any procedural requirements for third country removals. Instead, Congress entrusted the Executive Branch with ensuring that no alien will be removed to a country in which the alien will be tortured.”

The EO and the March 2025 Policy

On his first day back in office, January 20, 2025, President Trump issued Executive Order (EO) 14159, “Protecting the American People Against Invasion”, in which he directed DHS to take “all appropriate action” to deport removable aliens from the United States.

The next month, on February 18, ICE issued guidance directing its officers to review cases involving aliens who had been granted CAT withholding and deferral “to determine the viability of removal to a third country and accordingly whether the alien should be re-detained”.

Thereafter, on March 30, 2025, then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem issued more formal “Guidance Regarding Third Country Removals”, which requires immigration officers attempting to remove an alien to a third country to first determine whether the Department of State (DOS) has received assurances that the alien will not be persecuted or tortured there.

“If the United States has received such assurances, and if [DOS] believes those assurances to be credible, the alien may be removed without the need for further procedures.”

If no such assurances have been issued, or DOS doesn’t think the assurances are credible, DHS must then tell those aliens they are being removed to a third country and refer them to USCIS asylum officers, “generally” within 24 hours, for a fear screening if they assert a fear of persecution or harm.

If USCIS concludes “the alien would more likely than not be persecuted on a statutorily protected ground or tortured in the country of removal”, asylum officers must send their cases to immigration court for review if they haven’t been in removal proceedings, generally because they were subject to expedited removal.

If they were ordered removed following removal proceedings, ICE will either file a motion to reopen with the immigration court or designate another country of removal.

Enter Judge Murphy

On March 23, 2025, a group of aliens and “proposed class members” with final removal orders filed a “class action complaint” with the D. Mass. challenging first the February ICE guidance. The matter was referred to Judge Murphy, and five days later — two days before the Noem guidance — he issued a temporary restraining order (TRO), followed by a preliminary injunction on April 18, 2025.

That preliminary injunction required DHS to: give written notice to any alien under a final order facing removal to a third country; provide those aliens an opportunity to raise a claim they would be tortured in that third country; move to reopen an alien’s immigration court case if the alien had shown a “reasonable fear” of harm in that third country; and give those aliens 15 days prior to removal to move to reopen their cases if DHS didn’t find they had a reasonable fear.

In addition, Judge Murphy certified a class of aliens facing removal to third countries who could take advantage of the foregoing requirements, in possible contravention of language in section 242(f) of the INA that suggests only the Supreme Court can issue injunctive relief.

The First Circuit and the Supreme Court Got Involved — And Things Got Messy

On April 22, 2025, DOJ sought a stay pending appeal of Judge Murphy’s order from the First Circuit, and while the First Circuit denied an emergency stay on May 16, 2025, it also set the government’s appeal for briefing, which logically divested Judge Murphy of authority to issue any further orders in the matter.

That denial prompted the department, on May 27, 2025, to file an application for a stay of Judge Murphy’s injunction with the Supreme Court, which a majority of the justices granted “pending the disposition of” DOJ’s appeal in First Circuit in an order issued on June 23, 2025.

Keep the timing in mind as I explain that on May 21, 2025, Judge Murphy issued an “Order on Remedy for Violation of Preliminary Injunction”, along with a memorandum holding DHS had failed to provide “six non-citizen class members” a “meaningful opportunity” to make CAT claims before the department attempted to send them to South Sudan, finding they had only been given a 24-hour heads-up.

Specifically, Judge Murphy therein required DHS to give such aliens at least 10 days’ notification before a third-country removal to make a CAT claim, essentially modifying his April 18 order.

When the Supreme Court issued its order staying the April 18 injunction, those six were being held at a U.S. military base in Djibouti (on the Horn of Africa), and shortly after the justices acted, their counsel filed an “emergency motion” with Judge Murphy to enforce the May 21 order and prevent their transfer to South Sudan, or alternatively for the court to issue individual temporary restraining orders in their cases.

Apparently without waiting for DOJ to respond, Judge Murphy issued an electronic docket order finding his May 21 order “remains in full force and effect, notwithstanding today's stay of” his April preliminary injunction by the Supreme Court — and citing to Justice Sotomayor’s dissent from the June 23 Supreme Court order.

The next day, DOJ returned to the Supreme Court with a motion asking the justices to make clear their order applied to all the injunctive orders Judge Murphy has issued, including the May 21 order and memorandum.

On July 3, 2025, a majority of the justices granted that motion, clarifying for the parties and the lower courts that the “June 23 order stayed the April 18 preliminary injunction in full” and that the May 21 “remedial order” couldn’t “be used to enforce an injunction” the Court’s “stay rendered unenforceable”.

Even Justice Kagan — who had dissented from the June 23 stay — wrote to state that she did “not see how a district court can compel compliance with an order that this Court has stayed”, concurring in the majority’s “clarification” of its earlier order.

Onward — and Now Upward

That sent the case back down, and on February 25, Judge Murphy issued a final judgment ruling that DHS’s March 30, 2025, guidance and its subsequent July 9, 2025, guidance on “Third Country Removals Following the Supreme Court’s Order in Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D.” (which directed adherence to the March 30 guidance) were unlawful.

As the D. Mass. stated in its conclusion:

The Court DECLARES that class members have the right to meaningful notice before removal to any third country.

The Court DECLARES that class members have the right to a meaningful opportunity to raise a country-specific claim against removal before removal to any third country.

Simply put, Judge Murphy concluded that the two DHS policies didn’t comply with those rights.

That sent the matter back to the First Circuit, which on September 18 affirmed Judge Murphy’s latest order to the extent that it, inter alia, concluded it had jurisdiction to consider the aliens’ claims, entered class-wide relief, and held that the statutory withholding provision, section 241(b)(3) of the INA, and FARRA require DHS to give aliens notice and an opportunity to raise statutory withholding and CAT claims prior to a third-country removal.

Then on September 23, the circuit court dissolved its stay of Judge Murphy’s order that it had issued pending appeal, sending the department back to the Supreme Court the next day seeking a stay of that order and an “immediate administrative stay”.

As one legal expert has explained, “administrative” or “temporary” stays are “a little examined device that federal courts employ to freeze legal proceedings until they are able to rule on a party’s request for a stay pending appeal”. In other words, an administrative stay doesn’t resolve issues so much as it puts them on ice while they can be resolved.

At the heart of DOJ’s request for an administrative stay was its claim that:

The unexpected springing-back of [the] district court’s order has ... created substantial logistical problems with ongoing removal operations — including the cancellation of flights — and led to added expense, potential diplomatic issues, and the inability to remove dangerous criminals. For example, DHS informs us that it has already canceled a flight to three separate countries carrying 70 aliens with criminal convictions (including aggravated assault and serious drug offenses), and that the cancellation has required a new round of diplomatic engagement with each of the three countries. Those disruptions will only get worse.

More broadly, DOJ contends that under DHS’s third-country removal policy, prompt deportations only occur when the country “has credibly assured the Secretary of State that it will not persecute or torture anyone”, but that “absent such assurances, the alien will be given notice of his removal to that country and an opportunity to raise any fears of potential persecution or torture there”.

On September 29, the Supreme Court granted the stay, treated the application as a petition for writ of certiorari, and agreed to consider the government’s appeal, including on the question of whether the DHS third-country removal guidance is unlawful under the Constitution, the INA, or FARRA and its implementing regulations.

Key Questions

One practitioner explained that the circuit-court opinion “did not say what process a fear claim receives once raised. It called the evidentiary-hearing question neither ripe nor fully joined and left it to the district court. It did not reach the Constitution.”

That said, and while there are other issues in the case (including the major question of “whether the district court had authority to enter classwide declaratory relief”) as a practical matter, there aren’t that many major disputes surrounding third-country removals per se. Specifically, DOJ explains in its latest application that:

Everyone agrees that DHS may remove such an alien to a country not listed in the order (i.e., a “third country”) if that country is willing to accept the alien and certain other conditions are met. Everyone likewise agrees that the alien may not be removed to a country where he will be persecuted or tortured.

If the U.S. government has assurances no alien will be persecuted or tortured in a third country, does any alien have a right to contend he would be? And if an alien has no ties to a third country, how valid is a claim he’d be harmed there and how should it be assessed? The justices will soon mull those questions, albeit indirectly, in a case they’re already very familiar with.

text:
Only six of Indiana’s 92 county sheriffs have signed agreements to work with federal law enforcement on immigration cases. Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita says he hopes others follow his lead to change that.

Rokita’s office announced on Wednesday a partnership with U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, to improve the ability of state investigators to work with federal law enforcement.

The agreement with ICE falls under Section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act and aims to help deport illegal immigrants.

Such efforts are supported by the FAIRNESS Act, which Gov. Mike Braun signed into law in June.

The new law aims to hold employers of illegal immigrants accountable and discourage municipalities from being sanctuaries, according to a June statement from the governor’s office.

“Every county sheriff across the state should be — and can be — doing what we’re doing. And what sheriffs across the nation are doing,” Rokita said in a statement, adding that working with federal law enforcement is “a key part of how we deport illegal aliens under the FAIRNESS Act.”

Rokita said the agreements can open up opportunities to obtain federal funding to help with public safety.

Rokita’s office has aggressively pushed partnerships with ICE. It has sued sheriffs in St. Joseph and Monroe counties and Indianapolis Public Schools over cooperation levels.

title: New Civil Rights Monitor Poll from The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights ...
description:
Now in its fifth year, the Civil Rights Monitor shows a record of American values and attitudes on human rights.
Despite Fears on Race Relations, Core Civil Rights Values Remain Broadly Shared: 92% of voters say America’s diversity makes it stronger.
Black voters have seen this playbook before, which helps explain why they are both the most alarmed group in the electorate and are highly motivated to vote.
Disapproval of the Supreme Court Has Grown Every Year Since 2023: Disapproval of the Court now reaches 57% among all voters and 83% among Black voters, with 39% of all voters strongly disapproving.
A question long treated as a measure of white resentment now captures Black voters’ sense that their culture is under threat.
text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

September 30, 2026

Contact: press@civilrights.org

National poll also finds 71% oppose cutting Medicare and SNAP to fund ICE, 92% say America’s diversity makes it stronger, and a majority supports a Third Reconstruction

WASHINGTON — Voters are heading into the 2026 midterm elections with deep anxieties about their rights and the health of American democracy, according to a new national poll commissioned by The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights and conducted by polling firm Brilliant Corners Research. Now in its fifth year, the Civil Rights Monitor shows a record of American values and attitudes on human rights. This is a national survey of 1,000 likely voters, conducted by phone using professional interviewers from August 23 to September 6, 2026.

Key Findings

Voters Fear Interference in the 2026 Elections: 77% are concerned about political leaders pressuring election officials to change outcomes, 65% about the federal government trying to stop the elections by declaring a state of emergency, and 62% about ICE showing up at polling places to intimidate or interfere with voters.

Anxiety About Rights and Democracy Reached Poll Series Highs: 82% of voters are concerned that rights are being rolled back and 76% are convinced that democracy is under major threat, the largest year-over-year increases in the Civil Rights Monitor.

Voters Overwhelmingly Reject Cutting Social Programs to Fund ICE: 71% oppose taking money from programs like Medicare and SNAP to cover the agency’s budget increase from $10 billion to $85 billion, including 61% who strongly oppose.

A Majority Says Race Relations are Getting Worse: 53% of voters believe race relations in America are getting worse, a view that has reached a series high among Black voters, while only 14% believe they are getting better.

Black Voters are the Most Alarmed and the Most Motivated Group in the Electorate: They register a series high on the view that race relations are getting worse, 83% of them disapprove of the Supreme Court, and 83% are very concerned about their rights being taken away.

Despite Fears on Race Relations, Core Civil Rights Values Remain Broadly Shared: 92% of voters say America’s diversity makes it stronger.

Maya Wiley, president and CEO of The Leadership Conference, said: “What worries voters most right now ought to worry all of us, because they are describing threats to the machinery of democracy itself. Majorities of Americans fear political leaders pressuring election officials to change outcomes, a federal government willing to declare a state of emergency to stop the elections, and ICE showing up at polling places to intimidate voters. More than eight in 10 are worried that our rights and freedoms are being stripped away in this country. Black voters have seen this playbook before, which helps explain why they are both the most alarmed group in the electorate and are highly motivated to vote. The civil rights community will match that resolve, and we will spend this fall protecting every voter and every freedom under attack.”

The Issues

Immigration Enforcement Declined as a Priority: Border security dropped to 14% from 20% and deportations to 9% from 10%, a combined slide from 30% to 23% over the past year.

Voting Rights is a Top Issue in its First Year on the List: Protecting voting rights was chosen by 14% of voters, matching border security and outpacing abortion rights (10%) and fighting racial discrimination (9%).

ICE and Immigration Enforcement

A Majority of Voters Disapprove of ICE: 38% approve of the agency’s performance against 58% who disapprove, and opponents feel it more strongly, with 48% strongly disapproving compared with 25% who strongly approve.

Voters See ICE Violating Due Process and Rights: Half of voters strongly agree (rating their agreement 8 or higher on a scale of zero to 10) that ICE is violating due process and undermining people’s rights and the law, while 44% agree at that level that the growth and use of the agency is designed to intimidate people of color.

Critiques of ICE Differ by Community: Black voters agree most intensely that ICE is a political tool meant to reduce the number of Black and Brown people in the country (74%, compared with 40% among all voters).

71% Oppose Cutting Medicare and SNAP to Fund ICE: Voters oppose funding the agency’s growth from $10 billion to $85 billion out of social programs, with 61% strongly opposed.

Democracy and the 2026 Elections

Voter Motivation Remains High for a Midterm: 84% of voters say they will definitely vote in November, with a mean motivation score of 8.7 on a scale of zero to 10. 69% are dissatisfied with the direction of the country.

Voters Fear Efforts to Change Election Outcomes: 80% worry about foreign governments interfering with our elections, and 77% about political leaders pressuring election officials to change outcomes, with 55% very concerned about that pressure.

Majorities Fear Federal Interference at the Polls: 65% are concerned about the federal government trying to stop the elections by declaring a state of emergency, and 62% about ICE showing up at polling places to intimidate or interfere with voters.

A Majority of Voters Want Calmer Politics: 56% of voters say they would like to see our politics return to something calmer and less divided, compared with 36% who want leaders to keep up the pace of change while ensuring it helps families like theirs.

Race, Rights, and Discrimination

A Majority Says Race Relations are Getting Worse: 53% of voters believe race relations in America are getting worse, a view that has reached a series high among Black voters, while only 14% believe they are getting better.

Worry About White Supremacy has Risen Every Year Since 2023: Concern about the rise of white supremacy now stands at 57% overall, with 39% of voters very worried.

Disapproval of the Supreme Court Has Grown Every Year Since 2023: Disapproval of the Court now reaches 57% among all voters and 83% among Black voters, with 39% of all voters strongly disapproving.

Fewer Voters See Reverse Discrimination as a Big Problem: Agreement that reverse discrimination against white people is a big problem has fallen to 37%, with the decline concentrated among white voters, and only 32% agree that forced diversity and inclusion amounts to racism against white people.

Black Voters are Now Most Likely to Say Their Heritage is Under Attack: Agreement that “your heritage, traditions, and cultural identity is under attack in America” stands at 52% overall and is increasingly driven by Black voters, whose agreement has ranged from 71% to 83% in every poll since 2023 and stands at 81% today, while agreement among white voters has fallen from 54% in 2022 to 45%. A question long treated as a measure of white resentment now captures Black voters’ sense that their culture is under threat.

The Economy and Technology

71% Say the American Dream is Increasingly Out of Reach: Stagnant wages and rising costs drive that view, and 67% say the same about the concentration of power and wealth in the hands of a few.

Large Majorities Back a Higher Minimum Wage and Universal Healthcare: 74% want the minimum wage raised to match the cost of living and 71% support universal healthcare coverage, while narrower majorities back a universal basic income (53%) and a $25 minimum wage (51%).

83% Say Americans are Sacrificing Too Much Privacy to Big Tech: Voters say too much privacy is being given up for the convenience and profit of big tech, and they also view artificial intelligence as a threat to jobs (66%) and to democracy and elections (66%).

Half of Voters Want Data Center Construction Paused: 50% say construction should be paused or even banned until better regulations are in place, another 33% want companies to pay their utility and infrastructure costs in full and invest in community programs, and only 11% have no problems with it.

A Third Reconstruction

Voters Support a Third Reconstruction: Voters back the idea of a systemic, constitutional, and cultural overhaul to secure a robust multiracial democracy by 54% to 36%, including 32% who strongly support it. The concept would ensure voting rights, institute term limits for Supreme Court justices, and reduce income inequality through public programs.

Every Racial and Partisan Group Rated Voting Rights as the Top Priority: Protecting the freedom to vote earned the highest importance ratings of any civil rights work tested, rated 8 or higher out of 10 by 57% of white voters, 81% of Black voters, 88% of Hispanic voters, and 84% of Asian American voters.

Methodology

This is a national survey of 1,000 likely voters with an oversample of 100 Asian American likely voters, conducted by phone using professional interviewers from August 23 to September 6, 2026. The sample was drawn randomly from the voter file, geographically stratified for proportional representation, and weighted to the population demographics of voters in the file. The overall margin of error is +/- 3.1% at a 95% confidence interval, and margins for sub-groups are higher depending on sample size.

The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights is a coalition charged by its diverse membership of more than 240 national organizations to promote and protect the rights of all persons in the United States. The Leadership Conference works toward an America as good as its ideals. For more information on The Leadership Conference and its member organizations, visit www.civilrights.org.

In another win for the administration, the Supreme Court subsequently lifted limits the judge had imposed to protect a group of men from being sent to South Sudan.

text:
The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday let President Donald Trump's administration resume deporting migrants to countries other than their own without offering them the chance to show the ‌harms they may face, bolstering a tool his administration has used for rapid expulsions as part of his immigration crackdown.

The court granted the Justice Department's emergency request to put on hold Boston-based U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy's ruling that the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) policy to remove migrants to so-called third countries is unlawful. The court also agreed to hear arguments in the dispute in December, with a formal ruling on policy to follow.

The court has a 6-3 conservative majority. Its three ​liberal justices dissented from the decision to let the deportations immediately resume pending the final outcome of ​the litigation.

Murphy's ruling came in a class-action lawsuit filed by immigrant rights groups on behalf of migrants seeking to prevent the U.S. government from sending them to third countries without notice and a chance to assert the harms they could face.

More than 25,000 migrants have been deported to 29 ​countries under the policy implemented last year, according to a tally by human rights groups, with the vast majority going to Mexico.

The policy is ⁠one of a number of measures the ⁠administration has taken in its pursuit of Trump's goal of mass deportation. The Republican president has enforced ‌a sweeping crackdown on immigration — among his top priorities — since returning to office last year.

The administration has carried out third-country deportations to politically unstable South Sudan, which the U.S. State Department urges Americans to avoid due to the risks of crime, kidnapping and armed conflict, as well as Uganda, Equatorial Guinea, Liberia, the Central African Republic and other nations.

The Supreme Court previously sided with the administration in the legal challenge, suspending a preliminary order that Murphy issued earlier in the case halting the ⁠removals. In another win for the administration, the Supreme Court subsequently lifted limits the judge had imposed to protect a group of men from being sent to South Sudan.

The case began in 2025 after the DHS moved to step up deportations of migrants who cannot be returned to any country listed on their deportation orders.

Migrants with legal protection being sent home

The policy provided that migrants could be ‌swiftly removed without notice to third countries that have provided credible diplomatic assurance that they will not persecute or torture the individuals. For countries that have not provided such assurance, deportees would be notified of their destination and U.S. authorities would assess the likelihood of persecution or torture only if the individual raises such fear on their own.

In February, Murphy ruled that the policy violates immigration law procedures and due process protections under the U.S. Constitution's Fifth Amendment. Due process generally requires the government to provide ​notice and an opportunity for a hearing before taking certain adverse actions.

In its emergency filing to the Supreme Court, the Justice Department said third-country deportations are "an essential tool to remove certain aliens, including some of the worst criminal aliens."

But both Murphy and critics ⁠of the administration said the policy is also targeting migrants who had been granted legal protection from being sent back to their home countries.

The policy has resulted in deportees being ⁠unlawfully transferred by third countries back to their home countries from which the U.S. had already granted them protection, while others have been beaten, sexually assaulted, detained or have disappeared, ⁠the plaintiffs said ⁠in a court filing.

The administration is ignoring "the significant harm resulting from ​deporting thousands of longtime U.S. residents, many with no criminal history, to third countries without regard to the persecution or torture they face there," the plaintiffs said.

The case has been hotly contested since it began, and included findings by Murphy that the administration "repeatedly violated, or attempted to violate" his orders. Murphy in 2025 found that the administration had violated another order he issued requiring additional steps before attempting to send a group of migrants to South Sudan.

More than a dozen United Nations human rights experts have written to the U.S. government urging a halt to policies that they said on Monday were putting migrants at heightened risk of abuse, including torture and persecution, by deporting them to third countries.

"At gravest risk are children, women, persons with disabilities, victims of trafficking, ⁠LGBT persons, human rights defenders, stateless persons and other people ‌in extremely vulnerable situations," they said, without documenting individual cases.

name: Policy
title: U.S. poised to boot legal immigrants from Medicaid, including refugees and sex-trafficking victims
authors: Phil Galewitz, Andrew Jones, and Claudia Boyd-Barrett — KFF Health News, Phil Galewitz, Andrew Jones, Allison DeAngelis, Adam Feuerstein, Elaine Chen, Tara Bannow, Meghana Keshavan
description:
More than 281,000 immigrants from nine states and the District of Columbia are expected to lose Medicaid in October.
New Jersey expects 15,000 to 25,000 of its noncitizen residents to lose their Medicaid coverage.
Without health coverage, immigrants are likely to lose access to doctors, prescription drugs, and most other medical services.
Cutting off Medicaid coverage is just the first move to drop government health benefits provided to many lawfully present immigrants.
California expects about 148,000 immigrants to lose Medicaid coverage.
text:
Many lawfully present immigrants will be among the first people to lose Medicaid coverage under congressional Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which is expected to cut spending by more than $900 billion through 2034 for the state-federal health program for people with low incomes or disabilities. The law will strip many more immigrants of their Affordable Care Act plan subsidies and Medicare coverage next year.

Those losing their health benefits who were previously eligible include refugees of war, asylees who fled persecution, victims of sex trafficking, and interpreters who risked their lives assisting U.S. service members in Afghanistan — all of whom are in the country with the federal government’s permission. The law does not affect coverage for a few groups, including those who hold green cards.

The Congressional Budget Office, the nonpartisan budget scorekeeper, estimated the law’s changes eliminating Medicaid eligibility for many noncitizen adults with legal status would lead to about 100,000 more immigrants being uninsured by 2034.

KFF Health News asked several states how many Medicaid enrollees they had identified as being at risk of losing coverage under the provision. More than 281,000 immigrants from nine states and the District of Columbia are expected to lose Medicaid in October.

While some may be able to obtain coverage elsewhere, the state numbers suggest hundreds of thousands of immigrants nationally are at imminent risk of becoming uninsured.

The CBO declined to comment.

Florida alone identified nearly 177,000 immigrants who would no longer qualify for the state’s Medicaid program starting in October, said Anna Holaday, a spokesperson for the Florida Department of Children and Families. The agency verified the enrollees’ immigration status through government databases and sent notices to people to give them an opportunity to provide more information proving they remain eligible, Holaday said.

Arizona predicts nearly 28,000 could lose eligibility. New Jersey expects 15,000 to 25,000 of its noncitizen residents to lose their Medicaid coverage. In North Carolina, it’s about 29,000, and in Washington state it’s 11,000. Final numbers from states on how many Medicaid enrollees have been terminated from the program won’t be available until later this fall.

Lawmakers rely on the CBO to understand the budgetary and economic impacts of proposed legislation. Yet the federal agency did not publish estimates on the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s impact on noncitizens enrolled in Medicaid until a month after Congress passed the bill and Trump signed it into law.

Much of the attention around Medicaid changes in the law has centered on implementation of work requirements as a new condition of eligibility for many enrollees starting in January. The CBO estimates the requirements will increase the number of uninsured Americans by about 5 million by 2034.

Without health coverage, immigrants are likely to lose access to doctors, prescription drugs, and most other medical services. They still could qualify for coverage of emergency care under a separate program known as Emergency Medicaid.

“I came here to live a better life,” said Ahin, a refugee who left war-torn Syria for Turkey in 2011 and came to the U.S. in October 2024. She spoke with KFF Health News on the condition that she be identified by only her first name, out of concern for her privacy and security.

Soon after arriving in the U.S., she developed severe abdominal pain that required intestinal surgery. Those costs, along with ongoing visits to specialists, were covered by Medicaid.

“I’m really worried about this,” she said. “It’s truly a terrible situation.”

Ahin, 25, said she doesn’t know what she will do if she needs to go to the hospital — she wouldn’t be able to pay the bill. She lives in a small apartment in New Jersey with her mother. Medicaid has also been vital to her mother, who has asthma.

Health benefits wane for immigrants

The federal government required states to notify immigrants who will soon lose coverage, but immigrant rights advocates say some states did not begin sending letters until September. That’s given enrollees little time to react, including to respond if the state was mistakenly ending their coverage.

Cutting off Medicaid coverage is just the first move to drop government health benefits provided to many lawfully present immigrants. Under a change starting in January, the CBO estimates, about 1 million will lose eligibility for government subsidies to buy individual health coverage on Affordable Care Act marketplaces by 2034. And they will also lose access to Medicare, a change expected to affect about 100,000 immigrants, the agency forecasts.

Trump has argued that taxpayer-funded programs should be reserved for American citizens. As Congress debated the legislation in May 2025, the White House put out a news release with the misleading claim that the One Big Beautiful Bill Act would remove Medicaid coverage for people who are in the country without authorization.

Under long-standing law, people who are in the country without authorization do not qualify for the general Medicaid program that is funded by state and federal dollars.

The health coverage cuts are part of a broader Trump strategy to send a message that immigrants are not welcome in the United States, said Ben D’Avanzo, senior strategist for federal advocacy at the National Immigration Law Center. The Trump administration has also moved to kick people with legal status off the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, and tried to do the same with the children’s program Head Start until a federal judge intervened.

In addition to green card holders, people under age 19 and immigrants from Cuba, Haiti, or certain Pacific Island countries will not see their Medicaid coverage affected by the law.

A few states try to fill in the gaps

Some states are staving off the coverage loss using their own money. California expects about 148,000 immigrants to lose Medicaid coverage. But the state is spending $365 million for a separate program to keep them covered until July 2027, according to Tony Cava, a spokesperson for the California Department of Health Care Services.

New York and Pennsylvania also have state-funded health coverage for many of the immigrants who are affected.

Carlos Alarcón, health and public benefits policy manager with the California Immigrant Policy Center, an advocacy group, said taking away health coverage for immigrants will affect the health of the state as a whole. The fewer people who have access to healthcare, the easier it will be for contagious diseases to spread, as happened during the covid pandemic, he said.

Alarcón said he hopes the state-funded coverage will be extended under California’s next governor. Polling released in September showed Democrat Xavier Becerra, secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services under President Joe Biden, leading Republican Steve Hilton in the gubernatorial race. Becerra has vowed to issue an executive order to maintain health coverage for every Californian affected by federal cuts.

“I believe there’s folks in the legislature that will really want to fight to make sure that we restore things as much as we can,” Alarcón said.

Refugee assistance groups say they have been trying to educate people in their communities and direct them to health clinics that are government-funded or free.

“We’ve just been scrambling trying to find free medical care,” said Julianna Larsen, co-founder of the Arizona Refugee Center. “To not be a welcoming place is the most un-American thing I’ve ever experienced.”

Andrea Mendez Perez, director at Interfaith-RISE, a refugee resettlement organization in southern New Jersey, said the Trump administration has elongated the process for people to get green cards and is now taking away coverage from those without them. Before 2025, it typically took about six months to qualify for a green card, documentation that allows a foreign national to live and work permanently in the United States, she said. Today, it’s well over a year.

For many of these immigrants on Medicaid, losing their ability to get their prescribed medications “is a life-or-death situation,” Mendez Perez said.

Ahin, the Syrian refugee, applied for permanent residency soon after arriving in the U.S. two years ago. Mendez Perez said she should have her green card by now, which would have spared her from being dropped under the GOP law. “She is stuck in the middle and has no control.”

Colleen McCauley, policy and advocacy director at the Camden Coalition, a nonprofit that helps connect people to healthcare in southern New Jersey, said the loss of coverage is devastating.

“None of them did anything wrong,” McCauley said, “and they are losing coverage.”

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF—an independent source of health policy research, polling, and journalism. Learn more about KFF.

name: Policy
title: Refugee Coloradans work, pay taxes and build communities. Why strip away their healthcare?
authors: Kristy Beachy-Quick, Paula Schriefer, Chase Woodruff, Lindsey Toomer, Stephanie Rivera
description:
In July 2025, H.R.1 — the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” — revoked federal Medicaid eligibility for refugees and other categories of lawfully present immigrants.
For decades, the U.S. was a global leader in refugee resettlement.
CWS and other resettlement agencies help refugee Coloradans who are managing diabetes, heart disease and acute conditions requiring surgery and follow-up care.
Those contributions are measurable: Refugee Coloradans paid $127.1 million in state and local taxes and $233.3 million in federal taxes in 2023.
Maintaining healthcare access supports the wellbeing, stability and economic self-sufficiency of refugee families — and the communities we all call home.
text:
Congress has been shamefully complicit. In July 2025, H.R.1 — the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” — revoked federal Medicaid eligibility for refugees and other categories of lawfully present immigrants. The ugly result is that beginning Thursday, approximately 7,000 Coloradans — including refugees, asylees, humanitarian parolees, and trafficking survivors — are expected to lose healthcare coverage.

How has it come to this?

For decades, the U.S. was a global leader in refugee resettlement. Americans could take pride in offering some of the world’s most vulnerable displaced people an opportunity to safely start over. Long standing policy gave refugees access to modest benefits to help them succeed in integration, including immediate eligibility for Medicaid.

What changed? The first Trump administration justified deep cuts to refugee admissions partly by arguing the U.S. could help more displaced people through humanitarian assistance closer to home than by resettling them here. Yet it also proposed major foreign assistance cuts, even as the worldwide refugee population grew.

The current administration has gone further, gutting USAID while directing considerable taxpayer resources toward expanded immigration enforcement and sweeping deportations. This includes gratuitously re-vetting refugees already legally admitted to the U.S. and making costly agreements to deport immigrants to third countries with which they have no connection — a practice unacceptable to nearly two-thirds of surveyed Americans.

The contrast is stark: Federal resources are funding expanded enforcement and deportation while healthcare coverage and other humanitarian supports are being eviscerated.

The stakes of losing healthcare coverage are high for refugees and their communities. Some arrive with serious medical conditions requiring ongoing treatment. Many are recovering from trauma. CWS and other resettlement agencies help refugee Coloradans who are managing diabetes, heart disease and acute conditions requiring surgery and follow-up care. Losing Medicaid does not erase those needs. Instead, it will leave conditions untreated and shift greater pressure onto local hospitals, food banks, faith communities and nonprofits.

At the same time, refugees must support their families, and those of working age are expected to find employment and move toward self-sufficiency almost immediately upon resettlement. Medicaid access promotes the ability to enter and remain in the workforce, especially as refugees often face barriers to living-wage jobs with benefits when their education, experience or credentials are interrupted or unrecognized.

Reliable healthcare provides stability as resettlement agencies and organizations like Spring Institute for Intercultural Learning help newcomers develop skills, find jobs and advance careers. As refugees build livelihoods, their work supports their families while contributing substantially to our shared prosperity.

Those contributions are measurable: Refugee Coloradans paid $127.1 million in state and local taxes and $233.3 million in federal taxes in 2023. A U.S. Department of Health and Human Services analysis found that refugees and asylees generated tens of billions of dollars more in tax revenues over 15 years than they cost in government services. In Colorado, researchers estimate refugees generate $1.68 in economic activity for every $1 in assistance.

In short, refugees don’t simply receive public support. They work, pay taxes, care for their families and help fund public systems that we all rely on.

Whatever disagreements exist about U.S. immigration policy, these Medicaid changes starting Oct. 1 affect refugees who are already Coloradans raising families and striving for secure futures.

The urgent question is whether our country will honor the commitments made to them — or bear the ethical and practical consequences of increasing uninsurance, growing uncompensated care and destabilized families.

Congress should restore Medicaid eligibility for refugees and other affected humanitarian populations. Refugees have overcome enormous challenges and contribute tremendously when given the opportunity to start anew. Maintaining healthcare access supports the wellbeing, stability and economic self-sufficiency of refugee families — and the communities we all call home.

text:
June Sanson has lived in Collier County for about two decades, but says a surge in immigration encounters across Southwest Florida has led her to advocate for her neighbors.

Sanson, a legal observer with Rapid Response Alliance for Immigrant Safety and Empowerment, is among those helping migrant families and who has lived in Collier County since 2009, although relatives had already lived in the area since the 1980s.

Rapid Response Alliance for Immigrant Safety and Empowerment is a coalition of human rights leaders, advocates, civil rights attorneys and immigration law experts.

The group plans to protest later this week after federal agents on Sept. 23 wounded a U.S. citizen during a Naples Manor raid. Graphic images shared with the Naples Daily News and The News-Press show an ICE agent pointing a gun toward bystanders.

ICE did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

"When we hear of an ICE encounter, we go to the scene and we watch and record objectively," Sanson said. "We complete a report and submit that to the the RAISE coordinator here in Florida to be reviewed for civil rights violations."

Sanson added that "every one of these encounters seems to be a civil rights violation solely based on the color of people's skin."

"When when you see these encounters happen, it's always a person of color," Sanson reiterated. "It's never a white person. Never a white person that they stop."

Sanson said observers coordinate to make sure at least two bystanders are at every ICE encounter.

"One person can be recording and possibly calling out to the detainee their civil rights, like you have the right to remain silent, you have the right to request an attorney," Sanson explained.

She added that many of them have dash cams and wear vests to identify as legal observers.

Agent under scrutiny confronted legal observers in SW Florida before

Sanson explained that during one of their patrols, she and another legal observer pulled into an Immokalee gas station.

"I had turned around and started walking back toward the gas station where their vehicles were parked," Sanson said.

That is when according to her recollection, the agent she identified as injuring the U.S. citizen Sept. 22 previously pointed his gun at her.

According to Sanson, the agent pointed the gun at her and demanded that she move her vehicle.

Palm Beach Boulevard: The hotspot

Sanson said observers have noticed a pattern, making Palm Beach Boulevard a hotspot for immigration enforcement.

"They're out there every single morning," Sanson said. "It's really hard to miss that one."

Sanson said other areas, such as Immokalee or Bonita Springs, have seen a downward trend.

Detainees frequently moved out-of-state

Sanson said detainees are frequently moved out of state, making it difficult to ensure legal representation.

"It's very difficult for somebody that's in ICE custody to get any representation at all," Sanson said. "It's very difficult because they're moved around so quickly and hidden. And by the time they show up on the government website as being in custody, they're moved to another place."

Sanson said they have worked with Sanctuary of the South and with the Workers Circle, which provide affordable legal representation for detainees.

Sanson said she is aware of at least three U.S. who have been arrested as part of Lee County immigration sweeps, all charged with resisting arrest.

"It's oftentimes a violent detention for an immigrant. They're usually pushed to the ground, which isn't necessary to handcuff them," Sanson said. "Sometimes it's not violent, but it's often violent for the immigrant."

Sanson said "the entire community is traumatized."

"Our community members of color are very afraid," Sanson said. "They're afraid to go to their doctor's appointments. Children are afraid to go to school. They're afraid that they're going to come home to an empty house, and many of them do."

Sanson said community members plan to protest last week's assault on Oct. 2 at 11145 Tamiami Trail East, in Naples.

Since Florida's State Board of Immigration Enforcement began documenting ICE encounters and arrests across the state on Aug. 1, 2025, the Lee County Sheriff's Office is second statewide behind the Florida Highway Patrol when it comes to immigration encounters.

Through Sept. 29, the Lee County Sheriff's Office has logged 3,770 encounters and is third statewide behind the Florida Highway Patrol and the Martin County Sheriff's Office in encounters that lead to arrests on federal immigration charges, with 1,030 documented cases.

The Collier County Sheriff's Office leads the count in arrests on local and state charges and is the only statewide law enforcement agency to reach 1,000 arrests in that category.
